# keelwerk architecture

Date: 2026-11-04 (first version 2026-10-08, consolidated 2026-10-11). Status: specification,
complete: every question of the decision register is decided or, for the mail server, parked;
approved by Jens on 2026-11-04 (the name keelwerk was settled on 2026-10-28). Authors: the core architect and the data, interfaces
and platforms designers; consolidated with the review findings of 2026-10-11 by the synthesis
editor; the versioning and project-layout designs of addendum 3 and Jens's decisions of 2026-10-24
merged by the integration editor on 2026-10-24; the jobs, nodes and autoscaling design, the
design of encrypted personal data (decision 7b) and the pure-handler design (decision 50a, section
7.9) merged by the merge editor on 2026-10-25; brief addendum 5 and Jens's decisions of 2026-10-25
to 2026-10-28 (section 26.1) applied by the editor on 2026-10-28; the outcomes of the two M0 spikes
(section 26.2, register section M) and register section K2 applied on 2026-11-04.

This document is the design contract of the framework. [brief.md](brief.md) is the requirements
source of truth; this document says how those requirements are met and must not drop or
reinterpret any of them. Where it chooses between alternatives, an Architecture Decision Record in
[adr/](adr/) records why, and [roadmap.md](roadmap.md) orders the work into milestones. The
research notes under [research/](research/) are the evidence base.

It is one specification. Sections 1 to 13 define the kernel, the configuration model, actions
(with the pure handlers and the effect interpreter of section 7.9), authorization, execution and the
toolchain; sections 14 to 16 the data layer, events and sync, live
updates, and the transports and CLI; section 17 the shared accounts and authentication modules and
the two proof platforms; sections 18 to 20 versioning, rollouts and feature flags; section 21 nodes,
capacity and autoscaling; sections 22 and 23 the repository and the project layout; sections 24 to
26 the procedure for new requirements, traceability, and the decisions with the questions that
remain open.

Every library named here was checked against the npm registry between 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-28;
the version in parentheses is the one checked, and Appendix A lists them. Type-level claims name
the compiler versions that checked them.

## 1. Principles

1. **Definitions are values; everything else is derived.** An application is a TypeScript value
   built from module values, which are built from entity, action and policy values. Types are
   inferred from those values; schemas, documents, migrations and transports are generated from
   them. There is no second schema language and no decorator metadata.
2. **Selection is a value, and types follow it.** Which modules are part of an application is a
   `const` tuple. Every derived type (entities, actions, context) is computed from that tuple, so
   adding or removing a module changes the types at the same moment it changes the runtime.
   Declaration merging (`declare module`, `declare global`) is never used for anything that
   depends on the selection, because an augmentation applies whenever a file is compiled, not when
   a module is selected (research: module-systems.md, section 3.4).
3. **Hard dependencies are checked; soft influence is dropped silently.** A module `requires`
   what it cannot work without (compile-time and boot-time error when missing) and `contributes`
   to modules it merely enhances (ignored when the target is absent). This is what keeps the
   accounts and authentication modules independently toggleable while they influence each other.
4. **Actions are the only unit of behaviour.** Every read, write and subscription in the system
   is an action with a declared input, output, error set, execution mode and policy. Transports
   (GraphQL, REST, tRPC, CLI, JMAP, ...) are projections of the action registry onto a wire
   format; they never contain behaviour, never evaluate policies and never touch the data layer.
5. **Every action runs under a principal and inside a scope.** There is no unauthenticated,
   unscoped code path. The invoked action is the unit of authorization (section 8.4); reactions,
   timers and schedules run under the module's own service principal, never under the user who
   triggered them, and every escalation to the `system` principal names a reason that is logged.
   Tenant isolation is applied by the kernel and the data layer before any policy runs, so a
   policy mistake cannot cross a tenant boundary.
6. **Composition is order-independent.** Rules from several modules are a set: allow rules are
   OR-ed, deny rules override, the default is deny. Contributions are a set keyed by module id.
   Nothing depends on the position of a module in the tuple except deterministic tie-breaking of
   lifecycle order.
7. **Fail closed.** A missing requirement, a drifted schema, an action whose module is disabled
   for a backend, a load or a draft the module may not perform: each is an error, never a wider
   filter, a narrowed result, a loose type or a silent no-op. What a datastore lacks is not such a
   failure: the framework provides it itself, at a cost it reports, and never widens a filter or
   refuses to run because of the adapter (brief addendum 5, section 14.3.3).
8. **Nothing is deleted; everything is appended.** Live entities are an append-only event chain
   with a materialised current state. Deletion is an archive event that a restore event can
   undo. Erasure of personal data is crypto-shredding, which keeps the chain intact.
9. **The kernel stays small.** New requirements land as modules, adapters, policies or
   configuration. The kernel exposes extension points so that even transports and data adapters
   are modules. A kernel change requires an ADR.
10. **The compiler is the judge.** `tsc`, Biome and the test runner must see the same types the
    editor sees, with no language-service plugin. Module and app values carry named types, so
    declaration emit stays proportional to each package (section 13.11). The generated files in
    the type path, each module's manifest `module.generated.ts` (section 23.5) and the app's
    `keelwerk.generated.ts` (section 13.7), are plain committed TypeScript: the dev server
    rewrites them on every change, `tsc` checks them like hand-written code, and CI fails on drift
    (decision 59b).
11. **Handlers are pure; the kernel performs every effect.** Every part a module author writes is a
    function of its parameters and of the answers the kernel gives to the requests it yields, and
    everything it produces is in its return value: events, effect descriptions and a result.
    Imperative code exists only in the kernel, the deployment's infrastructure entries, transport
    and listener modules and effect executors. The kernel performs every effect and records it with
    its outcome, linked to the command and events that caused it, so the database and a full
    logbook rebuild from the chain (decision 50a, section 7.9).

## 2. Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Deployment** | One running installation of keelwerk: one build, one or more processes, possibly on several nodes, sharing one control store. |
| **Infrastructure** | What a deployment provides to every app it runs, listed in `defineDeployment`: data adapter factories, the job queue, blob stores, the HTTP host, secret providers, the erasure-ledger sink, tenant resolvers and listener port bindings (section 4.6). |
| **App** | A compile-time composition of modules: `defineApp({ id, modules: [...] })`. Its types are exact for that selection. The deployment platform and the mail server are two apps. |
| **Backend** | A runtime instance of an app inside a deployment, created at runtime without a redeploy: a name, the app it runs, its configuration, secrets, domains, quotas and tenants. Several backends may run the same app. |
| **Tenant** | An isolation unit inside a backend (a company, an organisation, an app, whatever the backend calls it). Data, authentication realm, configuration, secrets, domains and quotas are per tenant. |
| **Scope** | The pair (backend, tenant) an invocation runs in, or the backend level, or the deployment level. Every action declares the level it accepts. |
| **Scope key** | A deployment-wide unique key (a host name, a mail domain, a credential's public id, a webhook endpoint) that resolves to a scope before any tenant data is reachable (gap G2, section 17.7). |
| **Operator** | The person administering the deployment (Jens). A principal kind with deployment scope. |
| **Principal** | Who is acting: anonymous, user, service, operator or system, with the scope it belongs to, claims, roles and memberships (section 8.5). |
| **Module service principal** | The service principal `<module>.system` under which a module's reactions, timers and schedules run; governed by rules like any principal (section 8.4). |
| **Module** | A unit of composition with a string id. Owns entities, actions, policies, services, reactions and extension points; declares requirements, optional dependencies, contracts it provides, contributions and conditional parts. Written as a module base and a module literal, `defineModule(base, { ... })`, which the generator assembles from the module's directories as `module.generated.ts` (sections 4.1 and 23.5). |
| **Module base** | A module's declaration literal, `defineModuleBase({ ... })` in `base.ts`: identity, dependencies, configuration, extension points, entities, streams, flags and the data of contributions and conditional parts, against which parts are typed (sections 4.1 and 23.5). |
| **Part** | The one definition a source file exports (an action, a rule, a reaction, a service, a fill, a schedule, an effect, an effect executor, ...), typed against a module base and mounted by the generated manifest under the reference its file name and directory give (sections 4.1, 23.3 and 23.5). |
| **Generated manifest** | A module's `module.generated.ts`: the module literal that `keelwerk generate` and the dev server write from the module's directory conventions, mounting every part under the reference its path gives; committed and checked for drift in CI, while `base.ts` stays hand-written (decision 59b, section 23.5). |
| **Contract** | A named capability with a typed interface (`live`, `blobs`, `httpHost`) that modules list in `requires` or `optional` instead of a concrete implementation; a module or an infrastructure entry declares that it `provides` it (section 5.2). |
| **Maybe accessor** | The form in which a part reaches a module it lists as `optional`: `ctx.load.accounts.ifPresent((a) => a.profile.byId(id))` is a request answered with the inner request's answer, or `undefined` when the module is not selected, and composes with `yield*` like every request (decision 32b, sections 3.4 and 7.9.3). |
| **Entity** | A data structure owned by a module: fields, relations, indexes, events and the actions mounted on it. |
| **Field** | A typed column declared with the `field.*` builders. Emits a validator, a JSON Schema, a GraphQL type and a column definition. |
| **Action** | A named unit of behaviour mounted on an entity, a module or the app: a `query`, a `command` or a `subscription`. |
| **Action reference** | The dotted path of an action: `accounts.profile.deactivate`, `auth.login`, `app.health`. |
| **Request** | A plain value a pure handler yields with `yield*` and the kernel answers: a load (`ctx.load...`), an `ask` of a dependency's query, a flag, a new id, random bytes, the issue, reveal or verification of a secret, a computation, or, in `prepare` only, an inline effect. Answers the chain cannot reproduce are kept in the decision record (section 7.9.3). |
| **Effect** | A description of something to happen outside the decision, returned in a decision's `effects`: a kernel effect (`invoke`, `enqueue`, `setTimer`, `cancelTimer`, `settle`, scope-key claims) performed in the unit or at its commit, or an external effect declared with `defineEffect` and performed after commit, at least once, with its effect id as idempotency key. Every external effect has a `core.effect` record with its outcome (section 7.9.5). |
| **Effect executor** | The imperative code that performs one external effect, `defineEffectExecutor(base, effect, options)` under `src/executors/`: no data access, egress only, an output or a taxonomy error per attempt; the only imperative code a module author writes (section 7.9.5). |
| **External performer** | A program outside keelwerk that performs the effects of a `performer: 'external'` declaration: it holds a subscription over its pending effects and settles each through an action of the owning module, within a deadline; Launchway's agent is one (sections 7.9.5 and 17.3.4). |
| **Effect job** | The job that runs an external effect's executor after the requesting unit commits, on a process that advertises the executor's capabilities (sections 9.5 and 21.2). |
| **Continuation** | The own command an effect names with `continueWith`: the kernel invokes it under the module's service principal with the effect's outcome as input (`outcomeOf(effect)`), so outcomes re-enter pure code as input (section 7.9.5). |
| **Decision record** | What the kernel stores in the meta of each event about the decision that produced it: the part, the input digest, the snapshot position of every load, the recorded answers (ids, random values, the public parts of issued secrets) and the requested effect ids; with the chain it reproduces and explains every decision (section 7.9.6). |
| **Contribution** | Fields, relations, actions, policies or extension-point values a module adds to another module, active only when the target (and any extra `when` modules) are selected. |
| **Conditional part** | Fields, actions, reactions or policies a module adds to itself only when other modules are selected. |
| **Extension point** | A typed slot a module declares so that other modules can fill it without the owner importing them. The kernel's app-level extension points are how transports, resolvers and live carriers plug in; deployment-level points hold the infrastructure. |
| **Policy** | The set of rules for an entity's or a module's actions, one rule per file under `policies/<target>/` (decision 60b): allow or deny, with a `where` condition on the row acted on, an optional `check` on the row produced, a field list and a reason; a rule's id is `<module>.<target>.<file>` (sections 4.4 and 8.1). |
| **Condition** | A serialisable, typed filter AST over an entity's fields and relations, shared by authorization, the data layer and the live feed. |
| **Registry** | The runtime index built by `defineApp`: modules, entities, actions, policies, extension points, keyed by ids and references. |
| **API surface** | The serialisable description of one app's public interface, derived by the core from the registry; every transport, the CLI and every generated document read it (section 16.2). |
| **Field node** | The serialisable form of a field-model node inside the surface: kind, modifiers, constraints and access. |
| **Invoker** | The one in-process entry point that runs an action through the pipeline. Transports call it; so do listeners, the CLI, tests and the kernel when it performs the `invoke` effects modules return. |
| **Session** | The scope and principal the invoker resolved once for a transport request or a long-lived connection (`InvocationSession`, section 16.3.4). |
| **Carrier** | The transport-neutral description of where a request came from (host, path, headers, token, connection), used for scope and principal resolution. Handlers see a redacted form without credentials. |
| **Transport module** | A module that contributes a `TransportAdapter` to the kernel's `transports` extension point; a mount is one adapter attached to the HTTP host for one app. |
| **Invocation protocol** | The canonical JSON wire over HTTP and the operator Unix socket, served by the host for every app and used by the CLI, the typed client and tests (section 16.8). |
| **Artefact** | A file derived from the surface: the surface JSON, an OpenAPI document, a GraphQL SDL, the CLI manifest, a type fragment. |
| **Chain** | The append-only event log of an entity instance; "the chain" of the brief. |
| **Anchor** | A chain head written per scope to the deployment's ledger sinks outside the placement (scope id, position, hash, recorded time, writer), against which `keelwerk db verify` checks the chain (decision 35b, section 15.1.8). Not to be confused with a compaction snapshot's `anchor` (the hash of the last removed event, section 14.7.3), the DNS anchor host name (section 17.3.8) or JMAP's paging anchor (section 14.3.5). |
| **Namespace** | One event log, one set of framework tables and one copy of one app's tables on a placement: one per app on a shared-tables placement, one per tenant otherwise (section 14.2). |
| **Unit** | One transaction on one namespace, opened for one storage scope (section 14.3.2). |
| **Position** | A commit-ordered integer that orders the events of one scope inside a namespace; stream tokens, JMAP states and IMAP `MODSEQ` are positions (section 15.1.4). |
| **Live source** | What a subscription reads, built by its `source` as a description: an entity's changes, pokes, command receipts, stream records, a topic or the pending effects of an external performer; custom iterables exist only in kernel and listener code (section 15.4.2). |
| **Stream token** | The resume token every resumable emitted item carries: `v1.<epoch>.<position>.<scope>.<check>` (section 15.2.6). |
| **Control store** | The deployment-level database that holds backends, tenants, the scope directory, placements, namespaces, wrapped keys and migration history. |
| **Placement** | Where a tenant's data lives: an adapter binding plus a strategy (shared tables with a tenant key, a schema per tenant, a database per tenant, a different adapter). |
| **Node** | A host that runs keelwerk processes (a machine, a virtual machine, a Docker engine), recorded as `core.node` (section 21.1); not a Launchway node, which is tenant data (section 21.8). |
| **Named process** | An entry of `defineDeployment({ processes })`: roles, declared capabilities, slots per queue, placements, a provider and scaling limits, whose replicas the scaler counts (section 21.1). |
| **Lane** | The unit of fairness of the kernel job queue: one per scope, queue, capability set and priority class, with a cap, a weight and a virtual time (sections 9.5.2 and 9.5.3). |
| **Blind index** | The equality tag of a personal field: an HMAC of the normalised value under a field key derived from the tenant's index root key (or a per-subject key), stored beside the sealed column so that equality lookups and unique indexes work without decrypting; prefix, trigram, token and order tags extend the idea to the other declared capabilities (sections 14.7.9.2 and 14.7.9.6). |
| **Operator endpoint** | The deployment-level entry (operator Unix socket and operator host names) where deployment-scope actions are served. |
| **Receiver** | A mapping from an inbound webhook request (path, raw body, headers) to an action, filled into `transport-webhooks` (section 16.5.8). |
| **Edge provider** | The filler of the shared `edge` module's `providers` extension point: it renders the provider-neutral desired state of an edge (sites with their routes, upstreams and certificates) into its own configuration and maps the outcome of applying it to a status per site; `edge-caddy` is the first (decision 82a, section 17.3.7). |

## 3. Kernel

### 3.1 What the runtime is

The kernel is the `@keelwerk/core` package. It contains no transport, no database driver and
no business module. It provides:

- the configuration DSL (section 4) and the registry it builds;
- the invoker, its sessions and the request pipeline (section 9);
- the authorization engine (section 8);
- the condition AST, the pagination model and the error taxonomy shared by every other package;
- the lifecycle, the scope and principal model, the key service (section 14.7.4), the job queue
  contract (section 9.5), the app-level extension points through which transports, resolvers and
  live carriers plug in, and the deployment-level extension points that hold the infrastructure
  (section 5.6);
- the kernel write path, written once against the data adapter contract (section 14.3):
  kernel-internal repositories, the interpreter that drives pure handlers and answers their
  requests, kernel effects, `evolve`, merge rules, receipts, decision records and tokens; effect
  records with their effect jobs and continuations; and a computation pool that runs Argon2id off the
  event loop (section 7.9);
- the implicit `core` module, which owns the control entities (`core.backend`, `core.tenant`,
  `core.domain`, `core.placement`, `core.namespace`, `core.operatorToken`, for versioning, rollouts
  and flags `core.process`, `core.rollout`, `core.flag`, `core.suspension` and `core.apiUsage`, and
  for nodes and scaling `core.node` and `core.scaleDecision`, with `core.process` also recording
  each process's provider, instance, slots, reserved connections, drain and interruption, section
  21), the command receipts (`core.commandReceipt`), the effect records (`core.effect`, one stream
  per effect, with the attempt stream `core.effectAttempt`; section 7.9.6), and the operator and
  client actions (`core.introspect`, `core.me`, `core.capabilities`, `core.subjects.erase`,
  `core.retention.*`, `core.tenant.enter`, `core.tenant.move`, `core.tenant.setApiVersion`, and
  `core.flag.*`: `evaluate`, `restoreRules` and the operator actions behind `keelwerk flags`;
  sections 18 to 20).

Everything else is a module or an infrastructure entry in its own package. The two proof apps are
compositions of such packages (section 17).

### 3.2 Process model

- One deployment runs one build. Every process of the deployment loads the same deployment
  definition (`defineDeployment`, section 4.6), which lists the apps it can run and the
  infrastructure they share.
- A process has a role: `serve` (runs listeners and transports), `work` (runs queue workers,
  projections and the reaction dispatcher), or `all` (both; the development default). Roles are a
  start-up flag, not a different build. Named processes declare roles, capabilities (a process that
  sees real client addresses on port 25, a host with a clean address for outbound mail, a process on
  the edge host), slots per queue, placements, a provider and scaling limits (section 21; gap G9
  keeps the singleton leases). A `work` process runs action jobs for the queues it slots, and effect
  jobs only for executors whose capabilities it advertises (decision 50a; section 7.9.5 specifies
  effects and their executors).
- Processes share no memory. Coordination goes through the control store and the job queue, so
  any number of processes on any number of nodes can run the same role.
- A process serves every backend of the deployment. Which backends exist, which app each runs,
  and which tenants, domains and scope keys they have, is read from the control store and cached
  with a change feed; creating a backend or a tenant does not restart anything.
- Listeners are not only HTTP. A listener module contributes a `Listener` value (section 5.6); the
  deployment binds its ports; the SMTP listener of the mail app and the HTTP host are peers.

### 3.3 Lifecycle

The lifecycle is explicit and the same for every module. Phases run in this order:

| Phase | Who runs | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `compose` | `defineApp`, pure | Validates the module tuple at the type level and again at runtime (missing requirements and contracts, duplicate and reserved ids, conflicting fields, unknown contribution targets, dangling references, unknown execution overrides, identifier collisions), orders modules topologically by `requires` with tuple order as tie-break, applies contributions and conditional parts, builds the registry and derives the API surface. No I/O. |
| `setup` | Kernel, for each module in order | Registers what each module declares against the final registry: projections, indexes, schedules, effects and their executors. Module code does not run: modules only declare parts (section 7.9.1). Transports run their `check` against the surface. Runs before any adapter connects. |
| `connect` | Kernel | Opens the infrastructure listed in `defineDeployment` (data adapters, the control store, blob stores, secret providers, the ledger sink), verifies that it provides every deployment-level contract the apps require, then opens the placements the enabled backends need, checks the modules' declared raw-SQL dialects against their adapters and records the fallbacks the apps will use (section 14.3.3). Replays the erasure ledger and checks namespace epochs (section 14.7.6). Registers the process in `core.process` and compares its build manifest with `core.rollout`: it joins the finalized revision or the target, or refuses to start with `buildTooOld` or `targetConflict` (section 19.1). Runs the capability probes of its named process (section 21.2) and reserves its connection pool from each placement's budget, refusing to start with `connectionBudget` when a budget is spent (section 21.3). |
| `migrate` | Kernel | In development: plans and applies the schema diff per namespace, confirming destructive steps. In production: verifies that the applied history matches the committed migration files and refuses to start on drift. |
| `start` | Kernel, for each module in order | Starts the background work the modules declared: queue workers for their queues and executors, the reaction dispatcher, projections, schedules. Runs after data is available and before any listener accepts traffic. |
| `listen` | Kernel | The HTTP host mounts each app's transports and the invocation protocol; listener modules start on the ports the deployment binds. The process reports ready and is marked `ready` in `core.process`. |
| `stop` | Reverse order | The drain of section 21.6: the process is marked `draining` with a deadline (`processes.<name>.drainSeconds`, default 60, or a termination notice's if sooner) and stops taking jobs; listeners stop accepting, live streams end with `going_away`, consumer and singleton leases are released, and in-flight invocations and running jobs continue; at the deadline unfinished jobs are released; modules stop in reverse order, infrastructure closes, and the process deregisters and exits with code 0. |

A process that finds itself below the finalized revision, after a network partition for example,
stops (section 19.1).

Two runtime hooks exist beside the process lifecycle, because backends and tenants are created
while the process runs: `onBackendCreated(backend)` and `onTenantCreated(tenant)` (and their
`...Retired` counterparts). They are pure reactions (`defineHook`, section 7.9.2) that run under the
module's service principal and return a decision: events that provision per-tenant data (a mailbox
root, a default team) and effects the kernel performs, never migrations: tenant creation is a data
operation, the schema is already there.

### 3.4 Wiring: explicit, no container

There is no dependency-injection container, no decorators and no reflection. A module's code
reaches what it needs through the typed **context** parameter (section 7.6), and that context is
computed from the module alone: `DecideContext<M>` and its query, source and executor siblings
depend on the module's own definition, its `requires` and `optional` lists and the contracts it
declares, never on an app. Module packages are compiled and type-checked once, before any app that
selects them exists, and several apps share them; a handler type that depended on the app would need
an import of the app from the module package, which is a cycle. Concretely, the context is computed
from the module base (section 4.1), the value every part is typed against. Handlers are pure
(section 7.9): in a decision every member of `ctx` is a value, a pure function or a request or draft
constructor, and the kernel performs what the handler yields and returns.

- `ctx.load.<module>.<entity>`: request constructors for loads of the module's own entities (full
  rows, with the module's own authority) and of the entities of modules it `requires` (typed as
  present) or lists as `optional` (reached through the Maybe accessor below); `.forCaller()` narrows
  a load to the caller's plan. `ctx.write.<module>.<entity>`: draft constructors for the module's
  own entities and, on another module's entity, for the fields this module contributed to it;
  anything else goes through that module's actions or services (section 8.4). Handlers yield loads
  and return drafts; the kernel reads and writes (section 7.9.2).
- `ctx.services.<module>.<name>`: pure service functions of the module's dependencies, bound by the
  kernel to the providing module's context (section 5.5); they return values, requests or
  generators that callers delegate to with `yield*`, and call sites pass no context. Parts are typed
  against the module base, which holds no services, so a module's own code calls the `lib/`
  functions its services wrap.
- `ctx.extensions.<name>`: the values other modules contributed to this module's extension points,
  with behavioural values already bound to their contributor's pure context (section 5.5).
- Invocations are effects. A decision returns `invoke(action, input)` for actions of the module
  itself, passed by value as the part (`invoke(revokeSubject, input)`), and for commands of its
  required modules, named by reference (`invoke('accounts.profile.archive', input)`); the kernel
  runs them through the invoker under the current principal with their declared execution mode, a
  synchronous command of the same scope in a savepoint after the decision's events, and its result
  does not return to the caller. `enqueue(action, input)` runs a command after commit, in any scope
  (sections 7.6 and 7.9.5). A dependency's query is a request,
  `ctx.ask('accounts.profile.get', input)`, answered inside the unit.
- `ctx.flags`: flag requests for the flags of the module and of the modules it requires (the `when`
  modules included inside a conditional part), typed, answered from one snapshot per invocation and
  recorded in the envelope (section 20.3).
- `ctx.live`: present in subscription sources when the module requires the `live` contract, possibly
  undefined when it lists the contract as `optional`, absent otherwise; it builds source
  descriptions (section 15.4). The `blobs` contract gives effect executors and listeners their blob
  access (`ExecutorContext.blobs`); handlers hold `BlobRef` values (section 5.2, gap G5).

A module listed as `optional` is reached through a Maybe accessor (decision 32b, 2026-10-27):
`ctx.load.accounts` has one member, `ifPresent(f)`, a request that answers what `f`'s request
answers when `accounts` is selected and `undefined` when it is not, without touching the unit, so
`yield* ctx.load.accounts.ifPresent((a) => a.profile.byId(id))` is `Profile | undefined` and composes
with `yield*` like every other request (section 7.9.3). `ctx.services.<module>` of an optional
module has the same form. The composition-types spike wrote the auth module against it and against
the `| undefined` form (2026-11-04): the accessor composes with `yield*` and `ctx.all` and costs the
same (514 against 609 instantiations over a baseline of 219,196 at 30 call sites), so it stays
(decision 32b, confirmed). Its error message printed the module's whole loads type, so the accessor
has a short named type per module, referenced by declaration emit like the named module types of
section 13.11, and a type error names that type instead.

Inside a conditional part, the `when` modules count as required, so a reaction typed with
`within(authBase, whenAccounts)` sees `ctx.load.accounts` as present, without the accessor. Module
ids with hyphens appear in lower camel case in the context (`ctx.load.mailStore`,
`ctx.services.apiKeys`), while references keep the id (`mail-store.email.get`); a camel-case
collision between two selected modules is a compose error (section 5.1).

App-level types (`AppEntities<App>`, `AppActionTree<App>`, `AppClient<App>`) exist for what is
genuinely per app: app actions, clients, transports and the generated file (section 13.1).
Decorators are also excluded by the toolchain: sources run under Node's type stripping, which
allows only erasable syntax (section 13.3).

### 3.5 Multi-tenancy in the kernel

Every invocation carries a `Scope` resolved before anything else runs (section 9.2). The kernel
owns the control entities, the scope directory, the scope levels on actions, the principal
resolver extension point, the deployment-ordered tenant resolvers, and the admission stage that
applies per-tenant quotas (section 12.2). The operator principal is resolved by the kernel itself,
so the deployment can be administered even when no authentication module is enabled:

- on the operator Unix socket, connecting is proof of operator access (file mode 0600 inside a
  0700 directory, section 16.8.3); the static deployment secret serves only to bootstrap over that
  socket;
- remote operator profiles use short-lived operator tokens (`core.operatorToken`): issued over the
  socket or after an operator passkey login, expiring after 12 hours by default, revocable one by
  one, and audited at issue and use. The static secret is never accepted over the network.

Section 12 collects what each layer does.

## 4. Configuration DSL

The DSL is a set of plain functions exported by `@keelwerk/core`. Each returns the value it was
given, narrowed to literal types, so that later functions can compute over it. Nothing in the DSL
performs I/O; `defineApp` builds a registry, `defineDeployment` describes where it runs.

### 4.1 `defineModuleBase` and `defineModule`

A module is written as object literals, never as a builder chain. Three kinds of value make it up:

- the **module base**, `defineModuleBase({ ... })`: identity, dependencies, configuration, data
  needs, extension points, the principal reference its resolvers return (section 8.5), entities,
  streams, flags and the declarations of contributions and conditional parts, which is everything a
  handler's types depend on;
- **parts**, one literal each, typed against the base: `defineCommand`, `defineQuery` and
  `defineSubscription` (section 4.3), `defineRule` (section 4.4), `defineReaction` and
  `defineProcess` (section 7.7), `defineService` and `defineFill` (section 5.5), `defineSchedule`
  (section 9.5), `defineTopic` (gap G6), `defineHook` (section 3.3), and `defineEffect` and
  `defineEffectExecutor` (section 7.9.5);
- the **module literal**, `defineModule(base, { ... })`, which mounts the parts and is the module
  value apps select; the generator writes it as `module.generated.ts` from the module's directories
  (decision 59b, section 23.5).

```ts
import { contracts, defineCommand, defineModule, defineModuleBase, extensionPoint, field, shape, type ModuleBaseType, type ModuleType } from '@keelwerk/core'
import { accounts } from '@keelwerk/module-accounts'
// credential, session, toAccounts, whenAccounts, whenLive and the other parts come from their own files (section 23.5).

// The base: what every part is typed against.
const authBaseDef = defineModuleBase({
  id: 'auth',                       // literal; permanent; grammar and reserved ids in section 5.1
  version: '0.1.0',                 // the package's semantic version, enforced by `keelwerk surface diff` (section 18.6)
  requires: [],                     // hard dependencies: module values or contracts; compile-time and boot-time checked
  optional: [accounts, contracts.live], // soft dependencies: reached through ifPresent in the context (section 3.4)
  provides: [],                     // contracts this module implements (the live module provides contracts.live)
  config: shape({                   // per-backend configuration, validated when a backend is created
    sessionIdleMinutes: field.integer({ min: 5 }).default(720),
  }),
  data: { needs: [] },              // only a raw-SQL dialect, { sql: 'postgres' }: the one declared non-portability (section 14.3.3)
  extensionPoints: {                // typed slots other modules may fill (section 5.5)
    identityProviders: extensionPoint.set<IdentityProvider>(),
  },
  principalRef: shape({ credentialId: field.ref.own('credential'), sessionId: field.ref.own('session') }),   // what auth's resolvers put into a principal's ref (section 8.5)
  entities: { credential, session },            // section 4.2
  streams: {},                                  // records without a chain (gap G6)
  flags: {},                                    // section 20.2
  contributions: { toAccounts },                // defineContribution(accounts, { ... }): what auth adds to accounts (section 5.3)
  conditions: { whenAccounts, whenLive },       // defineCondition([accounts], { ... }): what auth adds to itself (section 5.4)
})
export interface AuthBase extends ModuleBaseType<typeof authBaseDef> {}
export const authBase: AuthBase = authBaseDef

// A part: one literal, typed against the base. ctx is DecideContext<AuthBase>; current is the credential row.
export const revoke = defineCommand(authBase, credential, {
  input: shape({ reason: field.string().optional() }),
  decide: (input, current, ctx) => [ctx.events.revoked({ at: ctx.clock.now(), reason: input.reason })],
})

// The module literal, which the generator writes as module.generated.ts from the directories
// (section 23.5): it mounts the parts under keys that are ids.
const authDef = defineModule(authBase, {
  actions: { login, logout, revokeSubject },             // module-level actions, section 4.3
  entityActions: { credential: { revoke } },             // actions mounted on own entities
  policies: { credential: { self, selfRevoke, alreadyRevoked }, login: { open } },   // one rule per file; the key path is the rule id (section 4.4)
  reactions: {},                                         // event handlers; keys are reaction ids (section 7.7)
  services: { verifyPassword, hashPassword },            // pure, typed functions for dependants, section 5.5
  topics: {},                                            // gap G6
  contributes: { toAccounts: { entityActions: { profile: { changePassword } }, policies: { profile: { self: profileSelf } } } },   // section 5.3; the generator aliases clashing names
  conditional: { whenAccounts: { reactions: { revokeOnDeactivation } } },                                      // section 5.4
  schedules: {},                                         // keys are schedule ids (section 9.5)
  lifecycle: { onTenantCreated },                        // hooks of section 3.3
  changes: {},                                           // version changes; keys are the ids the API ledger records (section 18.2)
  effects: {},                                           // external effects the module declares; keys are effect names (section 7.9.5)
  executors: {},                                         // their executors, keyed by effect name: the only imperative module code
})

// Every exported module value and its base have a named type (section 13.11): dependants' declaration
// files then reference `Auth` instead of copying its structure.
export interface Auth extends ModuleType<typeof authDef> {}
export const auth: Auth = authDef
```

Section 23 puts the base in `base.ts` and each part in a file of its own, and the generator writes
the module literal as `module.generated.ts` from the directories (decision 59b, 2026-10-28); tests,
spikes and the API sketch may write all three in one file, the module literal then by hand. Flags
and version changes are declarations that need no base: `defineFlag` (section 20.2), listed by the
base's `flags`, and `defineVersionChange`, listed by the module literal's `changes`; an app's dated
API versions are a `defineApiVersions` value (section 18.2).

- **Mounts.** An own entity is passed by value (`defineCommand(authBase, credential, { ... })`);
  another module's entity is named, inside a contribution: `defineCommand(within(authBase,
  toAccounts), 'profile', { ... })` mounts on `accounts.profile`. `within(base, declaration)` types
  a part of a contribution or conditional part: the target and `when` modules count as required,
  and rows include the contributed fields. Own actions are likewise used by value and other
  modules' actions by reference (section 7.6).
- **Checks.** A part's type records the base it was built against and its mount, and the module
  literal accepts it only where both match: `entityActions: { session: { revoke } }` fails at
  compile time and at boot. `defineModule` records each part's reference, so the registry resolves
  the value `revoke` to `auth.credential.revoke`.
- **Keys.** The keys of `actions`, `entityActions`, `reactions`, `schedules`, `topics`, `changes`,
  `effects` and `executors` are ids: renaming an action changes the API, and reaction, schedule,
  effect and version-change ids never change once released (an effect's name is part of its
  records, section 7.9.6). `policies` is keyed the same way, by target and then by rule, so the key
  path is the rule id (`policies.credential.self` is `auth.credential.self`); a rule over several
  actions or over a selector sits at the top level under its own name (section 4.4). With the
  generated manifest every key comes from a file or directory name (section 23.5).
- **Contributions and conditional parts** have two halves under one key: the base's
  `contributions` and `conditions` hold the declarations with the data they add, and the module
  literal's `contributes` and `conditional` hold the behaviour. Entries that share a (target,
  `when`) identity merge, because they are one migration track (section 14.6.1).

Why literals: Jens decided on 2026-10-24 (decision point 3, section 26) that modules are object
literals and never a builder chain. The first design used a chain because its callbacks could type
handlers from sibling declarations, which a single object literal cannot do: TypeScript cannot type
a property from its siblings. The base makes the chain unnecessary, because every part is typed
against a value that exists before it: `defineCommand(authBase, credential, { ... })` takes
`ctx.load`, `ctx.write`, `ctx.config`, the flag requests, the row and the event constructors from
`authBase` and `credential` alone, and the module literal only mounts values whose types are
complete.
`defineModule(base, { ... })` normalises the base and the literal into the module shape of
section 4.7, which is all `defineApp` ever sees; the type-level model is unchanged. Because the
base holds no services, a part's `ctx.services` lists only its dependencies' services, and a
module's own code calls the `lib/` functions its services wrap (section 3.4).

Why the named type: a module value's type is inferred and anonymous, and `requires`, `optional`
and the targets of contributions hold the full type of each dependency. Under `composite`,
declaration emit is mandatory and would copy every dependency's structure into each dependant's
`.d.ts`, recursively, until the compiler refuses with TS7056. `ModuleType<T>` is the identity;
extending it in an interface gives the value a name that emit references, and `ModuleBaseType<T>`
does the same for the base, which every part's type names. `keelwerk new module` scaffolds the
pattern, a GritQL rule flags an exported module, module base or app value without a named type,
and CI measures declaration size (section 13.11).

### 4.2 `defineEntity` and the field model

```ts
const credentialDef = defineEntity({
  prefix: 'cred',                              // TypeID prefix at the API boundary: cred_01j...; unique per app
  dataSubject: 'subject',                      // whose personal data a row holds (section 14.7.4)
  fields: {
    subject: field.subject().index(),          // the auth subject, a SubjectId (section 8.5)
    kind: field.enum(['password', 'passkey']),
    identifier: field.string({ format: 'email' }).optional().personal({ normalize: 'email' }),  // login name of password credentials; the unique index implies 'eq' (section 14.7.9)
    verifier: field.verifier(),                // password hash or passkey public key: hidden, sealed in events (section 6.6)
    label: field.string().optional().merge('lww'),
    lastUsedAt: field.instant().optional().maskable(),   // rules may hide it (section 8.1)
    revokedAt: field.instant().optional(),
  },
  relations: {},                               // reverse relations are added by contributions, see 6.3
  indexes: [{ fields: ['identifier'], unique: true, where: { kind: 'password', revokedAt: { isNull: true } } }],
  history: 'chain',                            // default; 'state', 'projection' or 'external' (section 6.6)
  tenancy: 'tenant',                           // default; 'backend' or 'deployment' for control data
  events: {                                    // domain events beyond the generated ones (section 15.1.5)
    revoked: shape({ at: field.instant(), reason: field.string().optional() }),
  },
  evolve: {                                    // how a domain event changes the state (pure)
    revoked: (state, e) => ({ ...state, revokedAt: e.at }),
  },
  invariant: (row) => row.kind !== 'password' || row.identifier !== undefined,   // checked on every post-image
  generated: { set: false },                   // credentials change only through auth's own commands
})
// The named entity type (section 13.11): the base's declaration file references `Credential`
// instead of repeating the entity's structure.
export interface Credential extends EntityType<typeof credentialDef> {}
export const credential: Credential = credentialDef
```

Every entity gets system fields the author never declares: `id` (UUIDv7, prefixed at the API),
`createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `archivedAt` (nullable; the tombstone), `version` (the stream version:
1 after creation, incremented by every event, used for optimistic concurrency) and, when
`tenancy` is `tenant`, a `tenantId` that no transport exposes and the data layer always filters
on. Positions, which order events across streams, are a separate concept (section 15.1.4).

The `field.*` builders are the single source for types, validation, JSON Schema, GraphQL types
and columns. The core defines the kinds and the modifiers; section 14.5.1 maps them to dialects.

| Builder | TypeScript type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `field.string()`, `field.text()` | `string` | `maxLength`, `pattern`, `format` ('email', 'uri', 'hostname') |
| `field.integer()` | `number` | stored in 64 bits, validated to the safe-integer range; `min`, `max` |
| `field.integer({ wide: true })` | `bigint` | decimal string on the wire |
| `field.decimal({ precision, scale })` | `string` | an exact canonical decimal; never a binary float |
| `field.float()` | `number` | IEEE 754 double, for measurements and introspected `real` columns |
| `field.boolean()` | `boolean` | |
| `field.instant()` | `Temporal.Instant` | UTC; millisecond precision as stored, finer digits rounded down at `validate`; RFC 3339 at the boundary (decision 19b, section 6.4) |
| `field.date()` | `Temporal.PlainDate` | ISO calendar date |
| `field.timeZone()` | `string` | an IANA zone name, validated against the runtime's time-zone database |
| `field.enum([...])` | union of the literals | |
| `field.json(schema)` | the schema's output type | any Standard Schema; stored as JSON |
| `field.ref(module, entity)`, `field.ref.own(entity)` | `Id<'module.entity'>` | a typed reference; where it may point is section 6.3; `own` names an entity of the declaring or contributing module |
| `field.subject()` | `SubjectId` | an opaque principal or data-subject id, branded: a plain string is rejected, and a helper that maps an id to a subject returns `SubjectId` (`asSubject(profileId): SubjectId`, section 8.5) |
| `field.serial({ per })` | `number` | allocated at insert, strictly ascending per partition, read-only (IMAP UIDs) |
| `field.set(inner)`, `field.list(inner)` | `ReadonlySet<T>`, `readonly T[]` | observed-remove set for merge `set`; CRDT list for merge `sequence` |
| `field.richText()` | `RichText` (an opaque document handle) | merge `richText`; an app needs a codec module (section 15.3.9) |
| `field.binary()` | `Uint8Array` | small payloads; large ones are blobs |
| `field.blob({ mediaType, maxBytes })` | `BlobRef` | a reference into a blob store; requires the `blobs` contract (gap G5) |
| `field.secret()` | entity fields: `SecretRef` in process; action inputs: `string`; write-only at the boundary | entity fields are sealed per value and read only through a reveal request (`yield* ctx.secrets.reveal(ref, reason)`) or, in an effect executor, `ctx.secrets.reveal` (sections 6.6 and 7.9.3); input values are redacted from logs, traces, receipts and errors |
| `field.verifier()` | `string`, hidden | a one-way verifier (password hash, token verifier); sealed per value in events (section 6.6) |

Modifiers, all chainable and all reflected in the type: `.optional()`, `.default(value)`,
`.unique()` (unique among non-archived rows; implies merge `exclusive`), `.index()`, `.hidden()`
(section 6.6), `.maskable()` (rules may hide the field from readers; section 8.1), `.personal()`
or `.personal({ subject?, queries?, normalize?, eq?, prefix?, contains?, order?, keys? })`
(encrypted per data subject in the chain and in state tables, queryable per declared capability;
`.unique()` and `.index()` on a personal field imply `'eq'`; sections 14.7.4 and 14.7.9),
`.stateOnly()` (kept in the state table, never written to events; section 6.6),
`.merge(type)` (section 15.3.4; default `lww` for scalars, `exclusive` for unique fields),
`.tag(n)` (a stable protobuf-style field number; allocated deterministically and recorded in the
module snapshot when omitted), `.describe(text)` and `.deprecated(reason)`. Every modifier returns
a field that keeps every earlier flag and the reference (section 4.7).

Entity options beyond the example: `partition: '<field>'` (an immutable field that partitions change
tokens, section 15.1.4), `searchIndexes` (section 14.3.3; an entry over personal fields adds `keys`
and `languages`, section 14.7.9.9), `projection` and `source` for the `projection` and `external`
history modes (sections 15.2.2 and 14.8.4), `rederive` (recomputes `stateOnly` fields during
rebuilds), and `retention: { suggest }` (section 14.7.1).

`shape({ ... })` builds an object schema from fields for action inputs and outputs. It is a
Standard Schema (section 6.5), so any library that accepts Standard Schema accepts it, and it is
walkable, so transports can project it exactly.

### 4.3 Actions

Actions are literals passed to `defineCommand`, `defineQuery` and `defineSubscription`. The first
argument types the handlers: a module base (section 4.1), a base narrowed to a contribution or a
conditional part with `within(base, declaration)`, or, for actions mounted on the app, the app's
selection, the `as const` tuple that `apps/<id>/src/modules.ts` exports (section 4.5). An entity
between the base and the literal mounts the action on that entity: an own entity by value, a
target's entity by name inside a contribution.

```ts
// One part per file (section 23); the generated module.generated.ts mounts them, from their paths:
//   entityActions: { credential: { revoke, active } }, actions: { login, whoami },
//   conditional: { whenLive: { actions: { sessionEvents } } }
export const revoke = defineCommand(authBase, credential, {
  input: shape({ reason: field.string().optional() }),
  errors: [alreadyRevoked],                              // closed set, section 10
  execution: 'sync',                                     // 'sync' | 'async' | 'either'
  scope: 'tenant',                                       // default
  decide: (input, current, ctx) => {                     // pure: the full current row in, events out
    if (current.revokedAt) throw alreadyRevoked({ id: current.id })
    return [ctx.events.revoked({ at: ctx.clock.now(), reason: input.reason })]
  },
  // output defaults to the entity row after the events are applied, masked for the caller
})

export const active = defineQuery(authBase, credential, {
  input: shape({ subject: field.subject() }),
  output: pageOf(credential),                            // a page of rows, cursor pagination
  read: (input, ctx) => ctx.target.query({               // a query description over the entity as the caller may read it under this action's rules
    where: { subject: input.subject, revokedAt: { isNull: true } },
    sort: [{ field: 'createdAt', direction: 'desc' }],
  }),
})

export const login = defineCommand(authBase, {
  input: shape({ identifier: field.string({ format: 'email' }), password: field.secret() }),
  output: shape({ sessionToken: field.string(), sessionId: field.ref.own('session'), expiresAt: field.instant() }),
  errors: [invalidCredentials],
  auth: { public: true },                                // no principal required; still scoped to a tenant
  execution: 'sync',
  hints: { http: { cookie: { set: { name: '__Host-keelwerk_session', from: 'sessionToken', expiresFrom: 'expiresAt' }, omitFromBody: ['sessionToken'] } } },
  *decide(input, ctx) { /* a generator: yields the credential load, the Argon2id check, an id and a token; returns the session's events (section 7.9.8) */ },
})

// principalShape and summarise() are module-local helpers, not framework exports; read returns the output itself
export const whoami = defineQuery(authBase, { output: principalShape, principal: 'user', read: (_, ctx) => summarise(ctx.principal) })

// The subscription exists only when a live module is selected: a part of the conditional part whenLive.
export const sessionEvents = defineSubscription(within(authBase, whenLive), {
  event: shape({ sessionId: field.ref.own('session'), kind: field.enum(['created', 'revoked']) }),
  principal: 'user',                                     // the gate admits user principals only; ctx.principal is narrowed
  source: (_input, ctx, resume) =>                       // resume: the stream token the client presented
    mapItems(
      ctx.live.entity('auth', 'session', { where: { subject: ctx.principal.subject }, after: resume }),
      (change) => ({ sessionId: change.id, kind: change.type === 'created' ? 'created' : 'revoked' }),
    ),
})
```

Every handler is pure (section 7.9). A command's `decide` is a plain function or a generator: it
yields requests with `yield*` (loads, flags, ids, computations) and returns a decision, events alone
or `{ events, effects, result }`; mounted on an entity it also receives the full current row, and
the kernel appends the events, evolves the state and returns the row. A synchronous command may add
`prepare`, the only place for inline effects (section 7.9.4). A query's `read` returns a query
description, which the kernel plans and runs, or the output itself, or is a generator that yields
loads first. The imperative `handle` form no longer exists. `source` builds a subscription's source
description; `mapItems` changes items and keeps stream tokens and control frames, so the
subscription stays resumable. `pageOf(entity)` and `rowOf(entity)` are the output shapes of entity
rows, which the shape stage masks (section 8.4). Section 7 defines the full option set.

### 4.4 Policies

A policy is the set of rules over one target: an own entity, an own module-level action, a list
of own module-level actions, or a selector across modules (gap G13). Each rule is a file of its
own (decision 60b, 2026-10-28), one `defineRule(base, target, { ... })` literal typed against the
base, with the members of section 8.1. A rule over one entity or one action lives in
`policies/<target>/<rule>.ts`, and its id is the module id, the target and the file name
(`policies/credential/self.ts` of `auth` is `auth.credential.self`); a rule over several actions or
over a selector lives in `policies/<rule>.ts` with the id `<module>.<rule>`. The generated manifest
mounts every rule file under that key path (section 23.5); because rules compose as a set (section
8.2), neither their order nor their split over files changes a decision, and allows and denies over
one target are still read together, as the files of one directory.

```ts
// modules/auth/src/policies/credential/self.ts: the rule auth.credential.self
export const self = defineRule(authBase, credential, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['read'],                                     // 'read' covers get, query, changes, queryChanges, watch, history
  principal: 'user',                                     // narrows ctx.principal: subject is a SubjectId, never null
  where: (ctx) => ({ subject: ctx.principal.subject }),  // typed condition over credential
  fields: ['lastUsedAt'],                                // the maskable fields this rule reveals
  reason: 'A user may see their own credentials.',
})

// modules/auth/src/policies/credential/self-revoke.ts: auth.credential.self-revoke
export const selfRevoke = defineRule(authBase, credential, { effect: 'allow', actions: ['revoke'], principal: 'user', where: (ctx) => ({ subject: ctx.principal.subject }) })

// modules/auth/src/policies/credential/already-revoked.ts: auth.credential.already-revoked
export const alreadyRevoked = defineRule(authBase, credential, {
  effect: 'deny',                                        // without `check`, a deny rule tests the row before the action
  actions: ['revoke'],
  where: () => ({ revokedAt: { isNull: false } }),
  reason: 'This credential is already revoked.',
})

// modules/auth/src/policies/login/open.ts and policies/whoami/signed-in.ts: rules over module-level actions
export const open = defineRule(authBase, login, { effect: 'allow', public: true })
export const signedIn = defineRule(authBase, whoami, { effect: 'allow', principal: 'user' })

// modules/members/src/policies/invitation/withdraw.ts: a transition; members may move an invitation
// from pending to withdrawn, and to nothing else.
export const withdraw = defineRule(membersBase, invitation, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['update'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => ({ status: 'pending', invitedBy: ctx.principal.subject }),   // the row acted on
  check: () => ({ status: 'withdrawn' }),                                      // the row produced
})
```

Entity rules carry a `where` condition over the row acted on (compiled to the data layer and
interpreted in memory) and an optional `check` over the row an action produces; module-level
rules carry a `when` predicate over context and input. Rule callbacks are plain pure functions of
the principal context: they yield nothing, and the flags they read come from the invocation's
snapshot (section 7.9.2). An interpolated `null` or `undefined` never matches; null tests use
`isNull` (section 8.3). Semantics and composition are in section 8. A contribution can add rules to
another module's entities (section 5.3).

`defineRule` checks what it can see: the keys of a returned condition against the target's fields
and relations (`unknownConditionFields`, section 8.3). A rule's custom action names and its policy
key need the module literal, which does not exist when the rule is typed, so `defineModule` checks
them: a mounted rule that names an action its target does not mount fails with
`unknownRuleActions`, and a policy key that names a target the rule does not cover fails with
`unknownPolicyTargets` (section 4.7).

### 4.5 `defineApp`

```ts
// apps/launchway/src/modules.ts: the selection
import { accounts } from '@keelwerk/module-accounts'
import { auth } from '@keelwerk/module-auth'
import { live } from '@keelwerk/live'
import { graphql } from '@keelwerk/transport-graphql'
import { rest } from '@keelwerk/transport-rest'
import { deployments } from '@launchway/module-deployments'
import { projects } from '@launchway/module-projects'

export const modules = [accounts, auth, live, projects, deployments, graphql, rest] as const   // order is a tie-break only

// apps/launchway/src/actions/health.ts: an app action, typed against the selection
export const health = defineQuery(modules, { /* app-level, referenced as app.health */ })

// apps/launchway/src/app.ts
import { defineApp, type AppType, type Row } from '@keelwerk/core'
import { health } from './actions/health.ts'
import { launchwayApi } from './api-versions.ts'
import { modules } from './modules.ts'

const launchwayDef = defineApp({
  id: 'launchway',
  modules,                                                 // the const tuple of modules.ts
  actions: { health },
  execution: { 'deployments.deployment.redeploy': 'async' }, // how external callers are answered (section 7.4)
  authorization: { mode: 'strict', decisionLog: 'denials' },
  policies: { disable: [], add: [] },                      // per-app rule overrides, section 8.7
  api: launchwayApi,                                       // defineApiVersions: the app's dated API versions (section 18.2)
  flags: {},                                               // app-level flags (section 20.2)
})
export interface Launchway extends AppType<typeof launchwayDef> {}
export const launchway: Launchway = launchwayDef

export type Profile = Row<Launchway, 'accounts.profile'>   // exact for this selection
```

Apps list only modules: data adapters, the HTTP host, blob stores and the queue are infrastructure
of the deployment (section 4.6), so an app never chooses a database. `defineApp` is uncallable
when the tuple is inconsistent; the error names the problem (`missingModules: 'accounts'`,
`conflictingFields: 'accounts.profile.lastLoginAt'`, ...). The checks are listed in section 4.7.
At runtime it repeats the same checks (for dynamic callers and JavaScript) and builds the
registry.

### 4.6 `defineDeployment`

```ts
// keelwerk.config.ts
import { byHeader, byHostname, byScopeKey, defineDeployment, env, secret } from '@keelwerk/core'
import { postgresAdapter } from '@keelwerk/adapter-postgres'
import { httpHost } from '@keelwerk/transport-http'
import { blobsFs } from '@keelwerk/blobs-fs'
import { ledgerFile } from '@keelwerk/core/ledger'

export default defineDeployment({
  apps: [launchway, mail],                                 // the catalogue a backend can be created from
  infrastructure: [                                        // fills the deployment-level extension points (section 5.6)
    postgresAdapter(),                                     // data adapter factory 'postgres' (section 14.3.7)
    httpHost({ listen: [{ port: 3000 }] }),                // provides contracts.httpHost; serves the invocation protocol for every app
    blobsFs({ root: '/var/lib/keelwerk/blobs' }),        // provides contracts.blobs (gap G5)
    ledgerFile({ path: '/var/lib/keelwerk-ledger/erasure.log' }),   // ledger sink outside placement backups: erasures and chain anchors (sections 14.7.6 and 15.1.8)
  ],
  control: { adapter: 'postgres', url: env('KEELWERK_CONTROL_URL') },
  placements: {                                            // where tenant data may live; chosen per tenant at creation
    default: { adapter: 'postgres', url: env('KEELWERK_DATA_URL'), strategy: 'shared-tables' },
  },
  tenantResolution: [byHostname(), byScopeKey(), byHeader('x-keelwerk-tenant')],   // deployment order
  ports: { 'smtp-in.mx': 25 },                             // listener ports belong to the deployment (gap G1)
  operator: { socket: '/run/keelwerk/operator.sock', hosts: ['ops.example'], bootstrapSecret: secret('KEELWERK_OPERATOR_SECRET') },
  keys: { masterKey: secret('KEELWERK_MASTER_KEY') },    // root of the key service (section 14.7.4)
  telemetry: { otlp: env('OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT') },
  rollout: { finalize: 'auto', graceSeconds: 600 },        // the defaults: finalization of rolling upgrades (section 19.4)
  anchors: { every: 'batch' },                             // the default: each scope's chain head to every ledger sink per notifier batch (section 15.1.8)
  processes: { home: { roles: ['serve', 'work'], slots: { '*': 4 } } },   // named processes (section 21.1)
  scaling: { maxProcesses: 8 },                            // the scaler's deployment-wide limits (section 21.4)
  queues: { 'mail-delivery': { running: 4, slo: 'PT2M' } },   // job limits per queue; slo: an ISO 8601 duration (sections 9.5.5 and 21.4)
})
```

A deployment names the apps it can run; backends are rows in the control store that reference an
app id. Creating a backend with a module selection that no app in the catalogue has means adding a
`defineApp` line and deploying, which is a configuration change, not a kernel change. The
alternative, selecting modules at runtime, cannot have exact types and is rejected (ADR 0003);
Jens decided for the compiled catalogue on 2026-10-25 (decision point 1, section 26), on the
condition that development always has the full, exact types of the app being built, which section
4.5 guarantees per app.

`defineDeployment` checks, at the type level and again at boot, that its infrastructure provides
every deployment-level contract any app's modules require (`missingInfrastructure: 'blobs'`). The
kernel job queue is built on the data adapters' job store and needs no entry (section 9.5); a
different queue implementation can replace it as an infrastructure entry. The deployment also
declares its named processes (`processes.<name>` with `roles`, `capabilities`, `slots` per queue,
`placements`, `provider`, `scale` and `drainSeconds`), the scaler's limits (`scaling`:
`maxProcesses`, `maxCostPerHour` and maxima per provider), the job limits per queue (`queues.<q>`:
`running`, `queued` and `slo`) and each placement's connection budget
(`placements.<name>.maxConnections`, default 80 percent of the server's `max_connections`); sections
9.5.5, 21.1, 21.3 and 21.4 specify them. `anchors.every` sets how often each scope's chain head is
appended to the ledger sinks: `'batch'`, the default, with every commit batch of the notifier and at
most once per second per scope, or an ISO 8601 duration such as `PT1M` (decision 35b, section
15.1.8). `queues.<q>.slo` is the target wait of the queue's due
jobs, from due to start, written as an ISO 8601 duration like every duration in this document's
configuration (default `PT30S`): `queues: { 'mail-delivery': { slo: 'PT2M' } }` asks the scaler to
start a due delivery within two minutes, and the scaler reads it in seconds (`sloSeconds`, section
21.4). Secret providers default to the process environment.

The deployment file has a default export and is found in this order: the file named by `--config`
or `KEELWERK_CONFIG`, then `keelwerk.config.ts`, then `.launchway/deployment.ts` (decision 90c,
section 16.9.1). An app repository carries its deployment in the `.launchway/` directory (section
23.1): `.launchway/deployment.ts` is the app's deployment file, as above (the app, data stores and
placements, ports, providers, scaling limits), and `.launchway/launchway.ts` holds what only the
deployment platform needs (domains and routes, previews, environment, node; section 17.3.1). Until
Launchway's rebuild (roadmap M4), the current Launchway deploys an app from
`.launchway/compose.yaml`, which runs `keelwerk start --config .launchway/deployment.ts`; Trail
(M3) is deployed that way. A deployment hosting several apps from published packages, as the
example above does, is what the rebuilt Launchway makes possible.

### 4.7 The type-level model

The derived types operate on the normalised module shape below, which `defineModule(base, { ... })`
produces from the module base and the module literal (section 4.1). The listing was checked on 2026-10-11 with TypeScript 7.0.2 and 5.9.3
(`--strict --exactOptionalPropertyTypes --noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) together with the fourteen
groups of positive and negative cases listed after it: every positive case holds, and every
negative case fails with the named check. The listing types instants as `Date`, as it was checked;
the DSL types them as `Temporal.Instant` (decision 19b, section 6.4), which no composition check
reads. The file with its cases costs 61,042 type
instantiations on TypeScript 7.0.2 (57,242 on 5.9.3). The composition-types spike of roadmap M0
(`spikes/composition-types`, 2026-11-04) built the type model of the whole DSL on this listing:
every case holds, every named check below is asserted as the exact `AppChecks` type and as a
failing call, and `docs/api-sketch.ts` type-checks against it.

The listing models the composition fold, not the whole DSL: its `defineModule(m)` takes the
normalised shape directly and applies the data-level module checks, which the DSL applies at
`defineModuleBase`, where the data lives (decided 2026-11-04 after the spike), and `contribute` and `whenPresent` build the normalised entries
that `defineContribution` and `defineCondition` declare. The module base, the parts typed against
it and the module literal, the module-local contexts of section 7.6, action input and output types
derived from the field model, `Insert` and `Patch`, and relations are the spike's work, against
the checklist at the end of this section. The core keeps these properties, as the spike did:

- every lookup is a mapped type over the union of module ids plus `Extract` by id; there is no
  recursion over the tuple, so depth is constant in the number of modules;
- contributions are a union of objects filtered by `to` and `when` and tagged with their
  contributor, not a tuple walk;
- a module literal without a key (`requires`, `contributes`) contributes nothing, which needs the
  distributive `infer` form (`Ms[number] extends infer M ? M extends { ... } ? ... : never : never`);
- a field defined by more than one source (own, a conditional part, a contributor) is a conflict
  whatever its types, which mirrors the boot check; comparing types cannot detect conflicts
  between subtype-related types (an enum and a string, a branded id and a string);
- positions are compared on the author's tuple: a mapped type over a variadic tuple
  (`[Core, ...Ms]`) numbers the spread elements from zero again, which hid a duplicate of the core
  module until reserved ids got their own check (found while checking this listing);
- every public derived type is named and wrapped in `Prettify`, so hovers show rows, not
  conditionals;
- the normalised shape also carries the module's `flags` and `changes` (sections 20.2 and 18.2);
  no composition check reads them, so the listing leaves them out;
- every type that can appear in a module value's type is exported by `@keelwerk/core`;
  otherwise declaration emit fails with TS4023 or TS2742 (checked with this listing), which
  TypeScript 7.0.2 reports as TS2883 (section 13.11);
- no DSL function that may be nested inside another const-generic call infers a defaulted literal
  type parameter: TypeScript infers such a parameter from the outer call's constraint, so in the
  spike an inline `defineContribution` inside `defineModuleBase` got `when: readonly Dependency[]`
  and was silently inactive. Such functions take the whole literal as one type parameter
  (`defineContribution`, `defineCondition`), and defaulted parameters use `NoInfer` (`defineEntity`);
  this is a rule for core authors (section 13.11);
- a single `any` in a module definition would collapse `UnionToIntersection`; module packages
  compile with `noImplicitAny` and a type test asserts that `AnyModule` constraints never
  mention `any`.

```ts
// ---- Helpers
type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {}
type UnionToIntersection<U> = (U extends unknown ? (x: U) => void : never) extends (x: infer I) => void ? I : never
type IsUnion<T, U = T> = [T] extends [never] ? false : T extends unknown ? ([U] extends [T] ? false : true) : never
type AllKeys<U> = U extends unknown ? keyof U : never
type TypeAt<U, K extends PropertyKey> = U extends unknown ? (K extends keyof U ? U[K] : never) : never
type Check<Problem, Key extends string> = [Problem] extends [never] ? {} : { readonly [K in Key]: Problem }

declare const entityBrand: unique symbol
export type Id<Ref extends string> = string & { readonly [entityBrand]: Ref }

// ---- Field model: every modifier returns a FieldDef that keeps all flags and the reference
type FieldKind = 'string' | 'integer' | 'instant' | 'enum' | 'ref'
interface FieldFlags { readonly optional: boolean; readonly defaulted: boolean; readonly hidden: boolean; readonly maskable: boolean }
interface NoFlags { readonly optional: false; readonly defaulted: false; readonly hidden: false; readonly maskable: false }
type Flag<F extends FieldFlags, K extends keyof FieldFlags> = { readonly [P in keyof FieldFlags]: P extends K ? true : F[P] }
interface AbsoluteRef { readonly module: string; readonly entity: string }
interface OwnRef { readonly own: true; readonly entity: string }

declare const valueType: unique symbol
export interface FieldDef<T, F extends FieldFlags = NoFlags, R extends AbsoluteRef | OwnRef | null = null> {
  readonly kind: FieldKind
  readonly flags: F
  readonly ref: R
  readonly [valueType]?: T
  optional(): FieldDef<T, Flag<F, 'optional'>, R>
  default(value: T): FieldDef<T, Flag<F, 'defaulted'>, R>
  hidden(): FieldDef<T, Flag<F, 'hidden'>, R>
  maskable(): FieldDef<T, Flag<F, 'maskable'>, R>
  unique(): FieldDef<T, F, R>
  index(): FieldDef<T, F, R>
}
type AnyField = FieldDef<unknown, FieldFlags, AbsoluteRef | OwnRef | null>

/** Own references name an entity of the declaring (or contributing) module; resolved per source. */
type ResolveFields<F, Owner extends string> = {
  readonly [K in keyof F]: F[K] extends FieldDef<infer _T, infer Fl, infer R>
    ? R extends { readonly own: true; readonly entity: infer E extends string }
      ? FieldDef<Id<`${Owner}.${E}`>, Fl, { readonly module: Owner; readonly entity: E }>
      : F[K]
    : never
}
type FieldValue<F> = F extends FieldDef<infer T, infer Fl, infer _R> ? (Fl extends { readonly optional: true } ? T | undefined : T) : never
type IsOptional<F> = F extends { readonly flags: { readonly optional: true } } ? true : false
type RowOf<F> = Prettify<
  { readonly [K in keyof F as IsOptional<F[K]> extends true ? never : K]: FieldValue<F[K]> } &
  { readonly [K in keyof F as IsOptional<F[K]> extends true ? K : never]?: FieldValue<F[K]> }
>

// ---- Actions carry kind, execution and phantom input and output types
type ActionKind = 'query' | 'command' | 'subscription'
type Execution = 'sync' | 'async' | 'either'
declare const ioTypes: unique symbol
export interface ActionDef<K extends ActionKind, I, O, X extends Execution> {
  readonly kind: K
  readonly execution: X
  readonly [ioTypes]?: { readonly input: I; readonly output: O }
}
type AnyAction = ActionDef<ActionKind, unknown, unknown, Execution>

// ---- Normalised definitions (what defineModule produces and defineApp consumes)
type HistoryMode = 'chain' | 'state' | 'projection' | 'external'
type GeneratorTemplate = 'watch'                       // closed, core-known set filled by modules
interface AnyEntity {
  readonly fields: { readonly [name: string]: AnyField }
  readonly history?: HistoryMode
  readonly generated?: { readonly [K in 'get' | 'query' | 'changes' | 'queryChanges' | 'set' | 'history' | GeneratorTemplate]?: boolean }
  readonly actions?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyAction }
}
interface AnyEntityPatch { readonly fields?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyField }; readonly actions?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyAction } }
interface AnyContract { readonly contract: string; readonly level: 'app' | 'deployment' }
interface AnyContribution {
  readonly to: AnyModule
  readonly when?: readonly AnyModule[]
  readonly entities?: { readonly [entity: string]: AnyEntityPatch }
  readonly actions?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyAction }
}
interface AnyConditional {
  readonly when: readonly (AnyModule | AnyContract)[]
  readonly entities?: { readonly [entity: string]: AnyEntityPatch }
  readonly actions?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyAction }
}
export interface AnyModule {
  readonly id: string
  readonly requires?: readonly (AnyModule | AnyContract)[]
  readonly optional?: readonly (AnyModule | AnyContract)[]
  readonly provides?: readonly AnyContract[]
  readonly generates?: readonly GeneratorTemplate[]
  readonly entities?: { readonly [entity: string]: AnyEntity }
  readonly actions?: { readonly [name: string]: AnyAction }
  readonly contributes?: readonly AnyContribution[]
  readonly conditional?: readonly AnyConditional[]
}
/** Module values get a named type, so declaration emit references it instead of copying the structure. */
export type ModuleType<T extends AnyModule> = T

// ---- Module-level checks (applied by defineModuleBase in the DSL, where the data lives)
type DepIds<L> = L extends readonly (infer R)[] ? (R extends { readonly id: infer I extends string } ? I : never) : never
type RequiresOf<M> = M extends { readonly requires: infer L } ? DepIds<L> : never
type RefsOf<Path extends string, F> = { [K in keyof F]: F[K] extends { readonly ref: { readonly module: infer RM extends string } } ? `${Path}.${K & string} -> ${RM}` : never }[keyof F]
type RefTarget<S extends string> = S extends `${string} -> ${infer T}` ? T : never
type BadRefs<Refs extends string, Allowed extends string> = Refs extends unknown ? (RefTarget<Refs> extends Allowed ? never : Refs) : never
type EntityRefs<Path extends string, Es> = { [E in keyof Es]: Es[E] extends { readonly fields: infer F } ? RefsOf<`${Path}.${E & string}`, F> : never }[keyof Es]
type UnguardedOf<Path extends string, Es> = {
  [E in keyof Es]: Es[E] extends { readonly fields: infer F }
    ? { [K in keyof F]: F[K] extends { readonly flags: { readonly optional: true } } | { readonly flags: { readonly defaulted: true } } ? never : `${Path}.${E & string}.${K & string}` }[keyof F]
    : never
}[keyof Es]
/** A reference may target the module itself (own), a hard requirement, or, inside a contribution or conditional part, its target and `when` modules. */
type RefsOutsideRequirements<M extends AnyModule> =
  | (M extends { readonly entities: infer Es } ? BadRefs<EntityRefs<M['id'], Es>, RequiresOf<M>> : never)
  | (M extends { readonly conditional: readonly (infer Cd)[] } ? (Cd extends { readonly when: infer W; readonly entities: infer Es } ? BadRefs<EntityRefs<`${M['id']}[when]`, Es>, RequiresOf<M> | DepIds<W>> : never) : never)
  | (M extends { readonly contributes: readonly (infer C)[] }
      ? (C extends { readonly to: { readonly id: infer T extends string }; readonly entities: infer Es }
          ? BadRefs<EntityRefs<`${M['id']}->${T}`, Es>, RequiresOf<M> | T | (C extends { readonly when: infer W } ? DepIds<W> : never)>
          : never)
      : never)
/** Contributed and conditional fields must be optional or defaulted: rows are inserted while those parts are inactive. */
type UnguardedFields<M extends AnyModule> =
  | (M extends { readonly conditional: readonly (infer Cd)[] } ? (Cd extends { readonly entities: infer Es } ? UnguardedOf<`${M['id']}[when]`, Es> : never) : never)
  | (M extends { readonly contributes: readonly (infer C)[] } ? (C extends { readonly to: { readonly id: infer T extends string }; readonly entities: infer Es } ? UnguardedOf<`${M['id']}->${T}`, Es> : never) : never)
type ModuleChecks<M extends AnyModule> = Check<RefsOutsideRequirements<M>, 'refsOutsideRequirements'> & Check<UnguardedFields<M>, 'contributedFieldsNeedDefault'>

export declare function defineModule<const M extends AnyModule>(m: M & ModuleChecks<M>): M
```
