```ts
interface CommandBus {
  dispatch<R extends string>(ref: R, input: unknown, ctx: KernelInvocationContext, options?: { prefer?: 'sync' | 'async'; commandId?: string }): Promise<Outcome<unknown>>
}
interface QueryBus {
  ask<R extends string>(ref: R, input: unknown, ctx: KernelInvocationContext): Promise<Outcome<unknown>>
}
interface EventBus {
  /** Called inside the command's unit; events are durable at commit. */
  publish(events: readonly EventEnvelope[], unit: Unit): Promise<void>
  /** Inline reactions run in the same unit; async reactions become jobs through the reaction dispatcher. */
  subscribe(selector: EventSelector, consumer: EventConsumer, options: { timing: 'inline' | 'async'; id: string }): void
}
```

The buses are internal to the invoker, and their context parameter (`KernelInvocationContext`:
scope, principal, unit, causation and trace) is kernel-internal. A module never calls them: it
returns `invoke` and `enqueue` effects and drafts from `ctx.write` and `ctx.events`, yields `ask`
requests, and declares reactions; the interpreter turns those into bus calls (section 7.9.4).

### 9.4 Transactions and the event chain

A synchronous command runs in one unit on the namespace of its scope (section 14.2): insert the
pending receipt, load the target with its version, drive the decision and answer its requests,
buffer the events (expected version), evolve and store the state, let inline reactions decide,
perform the kernel effects (invocations in savepoints, jobs and timers in the same unit), complete
the receipt, assign positions at the commit tail, commit. The unit also commits the effect records
of the effect descriptions the handler returned, written as effect jobs, and the external effects
run after commit through their executors, as section 9.5.2 describes (phases 6 to 9 of section
7.9.4). The events table is the outbox: nothing outside the unit observes anything before commit,
and wake-ups are sent after commit (section 15.2.5). Section 15.1 specifies the event store within
these constraints: one stream per entity instance, expected-version appends, commit-ordered
positions per scope, a hybrid logical clock per event, the actor and command id in the envelope.

### 9.5 Asynchronous work: jobs, timers and schedules

Asynchronous commands, async reactions, durable timers, schedules and external effects run on one
job queue (gap G3; ADR 0015, amended by [ADR 0025](adr/0025-nodes-capacity-and-autoscaling.md)). The
kernel queue stores jobs in the namespace through the data adapter's job store (section 14.3.9), so
a job is enqueued in the unit that causes it on every adapter (a command's jobs in the command's
unit; async reactions in the reaction dispatcher's unit, section 7.7; schedule runs in the
schedule's tick, section 9.5.6), carries the scope's row-level security and needs no relay. Under decision 50a no worker runs code that performs effects:
an action job (an asynchronous command, reaction, timer, schedule or continuation) is invoked
through the invoker and returns events and effect descriptions; an external effect (an SMTP
dialogue, a Docker Engine request) becomes an effect job in the same unit, run by its declared
executor where the executor's capabilities are advertised (section 7.9.5). Section 21 places and
scales the work ([research/jobs-nodes-autoscaling.md](research/jobs-nodes-autoscaling.md)).

#### 9.5.1 Jobs and the queue interface

```ts
interface JobSpec {
  readonly queue: string                                      // 'reactions', 'commands', 'timers', 'schedules', 'effects' or a module queue
  readonly run:
    | { readonly action: string; readonly input: unknown }    // through the invoker
    | { readonly executor: string; readonly effect: string }  // an external effect: its executor and effect record (decision 50a)
  readonly scope: Scope
  readonly principal: PrincipalRef                            // re-resolved when the job runs (section 7.4)
  readonly causation: { readonly eventId?: string; readonly commandId?: string; readonly actor?: ActorRef }
  readonly build: { readonly id: string; readonly revision: number }   // the enqueuer's build (section 19.2)
  readonly apiVersion?: string                                // external callers: the input as sent, at this API version
  readonly runAt?: Temporal.Instant
  readonly priority?: 'high' | 'normal' | 'low'               // set by module code, never by input
  readonly cost?: number                                      // fair-share units; default 1
  readonly key?: { readonly value: string; readonly onConflict: 'keep' | 'replace' | 'coalesce' }
  readonly ordering?: 'none' | 'fifo-per-key'
  readonly group?: { readonly id: string; readonly concurrency?: number; readonly rate?: string; readonly scope?: 'namespace' | 'deployment' }
  readonly capability?: readonly string[]                     // effect jobs: the executor's (section 21.2)
  readonly retry?: { readonly limit?: number; readonly delays: 'exponential' | readonly string[]; readonly maxDelay?: string; readonly giveUpAfter?: string }
  readonly heartbeatSeconds?: number                          // lease renewal, default 10; a lease lasts three
  readonly expireInSeconds?: number                           // the longest one attempt may run
  readonly deadLetter?: string
}
interface JobQueue {
  readonly capabilities: QueueCapabilities                    // keys, groups, fifoPerKey, heartbeat, schedules, fairLanes
  enqueue(job: JobSpec, unit: Unit): Promise<JobId>
  cancel(queue: string, key: string, unit: Unit): Promise<number>
  work(queue: string, handler: (job: Job) => Promise<void>, options: { readonly slots: number; readonly capabilitySets: readonly string[]; readonly revision: number }): Promise<{ drain(deadline: Temporal.Instant): Promise<number> }>
  schedule(id: string, expression: string, job: Omit<JobSpec, 'runAt' | 'scope' | 'principal'>, fanOut: 'backend' | 'each-tenant'): Promise<void>
  stats(selector: { readonly queue?: string; readonly backendId?: string }): Promise<readonly WorkClassStats[]>   // section 21.4
  explain(job: JobId): Promise<JobExplanation>                // why it waits: due time, cap, group, rate, key, capability, revision
}

// nodes.node.heartbeat (section 17.3.4), a kernel effect (section 7.9.5): the timer's job row commits in this
// unit and fires under the module's service principal; cancelTimer(key) is the inverse.
return {
  events: [ctx.events.heartbeat({ active: input.active })],
  effects: [setTimer({ key: `node-offline:${input.id}`, after: '45s', invoke: markOffline, input: { id: input.id } })],
}
export const refreshPublicAddressSchedule = defineSchedule(dnsBase, { every: '5m', invoke: refreshPublicAddress, scope: 'each-tenant', jitter: '30s' })
// modules/dns/src/module.generated.ts: schedules: { refreshPublicAddress: refreshPublicAddressSchedule }   (the key, from the file name, is the schedule id; schedules contribute to the core's `schedules` extension point)
// An effect executor's job options (section 7.9.5): the effect is its second argument, and its retries are
// mechanical; the five-day delivery schedule belongs to the submission's state machine (section 17.4.7).
export const smtpDeliverExecutor = defineEffectExecutor(mailDeliveryBase, smtpDeliver, {
  queue: 'mail-delivery',
  capability: ({ config }) => (config.relay ? [] : ['smtp-out']),
  group: ({ config, input }) => ({ id: `mx:${input.domain}`, concurrency: config.connectionsPerDomain, rate: '60/1m' }),
  retry: { delays: ['30s', '2m'], giveUpAfter: 'PT10M' },     // infrastructure failures only; SMTP replies are output
  run: (input, ctx) => deliverOverSmtp(input, ctx),           // imperative: the SMTP dialogue through the egress service (src/executors/lib/)
})
```

Asynchronous actions and async reactions set the same job options, `capability` apart (section 7.3).

#### 9.5.2 Where jobs live

- Per namespace: `kw_jobs` (open jobs: `scheduled`, `available`, `waiting`, `running`);
  `kw_job_lanes`, one row per scope, queue, capability set and priority class (cap, weight, `taken`,
  virtual time); `kw_job_lane_counts`, an `enqueued` and a `done` counter per lane; `kw_job_groups`
  (concurrency, token bucket, blocked-until); `kw_job_history` (outcome, attempts, timings and
  error, without input, seven days). Dead letters keep their input until replayed or discarded.
- Lane state is split by writer: what makes a job available (an enqueue tail, a promotion, a FIFO
  release) moves `enqueued`, takes move `taken` and the virtual time, completions `done`; groups
  count the same way. Takes lock only lane rows, so an enqueue burst never makes takers skip a lane,
  and a stale `done` only lowers a lane's room.
- A job due now is `available` and counted at its cause's commit tail, beside the scope's position
  counter (section 15.1.4); a later `runAt` (timers, retries, delayed sends) stays `scheduled` until
  the queue's fetcher promotes it, so lanes count only due work. FIFO followers are `waiting`;
  `replace` and `coalesce` act on a pending job of the same key and lane.
- Completion is a statement of the job's unit, conditional on its lease: success removes the row and
  writes history, a retryable failure schedules the next attempt, and the key's next `waiting` job
  becomes `available`.
- A job's unit runs the kernel's loads, then writes events, effect records, receipt and completion
  at its tail (section 7.9.4). No handler waits on the network inside a unit, so no long write
  transaction pins PostgreSQL's MVCC horizon. Database effects commit with the completion,
  effectively once; effect jobs run after commit, at least once, passing the effect id as
  idempotency key where the destination accepts one. Each outcome is recorded on its effect record,
  linked to its cause, and passed to the continuation the description names.

The queue tables, as the write-path spike built and measured them on PostgreSQL 18.6 (2026-11-04):

```sql
-- PostgreSQL, per namespace; MySQL and SQLite use the same columns with their own types (section 14.5.1). Every table
-- has forced row-level security over scope_id that also admits namespace-scope units (the take, section 9.5.3).
create table <root>.kw_job_lanes (
  id              bigint          generated always as identity primary key,
  scope_id        uuid            not null,             -- tenant id, or backend id
  queue           text            not null,
  capability_set  text            not null,             -- the capability set the lane's jobs need (section 21.2)
  priority        smallint        not null,             -- the class: high, normal, low
  cap             integer         not null,             -- running jobs at most (section 9.5.5)
  weight          integer         not null,             -- the scope's share
  taken           bigint          not null default 0,   -- written by takes only
  vtime           double precision not null default 0,  -- virtual time; written by takes only
  unique (queue, capability_set, scope_id, priority)
);
create table <root>.kw_job_lane_counts (
  lane_id         bigint          not null references <root>.kw_job_lanes (id),
  kind            text            not null check (kind in ('enqueued', 'done')),
  scope_id        uuid            not null,             -- the lane's scope, the row-level security key (below)
  value           bigint          not null default 0,   -- written by enqueue tails, promotions, FIFO releases, completions
  primary key (lane_id, kind)
);
create table <root>.kw_job_groups (
  id              text            primary key,          -- 'mx:example.com', 'backend:<id>'
  concurrency     integer,
  running         integer         not null default 0,
  blocked_until   timestamptz                           -- rate_limited with retryAfter, or the rate's next token
);
create table <root>.kw_jobs (
  id              bigint          generated always as identity primary key,
  scope_id        uuid            not null,
  lane_id         bigint          not null,
  queue           text            not null,
  state           text            not null check (state in ('scheduled', 'available', 'waiting', 'running')),
  run_at          timestamptz     not null default now(),
  revision        integer         not null,             -- the enqueuer's build revision (section 19.2)
  group_id        text,
  key             text,
  cost            integer         not null default 1,   -- fair-share units
  input           jsonb           not null,             -- the run: action and input, or executor and effect id
  worker          text,                                 -- worker, attempt and lease: the running attempt (section 9.5.4)
  attempt         integer         not null default 0,
  lease_until     timestamptz
);
create index kw_jobs_take on <root>.kw_jobs (lane_id, run_at, id) where state = 'available';
```

- `kw_job_lane_counts` carries the lane's scope: the enqueue bump runs in the causing tenant's unit
  under forced row-level security, and an update of a counter row the unit cannot see matches zero
  rows without an error, so a counter row without the scope would silently stop counting (the
  spike's first run did).
- These are the columns the take, the lane counters and the completions use. The rest of
  `JobSpec` (principal reference, causation, retry and lease options, dead-letter target) adds
  columns to `kw_jobs` in M1; groups, rates and FIFO keys were not exercised by the spike, so the
  group table's row-level security is settled with them, under the rule the lane counters follow.

#### 9.5.3 The fair take

```sql
-- PostgreSQL (MySQL: the same steps in two statements); a kernel namespace-scope unit only the queue tables'
-- policies admit. $sets: capability sets this process satisfies; $vmin: the least virtual time of the lanes with
-- available work, read in the take's unit before this statement; $lanes: lanes to lock, by default the batch size.
with picked as (
  select l.id, l.cap - (l.taken - d.value) as room from kw_job_lanes l
  join kw_job_lane_counts e on e.lane_id = l.id and e.kind = 'enqueued'   -- read, never locked
  join kw_job_lane_counts d on d.lane_id = l.id and d.kind = 'done'
  where l.queue = $queue and l.capability_set = any($sets) and e.value > l.taken and l.taken - d.value < l.cap
  order by l.priority, (l.taken - d.value) / l.weight, greatest(l.vtime, $vmin)   -- class, load per share, round robin
  limit $lanes
  for update of l skip locked
), share as (select greatest(1, ceil($batch::numeric / nullif(count(*), 0))) as n from picked)
select j.* from picked p cross join share s cross join lateral (
  select * from kw_jobs j
  where j.lane_id = p.id and j.state = 'available' and j.revision <= $revision
    and not exists (select 1 from kw_job_groups g where g.id = j.group_id and g.blocked_until > now())
  order by j.run_at, j.id
  limit least(p.room, s.n)
  for update skip locked) j;
-- Same transaction: jobs become 'running' with (worker, attempt, lease); lanes add the jobs to `taken` and cost / weight
-- to `vtime` (lifted to $vmin first); group rows are locked in id order and checked; a job over its limit goes back.
```

- Order: strict priority classes; then the least running work per unit of weight, which counts long
  jobs as load (Temporal's task-queue fairness weighs dispatches only); then virtual time, a
  weighted round robin (stride scheduling). Lifting a lane to `$vmin` means idleness earns no
  credit.
- Takers lock different lanes, then different jobs, sharing a batch over the lanes picked. Group
  rows serialise only takes of one group; counting under that lock replaces the count inside the
  take statement, which raced at `READ COMMITTED`.
- `$vmin` is the least virtual time of the lanes of the queue and capability sets that have
  available work (`enqueued > taken`), read in the take's unit; an idle lane that becomes busy is
  lifted to it.
- `$lanes` defaults to the take's batch size and is configurable per queue
  (`queues.<q>.takeLanes`). A take locks every lane it may use for the whole take unit with `skip
  locked`, so concurrent takers on few lanes come back empty while work is available: the
  write-path spike saw 44 to 59 % empty takes on one lane, 46 to 56 % on ten lanes with batches of
  10 or 50, and 9 % on 100 lanes with batches of 50. The take therefore reports the lanes it skipped
  as locked separately from "no work", and the fetcher acts on the difference (section 9.5.6).
- Known limit: the lane pick sorts every eligible lane, because the order by load per weight and
  virtual time cannot use an index. The take statement's p95 grew from 1.6 to 1.9 ms (1 to 10
  lanes) to 2.1 to 2.2 ms (100 lanes) and 4.3 to 4.8 ms (1,000 lanes). Lanes are per scope, queue,
  capability set and priority, so a placement with thousands of tenants needs a bounded candidate
  set (roadmap M5). Lane caps held: 0 of 325 samples over cap.
- The statement runs unmodified on PostgreSQL 18 (checked on 18.6): `limit least(p.room, s.n)`
  accepts the numeric share.
- SQLite, PGlite and the in-memory adapter (the conformance oracle) run the same steps under their
  single writer.

#### 9.5.4 Retries, leases and failures

- Retries follow the error taxonomy, in which executors report too: `unavailable`, `rate_limited`
  (honouring `retryAfter`, and blocking the job's group until then) and `conflict` with `retryable`
  are retried by the job's policy, with full jitter; every other kind fails the job at once. Domain
  waits (an image that does not exist yet, a deferred mail delivery) are state machines with timers,
  not job retries (section 7.9.5, decision point 75).
- The worker renews its running jobs' leases every `heartbeatSeconds`, one statement per namespace;
  a lease lasts three heartbeats. The next take reclaims an expired one: the job returns to
  `available`, the attempt counted as `unavailable`, `core.job_lease_lost`. Renewal and completion
  are conditional on (worker, attempt), so a paused or partitioned attempt fails at its completion
  statement and rolls back its own unit.
- Three consecutive lost leases make a job a dead letter, so a poison job cannot take the fleet down
  one process at a time. `expireInSeconds` aborts an attempt through its abort signal with
  `core.timeout` (retryable).
- Dead letters are a metric, an alert and a `keelwerk doctor` line; `keelwerk jobs
  replay|discard` handles them.

#### 9.5.5 Limits, priorities and backpressure

The job side of the quota model (section 12.2):

| Limit | Configured | Enforced | When reached |
|---|---|---|---|
| running jobs per tenant and queue (the lane's cap) | `queues.<q>.running` (a number or a share of live slots), per backend with tenant overrides | the take | jobs wait |
| running jobs per backend and queue | `core.quota.set` per backend | an implicit group `backend:<id>` | jobs wait |
| queued jobs per tenant and queue | `queues.<q>.queued`, default 10,000; backend and tenant overrides | the enqueue's commit tail | commands: `rate_limited` (`core.queue_full`, `retryAfter`); the reaction dispatcher pauses the scope until the lane is below 90 percent; timers and schedules are bounded by keys |
| share | weight per backend and tenant, default 1, operator only | the take's order | |
| priority | module code: `high` for liveness timers, `low` for bulk work | the take's order | lower classes wait; their age drives the scaler |
| destination concurrency and rate | `group` options of executors and actions, from module configuration | the take, under the group's row lock; `scope: 'deployment'` groups (M5) through control-store permits | jobs wait for a slot or a token |
| process slots | `processes.<name>.slots` (section 21.1) | the worker | |

Without a cap the take is work-conserving: one tenant may fill idle slots, and the fair order gives
the next free one to the least-served lane. Tenants cannot raise their own weight or caps (gap G10
configuration cannot reach them); `keelwerk jobs lanes` and `keelwerk doctor` show them.

#### 9.5.6 Workers, scopes and schedules

- Workers run only in processes with the `work` role, for the queues their named process slots, and
  take effect jobs only for executors whose capabilities the process advertises (section 21.2). One
  fetcher per queue promotes due jobs and takes batches for the slots, woken after commit by the
  notifier of section 14.3.7 (channel `kw_jobs`) and by a jittered poll every second. A take that
  skipped locked lanes is not "no work": a fetcher that saw skipped lanes takes again at once,
  after a short jitter, instead of waiting for the next wake-up or the poll (section 9.5.3). With
  per-tenant namespaces (M5), wake-ups pass through the control store, and each process sweeps the
  namespaces that rendezvous hashing over the live registry gives it.
- An action job runs through the invoker after the worker sets the scope and resolves the principal,
  so the gate and the item check run again against current state. An effect job runs its executor
  outside any unit; one short unit then records the outcome, enqueues the continuation (under the
  module's service principal) and completes the job.
- `each-tenant` schedules enumerate the tenants of the backends whose app contains the module and
  enqueue one job per tenant, with group concurrency per backend and the schedule's jitter; at most
  one run per tick and scope exists, however many processes run. Schedules run under the module's
  service principal with the schedule id as the reason.

#### 9.5.7 Implementations and the upgrade path

Decision point 6 was re-examined for many nodes against four families (research note): this
kernel queue; a PostgreSQL queue library (pg-boss 12.38.0); a broker (NATS JetStream or Redis
Streams) behind `JobQueue`; a durable execution engine. Jens decided for the kernel queue on
2026-10-26 (decision 6a). Only the kernel queue gives transactional enqueue on every adapter, row-level
security on payloads and one semantics in development, tests and production. pg-boss now has groups,
FIFO per key, heartbeats, Kysely enqueue and PGlite, but no MySQL, SQLite or in-memory store, no
scope predicate and no fair shares. Brokers need an outbox relay and carry payloads out of the
database; engines keep a second record of every step beside the event log, which records every
effect under decision 50a. The kernel queue stays.

- Ceiling: graphile-worker 0.18's benchmark reaches about 15,600 trivial jobs per second unbatched
  and 184,000 batched on one machine; Hatchet's maintainers reported that bursts above 5,000 tasks
  per second (about 25,000 transactions) outgrew a plain `SKIP LOCKED` queue. The ceiling is per
  placement. The write-path spike measured the take with four takers and trivial handlers on
  PostgreSQL 18.6 (2026-11-04): 417 to 718 jobs per second at batch 1, 4,020 to 5,500 at batch 10
  and 16,067 to 20,899 at batch 50, with completions batched per take. Each job completes in its
  own unit (section 9.5.2), so a placement's job rate is bounded by its unit rate (1,757 to 2,519
  units per second across eight tenants in the same environment), not by the take; the default take
  batch is 10. M2 measures again with real handlers. The proof platforms need well under 10 jobs
  per second.
- Upgrade path, keeping `JobQueue`, `JobStore`, `JobSpec` and the conformance suite: first more
  placements, partitioned `kw_jobs` and a transaction-mode pooler; then a dispatch tier, where
  leased fetchers per namespace and queue take fair batches and publish job ids on NATS JetStream
  work-queue subjects, and workers claim them by id with the same conditional statements. The broker
  carries ids only, so no tenant payload leaves the namespace and the broker needs no backup.
- A `queue-pg` entry on pg-boss remains possible for PostgreSQL-only deployments, not planned.

### 9.6 Live updates

```ts
interface ChangeFeed {
  /** Events after a position for one scope; reads committed events through read-only units. */
  read(scope: Scope, after: StateToken | null, selector: EventSelector): AsyncIterable<EventEnvelope>
  /** Wake-ups, never data: something may have been committed in this scope (section 15.2.5). */
  wake(scope: Scope): AsyncIterable<void>
}
interface LiveHub {
  entity<Row>(session: InvocationSession, entity: string, input: WatchInput<unknown>, resume?: StateToken): AsyncIterable<LiveFrame<EntityChange<Row>>>
  // pokes, stream records and topics: section 15.4.11
}
```

The live module subscribes to the change feed, re-evaluates the principal's plan per event
(section 8.4), masks fields and emits frames with stream tokens (section 15.4). Carriers (SSE
first, WebSocket second) are transports (sections 15.4.6 and 15.4.7); the poke-then-pull shape of
the client protocol is section 15.2.5. "Live updates on everything" follows from every entity
producing events or transient change records and from the generated `watch` on every entity.

### 9.7 Multi-tenancy in execution

Jobs, events, receipts and subscriptions carry the scope; a worker sets the scope and resolves the
principal from the job before any code runs; placements are resolved per scope, so two tenants on
different databases never share a transaction; positions are counted per scope, so one tenant's
writes never queue behind another's (section 15.1.4); quotas are enforced at `admit` and by lane
caps and queued caps per tenant and queue (sections 9.5.5 and 12.2).

## 10. Errors

One closed taxonomy, defined in core and serialised by each transport (the mapping table is in
section 16.4.6):

| Kind | Meaning | Retryable |
|---|---|---|
| `validation` | input or output does not match its schema; carries Standard Schema `issues` | no |
| `unauthenticated` | a principal is required and none was resolved, or presented credentials are invalid | no |
| `forbidden` | the gate, the item check or a write outside the module boundary was denied; carries rule ids and reason | no |
| `not_found` | scope, entity row or ids absent, or a target outside the plan | no |
| `conflict` | version or state mismatch, uniqueness, idempotency fingerprint mismatch, command in progress | sometimes (`retryable` set per case) |
| `rate_limited` | admission or a write denied by a rate or a quota (section 12.2) | yes for rates, with `retryAfter`; no for an exhausted quota (code `core.quota_exceeded`) |
| `not_implemented` | module or action not part of this backend's app | no |
| `unavailable` | backend suspended, placement unreachable, shutting down, timeout | yes |
| `unsupported` | a plan the field model does not allow (an operator a personal field did not declare, a restricted kind), a bounded scan past its limit, or a raw-SQL dialect the placement lacks; never a capability the adapter lacks, which the kernel provides (section 14.3.3) | no |
| `internal` | anything undeclared; message redacted outside development | no |

```ts
class KeelwerkError extends Error {
  readonly kind: ErrorKind
  readonly code: string                  // stable, module-prefixed: 'accounts.email_taken'
  readonly issues?: readonly { path: readonly PropertyKey[]; message: string }[]
  readonly details?: unknown             // typed by the ErrorSpec's data schema
  readonly retryable: boolean
  readonly retryAfter?: number           // seconds
  readonly rules?: readonly { id: string; effect: 'allow' | 'deny' }[]
}
const emailTaken = defineError('accounts.email_taken', { kind: 'conflict', data: shape({ email: field.string() }), message: 'This e-mail address is already in use.' })

/** The one serialised form, used by every transport, the sync protocol and receipts. */
declare function toWire(error: KeelwerkError, audience: 'public' | 'operator' | 'development'): WireError
```

`toWire` decides once what an audience sees: operator principals and development get rule ids and
unredacted `internal` messages; everyone else gets the code, the kind, the message and the deny
reason (`WireError`, section 16.4.6). The core registers its own codes: `core.forbidden`,
`core.version_mismatch`, `core.state_mismatch`, `core.idempotency_mismatch`,
`core.command_in_progress`, `core.cursor_mismatch`, `core.malformed_request`,
`core.payload_too_large`, `core.csrf`, `core.token_scope_mismatch`, `core.live_unavailable`,
`core.quota_exceeded` and `core.timeout`. A command that exceeds its timeout is rolled back and reported as `unavailable`
with code `core.timeout`, retryable under the same command id.

Versioning, rollouts and flags add codes within the same kinds (section 18.8):
`core.api_version_invalid` and `core.api_version_unknown` (`validation`), `core.api_version_retired`
and `core.protocol_retired` (`not_found`), `core.rollout_in_progress` and `core.feature_suspended`
(`unavailable`), `core.version_change_failed` (`internal`), `core.feature_disabled` (`forbidden`)
and `core.rollout_not_finalized` (`conflict`). The shape-stage row check fails with
`core.row_outside_plan` (`internal`, section 8.4), and an `asOf` read before a stream's compaction
horizon with `core.history_compacted` (`not_found`, section 14.7.1). The job queue adds
`core.queue_full` (`rate_limited` with `retryAfter`, section 9.5.5), `core.job_lease_lost` (an
attempt counted as `unavailable`, section 9.5.4) and `core.capability_unplaceable` (`unsupported`,
section 21.2); queries over encrypted personal fields add `core.personal_operator`,
`core.personal_needle_short` and `core.scan_limit` (all `unsupported`, section 14.7.9). The effect
interpreter adds `core.effect_in_unit` (an inline effect requested inside the unit) and
`core.reaction_depth` (inline reactions nested deeper than 8), both `internal`, and
`core.effect_outcome_unknown` (an effect settled as `abandoned`, whose destination may have acted)
and `core.effect_deadline` (an external effect settled as `failed` at its deadline), both
`unavailable`, not retried by an executor and handed to the continuation as the outcome's error
(section 7.9). The taxonomy itself is unchanged.

Declared errors become typed unions in GraphQL, typed results of `attempt` in the typed client,
documented responses in OpenAPI and exit codes in the CLI. Error codes are part of the public
contract and are never reused.

## 11. Observability

- Tracing and metrics through OpenTelemetry (`@opentelemetry/api` 1.9.1; SDK 2.x in the
  deployment package). The invoker opens one span per invocation with attributes
  `keelwerk.app`, `.backend`, `.tenant`, `.module`, `.entity`, `.action`, `.kind`,
  `.transport`, `.execution`, `.outcome`, `.api_version`, `.build` (build id and revision) and
  `.flags` (the flags read, with variant and reason) and the matched rule ids; transports, the data layer and
  the queue add child spans; W3C `traceparent` is propagated in and out and stored in every event
  envelope, so live deliveries, async reactions and webhooks link back to the command that caused
  them. Section 16.11 adds the interface layer's spans and metrics.
- Metrics: invocations and durations by action and outcome, job queue depth, age and dead letters
  (with the job and scaling metrics of section 21.9: `keelwerk.jobs.due`, `.oldest_due`,
  `.lanes.capped`, `.unplaceable`, `.wait`, `.run`, `.take.duration` and `.outcomes` by kind and
  outcome, and `keelwerk.slots`, `.processes`, `.connections.reserved` and `.scaler.desired` per
  named process), event append rate per namespace, projection and change-feed lag, live
  subscriptions, per-tenant quota usage (section 12.2), and `keelwerk.flags.evaluations` by flag,
  variant and reason.
- API usage counters: requests per day, backend, tenant, API version and transport, per action or
  field for deprecated items, flushed at `complete` into `core.apiUsage` (section 18.5).
- Logs are structured, carry the scope ids and request id, and go through `ctx.log`; no module
  writes to `console`. The default `Logger` implementation in the deployment package is pino
  10.4.0 writing JSON lines to standard output; the core depends only on the `Logger` interface.
  `.personal()`, secret, verifier and hidden values are redacted in logs, traces and decision logs.
- The decision log (section 8.6) and the command receipts give an audit trail of who did what;
  receipts record the transport, the remote address after trusted-proxy rules and the user agent
  (gap G12); the chain itself is the audit trail of what changed. An `audit` module can persist
  them.
- Health: `app.health` (liveness) and `app.ready` (readiness: control store, placements, queue)
  are app-level actions every transport exposes; `keelwerk doctor` runs them from the CLI.
- Development: the invoker can emit a per-invocation explanation (stages, timings, plan, matched
  rules) when `KEELWERK_EXPLAIN=1`.

## 12. Multi-tenancy and one deployment

### 12.1 What each layer does

The brief makes this cross-cutting; this section collects the statements of each layer.

| Layer | How it handles backends and tenants |
|---|---|
| Kernel | Control entities `core.backend`, `core.tenant`, `core.domain`, `core.placement` and `core.namespace` (tenancy `deployment`) and the scope directory; API version pins per backend, tenant and credential (section 18.3); the process registry `core.process` (section 19.1); `core.commandReceipt` with tenancy `invocation` (rows carry their command's scope); operator actions with `scope: 'deployment'`; runtime creation without restart; per-backend module configuration and per-tenant overrides; `onBackendCreated` and `onTenantCreated` hooks for provisioning; a change feed over the control store keeps every process's directory current. |
| Pipeline | `resolveScope` runs first on every request or connection, followed by `resolvePrincipal` and `resolveVersion`, using the deployment-ordered tenant resolvers (host name, path prefix, header, scope key from tokens, receivers and listeners such as the SMTP recipient domain); the same resolvers serve every transport, the CLI and non-HTTP listeners; actions declare the scope level they accept and the gate rejects a mismatch. |
| Data layer | Placement per tenant (shared tables with a tenant key, schema per tenant, database per tenant, or a different adapter), chosen at tenant creation and changeable by a move; the adapter injects the scope predicate into every statement; PostgreSQL row-level security as a backstop; positions, consumer checkpoints and usage counters per scope; migrations per namespace; application code never sees the strategy (section 14.9), nor the adapter's capabilities: what an adapter lacks the kernel provides at a cost `keelwerk doctor` reports, so a tenant can be placed on any adapter, a module's declared raw-SQL dialect being the one condition (section 14.3.3, brief addendum 5). |
| Authorization | Scope is applied before and outside policies (section 8.8); the operator principal and explicit, logged tenant entry; no rule can widen a scope. |
| Execution | Jobs, events, receipts, subscriptions and checkpoints carry the scope; workers adopt it and resolve the principal again before running; quotas, and lane caps and queued caps per tenant and queue (sections 9.7 and 12.2). |
| Transports | Fill the carrier and never resolve tenants themselves; the HTTP host routes by the resolved app; cookies, CORS and CSRF checks follow the tenant's origins; generated documents are per app, served per backend (section 16.12). |
| CLI | A profile names a deployment, a backend and a tenant (or the deployment level for operator work); the token in the profile is resolved like any other principal; every command accepts `--backend` and `--tenant` overrides; operator commands create backends and tenants at runtime. |
| Secrets and configuration | Per backend with per-tenant overrides, sealed by the key service under backend and tenant keys, never in the app code or the environment of a tenant (section 5.7). |
| Isolation guarantee | A tenant principal reaches only its own tenant's data and the backend-level data of its own backend, through backend-scope actions that cannot touch tenant entities; deployment-scope actions exist only at the operator endpoint; every operator entry into a tenant is logged (sections 8.8 and 12.3). |

### 12.2 Quotas

The brief lists quotas among the dimensions in which tenants are isolated. The model:

| Dimension | Configured | Counted | Enforced |
|---|---|---|---|
| request rate (per tenant, per principal, per action class) | `core` quota configuration per backend, with tenant overrides | token buckets in the tenant's namespace, refilled by time; each process takes a small allowance at a time so the shared row is touched rarely | `admit`: `rate_limited` with `retryAfter` |
| concurrent invocations per tenant | as above | per process, reconciled through leases in the control store | `admit` |
| storage: rows, event bytes and blob bytes per tenant | as above; modules may declare finer dimensions (`mail-store`'s bytes per mail account) | usage counters per scope, updated in the commit tail of the unit that changes them (blob bytes when a blob is adopted or purged) | the commit tail: `rate_limited` with code `core.quota_exceeded`, not retryable |
| running jobs per tenant and queue | `queues.<q>.running` per backend, with tenant overrides (section 9.5.5) | the lane's `taken` and `done` counters | the take, by the lane's cap: excess jobs wait |
| queued jobs per tenant and queue | `queues.<q>.queued` (default 10,000), with backend and tenant overrides | the lane counters (section 9.5.2) | the enqueue's commit tail: `rate_limited` with code `core.queue_full` and `retryAfter` |
| share of a queue | a weight per backend and tenant (default 1), operator only | the lane's virtual time | the take's order |
| live subscriptions and connections per tenant | as above | deployment-wide, through leases in the control store; per-process counters for the fast path | `admit` at subscribe time |

- Quota dimensions are declared like configuration (`quotas: { storageBytes: quota.bytes().default('10GiB') }`
  on a module or on the core) and changed through operator actions (`core.quota.set`), or through
  tenant-editable configuration where a backend allows it.
- Usage counters are maintained per scope inside the namespace, so they commit with the data they
  count; the counters of one tenant never contend with another tenant's, because positions and
  counters are both per scope (section 15.1.4).
- Usage is a metric per tenant and dimension; `keelwerk doctor` lists tenants above 80 percent
  of a limit.

### 12.3 Scope boundaries, cross-scope work and outbound connections

- A unit is opened for one scope. A backend-scope or deployment-scope unit refuses tenant-tenancy
  entities: plan compilation fails with `unsupported`, and PostgreSQL row-level security denies
  the statement as well. Cross-tenant work happens only in kernel fan-out, one tenant-scope unit
  per tenant (schedules with `each-tenant`, retention, migrations of data). The adversarial
  isolation suite covers these cases (section 14.10).
- A tenant command reads backend-level entities in a separate read-only snapshot, never inside its
  own transaction, whether or not the backend's home namespace is co-located with the tenant's.
  A command of another scope runs only after commit, through an `enqueue` effect; no receipt
  returns to the decision, which names the command id (`enqueue(action, input, { commandId })`)
  when someone must follow it (section 7.9.5). Snapshot and atomicity semantics are therefore the
  same on every placement.
- Effect executors that connect to hosts named by tenants or by DNS (MX targets, MTA-STS policy
  hosts, outbound webhooks) use the core's egress service (`ctx.egress.fetch`, `ctx.egress.connect`
  of the executor context, section 7.9.5); handlers connect nowhere. The egress service resolves the
  name, refuses loopback, private (RFC 1918 and RFC 4193), link-local and other special-purpose
  addresses unless the deployment allowlists them, pins the checked address for the connection, and
  records the destination on the span. A home installation that hosts PostgreSQL, Caddy's admin API
  and other services on its LAN is otherwise one tenant-supplied host name away from them.

## 13. Types and toolchain

### 13.1 Live types and generated files

The types of what is in the database are inferred from the entity definitions through
`AppEntities<App>` and the module-local types of section 7.6; the editor, `tsc`, Biome and Vitest
see the same types, and no row type is ever generated. A TypeScript language-service plugin is
not used: plugins never run under `tsc`, and TypeScript 7.0 ships no plugin API (research:
data-layer.md section 6, interfaces-and-devx.md section 5.4).

Two kinds of TypeScript file are generated, both committed, both rewritten by the dev server
(`keelwerk dev`) on every change and both checked by `tsc` like hand-written code:

- each module's manifest, `src/module.generated.ts`: the module literal that mounts every part of
  the module's directories under the reference its path gives, and the module's package entry
  (decision 59b of 2026-10-28, section 23.5);
- next to each app, `keelwerk.generated.ts`, which re-exports `AppEntities`, `Row`, `ActionRef`,
  `AppActionTree` and the typed client for that app, so application code imports from one place
  and the app-level fold is instantiated once (section 13.7). Module packages never import it:
  their handler types are module-local.

`keelwerk generate --check` fails CI when either kind, the migrations, the OpenAPI document, the
SDL or the CLI manifest drift from the definitions. Tables the framework does not own are described
by entity definitions that `keelwerk db introspect` writes (section 14.8.4), so there is one type
mechanism; their drift against the live catalogue is checked at `connect`, in `keelwerk dev` and
by `keelwerk db introspect --check`.

### 13.2 Toolchain

| Tool | Version checked (2026-10-08 to 2026-10-28) | Role |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript | 7.0.2 (builds and checks; still the latest on 2026-10-28, with `lib.es2025` and `lib.esnext.temporal` bundled); 6.0.3 pinned only for tools that need the compiler API; 5.9.3 used for cross-checks | `tsc -b` with project references |
| Node.js | 26 (26.12.1 of 2026-10-21; promotion to LTS due in the last week of October 2026; checked by the lead on 2026-10-27) | runs `.ts` sources directly through type stripping; ships `Temporal` natively, so no polyfill (decision 19b); `node:crypto` provides Argon2id and AES-256-GCM |
| `@types/node` | 26.6.5 (2026-10-09, checked 2026-10-28) | the Node 26 declarations that `"types": ["node"]` loads |
| pnpm | 11.21.0 locally | workspace |
| Biome | 2.5.15 | the only formatter and linter |
| Vitest | 5.0.3 with `--typecheck`; expect-type 1.4.0 | unit, integration and type tests |
| @ark/attest | 0.57.0 (alpha; needs TypeScript 6) | instantiation budgets on the composition types |
| OpenTelemetry | api 1.9.1, SDK 2.x | section 11 |

Compiler options are in section 13.3. Consequences the DSL respects: no enums, no namespaces, no
parameter properties, no decorators; relative imports carry `.ts`.

**Baseline policy** (decision 28a, raised on 2026-10-27): the latest major of TypeScript and of
Node, always; the baseline follows each new major, and backfills or polyfills exist only for what
the baseline lacks, never as a lower target. Today the baseline is TypeScript 7 and Node 26. Every
package declares `"engines": { "node": ">=26" }`, CI runs on Node 26 only (the matrix has one
runtime entry), and the deployment image (the `keelwerk` container of section 17.5.2) is built on
a Node 26 base image. Node 26 ships `Temporal`, so instants are `Temporal.Instant` from the start
with no polyfill (decision 19b, section 6.4). The checks this document records on Node 24.21.0
(sections 13.4, 14.3.7, 14.7.9.3 and 17.2.2, Appendix B) were made before the baseline moved; the
M0 spike runs them again on Node 26 and records the results here.

### 13.3 TypeScript configuration and project references

`tsconfig.base.json`, shared by every package:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2025",
    "lib": ["es2025", "esnext.temporal"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "types": ["node"],
    "strict": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "customConditions": ["@keelwerk/source"],
    "composite": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "sourceMap": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
```

- `target` and `lib` follow the newest yearly edition the baseline runs, `es2025` on Node 26, and
  `lib` adds `esnext.temporal`, the `Temporal` declarations TypeScript 7.0.2 bundles
  (`lib.esnext.temporal.d.ts`, checked in an installed 7.0.2 on 2026-10-28), because `Temporal` is
  not yet part of a yearly library.
- Every package's `tsconfig.json` extends it and sets `rootDir: "src"` and `outDir: "dist"`
  explicitly (TypeScript 6 and 7 require an explicit `rootDir` when the common source directory
  differs, error TS5011), lists its `references`, and excludes tests.
- `isolatedDeclarations` is enabled only in packages whose exports are explicitly typed (core
  internals, adapters, the client, the CLI). It cannot be enabled in packages that export DSL values
  (modules, apps, transport modules, examples): TypeScript 7.0.2 rejects `export const accounts =
  defineModule(...)` with TS9010 and TS9013, because the type comes from inference (Appendix B);
  the composition-types spike counted 41 such errors (TS9010, TS9013, TS9016, TS9017) in one
  synthetic module package. The named-type pattern of section 4.1 keeps the inference and still
  needs the full checker for declaration emit.
- The core compiles with `isolatedDeclarations` on, so the core module's own value cannot use the
  named-type pattern, which needs an inferred type and fails there with TS9010: its base and module
  types are written by hand (`CoreBase`, `Core`; found by the composition-types spike,
  2026-11-04).
- The root `tsconfig.json` is a solution file (`"files": []` and the references of every package);
  `tsc -b` builds the graph with TypeScript 7.0.2.
- Unit and type tests live next to sources (`*.test.ts`, `*.test-d.ts`); integration tests live in
  each package's `test/` directory (section 23.8). Each package has a `tsconfig.test.json` (no
  emit, includes both, references the package), which Vitest's type checker uses; `tsconfig.json`
  excludes them.

### 13.4 Workspace packages from source

Workspace packages are consumed as TypeScript source in development and as JavaScript when
published, through one export condition:

```json
{
  "name": "@keelwerk/core",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": { "@keelwerk/source": "./src/index.ts", "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" },
    "./wire": { "@keelwerk/source": "./src/wire/index.ts", "types": "./dist/wire/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/wire/index.js" }
  },
  "publishConfig": {
    "exports": {
      ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" },
      "./wire": { "types": "./dist/wire/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/wire/index.js" }
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"]
}
```

- `keelwerk dev` runs Node with `--conditions=@keelwerk/source`, and TypeScript resolves the same
  condition through `customConditions`, so an edit in any workspace package is live in the running
  app without a build step.
- This works because pnpm links workspace packages: Node resolves the link to the real path outside
  `node_modules`, where type stripping is allowed. Node refuses type stripping for files under
  `node_modules` (`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING`), so the published manifest must not
  carry the source condition; pnpm's `publishConfig.exports` replaces `exports` at pack time. Both
  behaviours were checked with Node 24.21.0 (Appendix B); the M0 spike checks them again on Node 26
  (section 13.2).
- Production runs the JavaScript that `tsc -b` emits (`keelwerk start` runs `dist`), so production
  does not depend on type stripping at all.
- Library packages such as `@keelwerk/core` keep `src/index.ts` (and subpath entries such as
  `src/wire/index.ts`) as curated entry files of named re-exports. Module packages point `"."` at
  `src/module.generated.ts`, the generated module literal, instead of `src/index.ts`, and have no
  other entry (sections 23.5 and 23.7).

### 13.5 Project layout

The framework repository follows section 22 and keeps one example app, `examples/portal`, for its
own CI; every platform built on keelwerk lives in its own repository and depends only on the
published packages (decision 48c, 2026-10-27). An application repository built on keelwerk has
the layout of section 23.1: the deployment in `.launchway/` (decision 90c), one package per app under
`apps/<id>/` with `src/modules.ts` (the selection) and `src/app.ts` (`defineApp` with its named
type), every module a package under `modules/<id>/` in the module layout of section 23.2,
`scripts/` with one task per file, and `knip.json` beside `biome.json` at the root. Section 23
also states the single-purpose rule, the names and the tooling that keeps them.

### 13.6 `keelwerk dev`

`keelwerk dev` is a supervisor with three kinds of children:

1. **The type checker**: `tsc -b --watch --preserveWatchOutput` with TypeScript 7.0.2. Diagnostics
   stay visible in the status line; they do not stop the app, because type stripping does not need
   types, but `keelwerk build` refuses them.
2. **The probe**: a short-lived Node process that imports the deployment file (section 4.6), composes every
   app, derives the surfaces and asks every producer for its artefacts. A fresh process runs after
   each change, because an ECMAScript module graph cannot be unloaded. Before it starts, the
   supervisor rewrites the manifest of every module whose directories changed (section 23.5): a
   scan of file names, directories and each part's export that imports nothing, so a new, moved or
   deleted part is mounted or unmounted within the same cycle. The probe writes only the artefacts
   whose content changed (atomic rename), so the type checker and the editor see new types within
   one cycle and no watch loop starts. Module definition files must be free of I/O at import time;
   the probe has a 10-second limit and names the import that hung.
3. **The app**: one process with role `all`, the dev operator socket `.keelwerk/dev.sock`,
   `KEELWERK_EXPLAIN=1` and the source condition. Before it starts, the data layer synchronises
   the development database (expand steps at once, contract and rebuild steps after a confirmation
   in the terminal, section 14.6.4).

The supervisor watches the workspace with recursive `fs.watch` (ignoring `node_modules`, `dist`,
`generated`, `.keelwerk` and the `*.generated.ts` files it writes itself), debounces changes for
100 milliseconds, then rewrites the changed module manifests and runs the probe, the database
synchronisation and a restart of the app (stop phase with a 2-second deadline). The target is a
restart under one second for the proof apps, to be measured. It prints one line per invocation from
the explain stream, for example `POST /api/accounts/register → accounts.register 201 12 ms allow
accounts.register.open`. Only in development do transports serve GraphiQL, the API reference page
and verbose problem details.

### 13.7 Generated artefacts

| Artefact | Producer | Written by | Committed | Checked by | At runtime |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `src/module.generated.ts` (every module package) | core: the module literal from the directory conventions (section 23.5) | `dev` on change, `generate` | yes | `generate --check` | the package entry: the module value apps import |
| `src/keelwerk.generated.ts` | core, plus type fragments from transports | `dev` on change, `generate` | yes | `generate --check` | not loaded (types only) |
| `generated/api-surface/<app>/<api version>.json` | core | `dev`, `generate` | yes | `generate --check`, `surface diff` | recomputed in memory; the hash is compared at boot (warning in development, configurable in production) |
| `generated/api-surface/<app>/ledger.json` | core | `surface version new` (explicit) | yes | `generate --check` against `defineApiVersions`; `surface diff` keeps released entries unchanged | read at `compose` for module version changes (section 18.2) |
| `generated/openapi/<app>/<api version>.json` | `transport-rest` | `dev`, `generate` | yes | `generate --check`, OpenAPI schema validation | recomputed by the same function and served with per-backend `servers` |
| `generated/graphql/<app>/<api version>.graphql` | `transport-graphql` | `dev`, `generate` | yes | `generate --check` | the schema object is built from the surface; its printed form equals the file |
| `generated/cli/<app>/<api version>.json` | `@keelwerk/cli` | `dev`, `generate` | yes | `generate --check` | not used; the CLI builds from the surface |
| `TrpcRouter` type alias | `transport-trpc` | type fragment in the generated file | yes | `generate --check` | the router value is built from the surface |
| migrations and module snapshots | data layer | `db generate` (explicit, never by the watch loop) | yes | `generate --check` (definitions against snapshots), `db check` | production verifies the applied history |
| entity definitions for external tables | data layer | `db introspect` (section 14.8.4) | yes | `db introspect --check` | no |

The generated TypeScript file re-exports what application code needs, so the app-level type fold is
instantiated once:

```ts
// Generated by keelwerk 0.1.0 from src/app.ts. Do not edit. Format keelwerk.generated/1, API version 2027-01-12, surface sha256-3q2F...
import type { ActionRef as ActionRefOf, AppActionTree, AppEntities, Row } from '@keelwerk/core'
import type { AppClient } from '@keelwerk/client'
import type { TrpcRouterOf } from '@keelwerk/transport-trpc'
import type { Portal } from './app.ts'

export type App = Portal
export type Entities = AppEntities<App>
export type Actions = AppActionTree<App>
export type ActionRef = ActionRefOf<App>
export type Client = AppClient<App>
export type RowOf<R extends string> = Row<App, R>
export type TrpcRouter = TrpcRouterOf<App>               // type fragment of transport-trpc
export const apiVersion = '2027-01-12'                   // the head the types describe; createRemoteClient sends it (section 18.2)
```

Rules for every artefact: LF line endings, a trailing newline, sorted keys, two-space JSON
indentation, no timestamps, a header naming the producer and its version, the format, the API
version and the surface hash. Documents derived from the surface exist once per supported API
version (section 18.2). Biome excludes
generated paths from linting and formatting (`"!**/generated"`, `"!**/*.generated.ts"`) but keeps
them indexed for type-aware rules.

### 13.8 `keelwerk build` and CI

CI runs, in order, on Node 26 (the baseline of section 13.2):

1. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`;
2. `biome ci` (formatting and linting, no writes), then `knip` (unused files, which are forgotten
   mounts, unused exports and dependencies) and `keelwerk doctor --layout` (the layout pass of
   section 23.13);
3. `tsc -b` with TypeScript 7.0.2 (checks every project and emits `dist`);
4. `vitest run` with type checking (unit, integration and type tests);
5. `keelwerk generate --check` (the module manifests, the apps' generated files and every artefact
   of section 13.7);
6. `keelwerk db check` (section 14.8.5);
7. the transport conformance suite of section 16.3.8, the adapter conformance suite of section
   14.10 and the dual-evaluation suite of section 8.6 on every adapter the milestone ships
   (PostgreSQL, PGlite and in-memory from M1; MySQL and SQLite from M5, roadmap.md);
8. the type budgets of section 13.11: instantiation counts per app with
   `tsc -p <app> --extendedDiagnostics` (and `--generateTrace` for diagnosis; both work on
   TypeScript 7.0.2, Appendix B), declaration size per module package, and no TS7056, TS2742 or
   TS4023; attest benchmarks for the core's composition types run on TypeScript 6.0.3, which
   attest still needs;
9. `keelwerk surface diff --base origin/main` (section 18.6): derives the surface of every API
   version of each app on both sides and classifies every change as breaking (an action or an
   output field removed; an output field made optional; a new required input field; an input type
   narrowed or an input enum value removed; an execution mode changed away from `sync`; an error
   code given another kind), dangerous (an output enum value or a union member added, which
   exhaustive clients must handle), additive or neutral. A breaking change to a supported version
   fails, whatever the changelog says; dangerous changes need a changelog acknowledgement. Each
   changed module package's own surface and declaration files must fit its semantic version bump.

`keelwerk build` runs steps 2 to 6 and 9 locally, the layout pass included, then emits JavaScript
for production.

### 13.9 Biome preset and framework lint rules

`@keelwerk/biome-config` publishes a Biome 2.5.15 configuration that projects extend with
`"extends": ["@keelwerk/biome-config/biome"]`. Biome stays the only formatter and linter, with
its formatter with single quotes, two-space indentation and 100 columns (the style of
`docs/api-sketch.ts`, fixed 2026-11-04). The preset enables these rules as errors:

| Rule (group) | Why |
|---|---|
| `noExplicitAny` (suspicious) | one `any` in a module definition collapses the composition types (section 4.7) |
| `noConsole` (suspicious) | logs go through `ctx.log` (section 11) |
| `noImportCycles` (suspicious) | the package graph is a DAG (section 22) |
| `noTsIgnore` (suspicious) | `@ts-expect-error` makes a negative type test fail when the error disappears |
| `noEnum`, `noNamespace`, `noParameterProperties` (style) | erasable syntax only, for Node's type stripping |
| `useImportType`, `useExportType` (style) | `verbatimModuleSyntax` |
| `useNodejsImportProtocol` (style) | `node:` specifiers for built-ins |
| `noProcessEnv` (style), `noProcessGlobal` (correctness), `noGlobalAssign` (suspicious), everywhere except the deployment file (`.launchway/deployment.ts` or `keelwerk.config.ts`) | configuration comes from `ctx.config`, secrets from `field.secret()`, deployment values from `env()`; no hidden channel through the process or a global (section 7.9.6) |
| `noNodejsModules` (correctness), in module packages outside `src/executors/` | `node:*` modules perform effects or need the event loop; handlers yield requests instead, and the core's pure primitives come from `@keelwerk/core/crypto` (section 7.9.3) |
| `noNonNullAssertion` (style) | `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` results are meant to be handled |
| `noDefaultExport` (style) | named exports everywhere except the deployment file (an override) |
| `useImportExtensions` (correctness) | relative imports carry `.ts`, as Node and `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` need |
| `noUnusedImports`, `noPrivateImports` (correctness) | hygiene; `@private` internals stay private |
| `noFloatingPromises`, `noMisusedPromises` (nursery) | in the imperative code that remains (kernel, executors, transports, listeners), unawaited work escapes its span and its abort signal; the exact Biome version is pinned, so nursery behaviour does not drift |
| `noRestrictedImports` (style) | the package-kind boundaries below, and per-directory patterns of the layout (section 23.12) |
| `useFilenamingConvention` (style), `filenameCases: ["kebab-case"]`, `requireAscii` | file names are `kebab()` of their export (section 23.4) |
| `useNamingConvention` (style), `strictCase` | identifiers without consecutive capitals, so the name mapping reads back |
| `noBarrelFile`, `noReExportAll`, `noNamespaceImport` (performance); `noExportedImports` (style) | no re-exporting files, `export *`, `import * as` or exported imports (section 23.3) |
| `useExportsLast` (style) | a file's exports are its last statements |
| `noExcessiveLinesPerFile` (style), 300 non-blank lines, as a warning | a file long enough to hold two purposes |

Biome's recommended `noBannedTypes` (complexity) stays on everywhere, core type modules included,
with no relaxation in the preset. The type model needs the empty object type, so the core defines
it once as `Empty` (`type Empty = Record<never, never>`) and uses that name instead of `{}`; the
composition-types spike, which wrote `{}`, drew 67 warnings from the rule (2026-11-04).

Overrides exempt the entry files of library packages from the barrel rules, migrations and
generated paths from the naming rule, and scripts and tests from the import-effects plugin below.

Package-kind boundaries, as `overrides` with `includes`:

- module packages may not import adapters, transports, database drivers (`pg`, `mysql2`,
  `better-sqlite3`), `kysely` or `drizzle-orm`: handlers reach data through `ctx.load` and
  `ctx.write`, and the SQL escape hatch is a read request over an adapter capability (section
  14.3.8), not an import; outside `src/executors/` they may not import `node:*` modules or HTTP and
  SMTP clients either (`noNodejsModules` and `noRestrictedImports` overrides), while executors and
  their `src/executors/lib/` may;
- transport packages may not import module packages, adapters or the data package: transports see
  only the surface and the invoker;
- the core imports nothing from the workspace.

GritQL plugins shipped in the same package, each with tests:

| Plugin | Flags |
|---|---|
| `no-selection-augmentation.grit` | `declare module '@keelwerk/...'` and `declare global` in module and app packages (principle 2) |
| `named-module-types.grit` | an exported `defineModuleBase(...)`, `defineModule(...)` or `defineApp(...)` value without a named type annotation (section 4.1), in `base.ts`, `app.ts` and hand-written module literals of tests and spikes; the generator writes the named type into every `module.generated.ts` |
| `no-null-in-conditions.grit` | a literal `null` as a comparison value in a rule's `where` or `check` (section 8.3) |
| `as-system-reason.grit` | `system()` without a reason or with an empty string, as in `invoke(action, input, { as: system('') })` |
| `pure-parts.grit` (replaces `pure-deciders.grit`) | `Temporal.Now.*`, `Date.now()`, `new Date()` without arguments, `Math.random()`, `performance.now()`, `crypto.*`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `queueMicrotask`, `fetch` and a bare `yield` of a request, in module sources outside `src/executors/` (use `ctx.clock`, `ctx.newId`, `ctx.random`, `yield*` and effects; section 7.9.6) |
| `no-module-state.grit` | top-level `let` and `var`, and calls that mutate a top-level binding (`push`, `set`, `delete`, property assignment), in module sources |
| `no-await-in-parts.grit` | `async` and `await` in pure parts outside `src/executors/`: handler types already exclude promises, and this rule says so readably |
| `error-code-format.grit` | `defineError` codes that do not match `<module>.<snake_case>` |
| `one-export.grit` | a second exported value in a source file, outside assembly files (`base.ts`, `app.ts`, `modules.ts`), generated files, library entries and tests (section 23.3) |
| `no-import-effects.grit` | top-level expression statements, `await` and bare imports, outside tests and scripts |
| `wiring-only-assembly.grit` | a function or arrow function in `base.ts`, `app.ts` or `modules.ts` |

The last three, like `pure-parts`, `no-module-state` and `no-await-in-parts` (module sources, minus
`src/executors/` where the rule says so), are scoped with `includes`, because GritQL cannot read the
file path; checks that need paths belong to the layout pass of `keelwerk doctor` (section 23.13).
Modules are object literals (section 4.1), so no rule guards a chain of steps.

```grit
or {
  `system()`,
  `system($reason)` where { $reason <: or { `""`, `''` } }
} as $call where {
  register_diagnostic(span = $call, message = "system() needs a reason: it is written to the audit log.", severity = "error")
}
```

The patterns above are sketches; the package finalises them against fixtures. Checks that need
the registry rather than syntax (module ids against the grammar and the two reserved ids `core` and
`app`, camel-case collisions,
error-code prefixes against the declaring module, unique TypeID prefixes) run at `defineModule`,
`defineApp` and boot.

### 13.10 Type tests

- Every package has `*.test-d.ts` files checked by Vitest 5.0.3 with `--typecheck`, using
  `expectTypeOf`; a check on 2026-10-10 confirmed that Vitest's type checker runs on TypeScript
  7.0.2 and reports failing assertions (Appendix B).
- The core's suite contains the fourteen cases of section 4.7, the context rules of section 7.6
  (each module compiles with no app in scope; `ctx.load.accounts` is reached through `ifPresent`
  under `optional` and present in a part typed with `within(base, whenAccounts)`; `ctx.live` follows
  the contract; parts in separate files, mounted by the generated manifest, produce the module type
  of the same module written in one file; an `async` handler fails to compile; generator answers are
  typed per request), the policy typing (a condition cannot name a field or relation that the rule's
  modules do not provide; read rules list only maskable fields; `principal: 'user'` narrows the
  subject), the named checks of section 4.7 with a passing and a failing case each, and the
  generated file's exports.
- TypeScript does not excess-check an object literal returned from a callback: a rule's
  `where: () => ({ owner: 'x' })` passed a plain `Condition<E>` return type on an entity without
  `owner` (composition-types spike, 2026-11-04). Every callback-returned literal in the DSL
  therefore needs a named check that infers the literal and checks its keys by name, as
  `unknownConditionFields` does for rules (section 8.3), and a failing case in the suite; a
  declared return type alone checks nothing.
- `@keelwerk/testing/types` exports assertion helpers for application authors:
  `ExpectValidApp<A>` (no `defineApp` check properties), `HasEntity<App, 'accounts.profile'>`,
  `HasAction<App, 'accounts.profile.changePassword'>`, and the client types `InputOf`, `ResultOf`
  and `EventOf` for asserting what a transport will accept and return.
- `keelwerk new module` scaffolds the toggle cases: the module alone, the module with each module
  in its `optional` list, and the conditional parts present only in the latter.
- Transport packages carry type tests of their derived types (the cases of Appendix B for tRPC,
  the result types per execution mode for the typed client, `Readable<App, Ref>` for masks) and an
  instantiation budget on their fixture app.

### 13.11 Type budgets and declaration emit

Two costs grow with the number of modules and are guarded in CI: in this repository on the portal
example and the synthetic apps of the M0 spike, and in each platform's own repository on its app,
with the same checks from the published preset (decision 48c).

**Declaration emit.** Every package is `composite`, so `tsc -b` must write a `.d.ts` for every
exported value. Module values have inferred types, and `requires`, `optional` and
`contributes[].to` hold each dependency's full type; without a name, the emitter copies every
dependency's structure into each dependant, recursively. Checked on 2026-10-11 with TypeScript
7.0.2 and the section 4.7 listing (types exported): in a chain of ten modules, each requiring its
two predecessors and holding two entities of four fields, the inferred pattern emitted 1.1, 2.2,
4.6, 8.4, 15, 26, 45, 76, 130 and 219 KB; with the named-type pattern of section 4.1 every module
emitted about 1.3 KB. The review measured the same growth on TypeScript 5.9.3 and 6.0.3, up to
TS7056 ("inferred type of this node exceeds the maximum length the compiler will serialize") at
the tenth module of a larger chain. Both proof apps are that deep (`previews` requires
`deployments`, which requires `projects` and `nodes`; `smtp-submission` requires `mail-delivery`,
which requires `mail-store`, which requires `mail-domains`). Rules:

- every exported module and app value has a named type (`ModuleType`, `AppType`), scaffolded by
  `keelwerk new module` and enforced by `named-module-types.grit`; every exported entity has one
  too, in the same style (`export interface Profile extends EntityType<typeof profile> {}`, section
  4.2), because `base.d.ts` otherwise repeats each entity's type;
- every type that can appear in a DSL value's type is exported by `@keelwerk/core`, or emit fails
  with TS4023 or TS2742, which TypeScript 7.0.2 reports as TS2883: the core package's entry exports
  every type that can appear in a part or module type (about 120 names in the spike);
- the declared return types of part functions are written out as `ActionPart<...>` with computed
  types, never as an alias with its raw arguments: emit writes an alias in a declared return type
  with the arguments as given, which copied the entity and input shapes into every part file and
  brought a synthetic module to 21 KB, against 12.3 KB written out;
- no DSL function that may be nested inside another const-generic call infers a defaulted literal
  type parameter; such functions take the whole literal as one type parameter, and defaulted
  parameters use `NoInfer`. Measured failure: an inline `defineContribution` inside
  `defineModuleBase` inferred `when: readonly Dependency[]` from the outer constraint and the
  contribution was silently inactive (section 4.7);
- CI builds the portal example and the synthetic apps here, and each platform repository builds its
  app, under the pnpm layout and fails on TS7056, TS2742, TS4023 or TS2883, and when a module's
  declarations exceed the budgets: 6 KB per `module.generated.d.ts` and 16 KB per module package
  `.d.ts` in total.

Measured on 2026-11-04 by the composition-types spike under the pnpm layout: a synthetic module
emits 12,317 B in 11 files (`module.generated.d.ts` 2,880 B, `base.d.ts` 4,078 B, the two entities
865 and 1,323 B, parts 355 to 539 B each), the same at depth 3 and at depth 40; the fixture modules
emit 1.1 KB (teams) to 21.4 KB (auth, 21 files, manifest 5.6 KB) before the named entity types. The
build is clean at 3, 12, 25 and 40 modules with no TS7056, TS2742, TS4023 or TS2883.

**Instantiations.** CI runs `tsc -p <app> --extendedDiagnostics` on the portal example and the
synthetic apps here, and on Trail's, Launchway's and later the mail server's app in their own
repositories, and fails when the instantiation count exceeds the budgets set from the spike's synthetic apps with
parts typed against their bases (section 4.7 lists the measurements, about 15 % headroom):

| Count | 25 modules | 40 modules |
|---|---|---|
| fold: the app over the modules' `.d.ts` | 450,000 | 960,000 |
| whole program | 1,550,000 | 2,600,000 |

Typing parts against their bases costs about 36,000 instantiations per module, linear in the
module count, and parts in files cost 0.8 % more than one file per module, so the one-part-per-file
layout of section 23 has no type-check price worth naming. attest benchmarks guard the composition
types in `@keelwerk/core`.

**The generated manifest in the budget.** `tsc` sees `module.generated.ts` as written, so the
budgets and traces measure the generated literal itself: one import and one entry per part, the
same shape as the hand-written literal it replaces (decision 59b). The spike's synthetic modules
are produced by the generator, so the recorded budgets include its output, and `--generateTrace`
attributes check time to the manifest's mounts like any other file; a generator change that grows
the manifest's type cost fails the budget like any other change.

### 13.12 `keelwerk doctor`

Checks the environment and the project, then the running backends:

- Node 26 or later (the baseline, section 13.2); TypeScript 7.0 for builds (and 6.0 only where
  attest runs); the pnpm version;
  the Biome version the preset expects;
- every `tsconfig.json`: the options of section 13.3, an explicit `rootDir`, `customConditions`
  with the source condition, `isolatedDeclarations` only where it can work;
- project references complete: every workspace dependency of a package is referenced (computed
  from `package.json`);
- package manifests: the source condition in `exports`, absent from `publishConfig.exports`;
- artefacts fresh (`generate --check`);
- named types on exported module, module base and app values, and declaration sizes within budget;
- the layout pass (`--layout` runs it alone): placement of files in their kind's directory, names
  derived from exports, the generated manifests up to date and every declaration listed in
  `base.ts`, and the package shape (section 23.13);
- flags past their expiry or otherwise stale, and release or experiment flags expiring more than
  40 days after their first build (section 20.7);
- the personal-data pass (section 14.7.9.12): each personal field's capabilities, leaks, key scope
  and normaliser and, on a running deployment, its index rows and bytes per tenant, with warnings
  for equality indexes on low-entropy fields, `prefix.min` below 3, `contains.bits` above 12, every
  `order` field, tenant-keyed search indexes, indexes built under another Unicode version, failed
  reindex jobs and backups still holding plaintext of fields made personal later;
- the deployment: operator socket permissions, master key present, control store reachable, the
  control store on a different database cluster than the placements or an erasure-ledger sink
  configured (section 14.7.6), external-table drift, dead letters and parked streams, queued caps
  above 80 percent, capped lanes and unplaceable work (sections 9.5.5 and 21.2); then `app.health`
  and `app.ready` per backend;
- the data layer's fallbacks: per placement, every capability its adapter lacks that a selected app
  uses, the kernel path that replaces it and its cost (section 14.3.3, brief addendum 5);
- chain anchors: a scope whose newest anchor is older than its cadence, and a ledger sink that
  refused an append (section 15.1.8).

## 14. Data layer

This section specifies the data adapter boundary, placements and namespaces, the column mapping of
the field model, migrations per module, retention and erasure, the live types of stored data, and
how the data layer handles tenancy. Section 15 continues with the event log, consumers, offline
sync and live updates. ADRs [0006](adr/0006-data-adapter-boundary-namespaces-and-migrations.md),
[0007](adr/0007-event-log-positions-and-projections.md),
[0008](adr/0008-offline-sync-and-merge-rules.md),
[0009](adr/0009-personal-data-retention-and-erasure.md) and
[0027](adr/0027-encrypted-personal-data-and-queries.md) record the decisions. The PostgreSQL
statements this section relies on (the commit-tail counter, including the reuse of a rolled-back
allocation, and the unique-violation code of expected-version conflicts) and the `xid8` visibility
scheme it rejects were run on PostgreSQL 18.3 through PGlite 0.5.8 on 2026-10-11; PGlite has a
single connection and cannot exercise lock waits, so the write-path spike measured concurrent
multi-tenant writers on PostgreSQL 18.6 over TCP on 2026-11-04 (`spikes/write-path/REPORT.md`;
sections 7.9.4, 9.5, 14.3.6, 14.3.7 and 15.1.4 carry its results).

### 14.1 Principles

1. **The entity model is the only schema.** Columns, indexes, migrations, event payloads, merge
   metadata and the types of everything stored derive from the field model of section 6. No
   adapter has a second schema language; tables the framework does not own are
   described by entity definitions as well (section 14.8.4).
2. **The chain is the source of truth; tables are projections.** For `history: 'chain'` entities
   the event log is authoritative and the state table is an inline projection that can be rebuilt
   from it. Every other table is either a projection of the log or explicitly declared as not
   being history (`state`, `external`).
3. **Tenancy is applied below everything.** A unit of work is opened for one scope; the adapter
   adds the scope predicate to every statement and every event read, and PostgreSQL row-level
   security repeats it. No caller can pass another tenant.
4. **Fail closed.** An operator an adapter cannot express, a capability a module needs but the
   placement lacks, a drifted schema, a client clock too far ahead, a change report the server
   cannot compute exactly: each is an error or a forced resynchronisation, never a wider filter or
   a silent gap.
5. **Never disclose, never silently miss.** A change report (`changes`, `queryChanges`, live
   events, sync pulls) contains an id only if the principal could read the row at the client's
   position or can read it now. When the server cannot decide, it tells the client to
   resynchronise.
6. **Stored formats are final from the first milestone.** Later milestones add tables, columns and
   protocols; they never reinterpret an event, a position or a token written earlier. Every event
   carries its hybrid logical clock, actor, command id, client fields, before-images and hash from
   day one, even while nothing reads some of them.
7. **Deterministic replay.** Author `evolve` functions, the generic field-operation evolve and
   every merge rule are pure functions of the stream in version order, so a table rebuilt from the
   log equals the table maintained inline, and convergence can be property-tested.

### 14.2 Storage model at a glance

```
deployment
├── control store                         namespace "control", deployment scope
│     core entities: backends, tenants, domains, placements, namespaces, wrapped tenant keys,
│     erasure ledger, retention rules; their own event log (the directory change feed)
└── placement "default"                   adapter postgres, strategy shared-tables
      ├── namespace "launchway"           root: PostgreSQL schema launchway
      │     framework tables  kw_events  kw_positions  kw_shapes  kw_consumers  kw_parked
      │                       kw_jobs  kw_job_lanes  kw_job_lane_counts  kw_job_groups  kw_job_history
      │                       kw_serials  kw_usage  kw_subject_keys  kw_value_keys  kw_index_keys
      │                       kw_subject_refs  kw_tombstones  kw_stream_records  kw_migrations
      │     module tables     core__command_receipt  accounts__profile  auth__credential  auth__session ...
      └── namespace "mail"                root: PostgreSQL schema mail
            framework tables  kw_events ...
            module tables     accounts__profile  mail_store__email  mail_store__mailbox ...
```

- A **namespace** owns one event log, one set of framework tables and one copy of the tables of
  one app. A `shared-tables` placement holds one namespace per app of the deployment's catalogue
  (optionally restricted per placement); `schema-per-tenant` and `database-per-tenant` placements
  hold one namespace per tenant. Inside a namespace, positions, consumer checkpoints, serials and
  usage counters are kept per scope (a tenant, or a backend for backend-level entities), so
  tenants that share a namespace never share a position space (section 15.1.4).
- A **unit** is one transaction on one namespace, opened for one storage scope. All data access of
  one invocation runs in one unit (section 14.3.6).
- The namespaces of every app on every placement are provisioned and migrated in the `migrate`
