the CLI's project mode uses the same mechanism with the operator principal (section 16.9.1).
`host.fetch(request)` on a test runtime calls the HTTP host without a port, which the conformance
suite uses for the HTTP transports.

### 16.9 The CLI

#### 16.9.1 One binary, three connections

`@keelwerk/cli` provides the `keelwerk` binary, built with Stricli 1.3.0 (`@stricli/core`,
`@stricli/auto-complete`). Its command contexts are injected objects, so command tests never touch
process globals.

| Connection | When | Principal |
|---|---|---|
| project | inside a project: the file named by `--config <path>` or `KEELWERK_CONFIG`, else a `keelwerk.config.ts` that default-exports `defineDeployment` in the working directory or an ancestor, else `.launchway/deployment.ts` there (decision 90c) | framework commands run on the local definitions; action commands go to `.keelwerk/dev.sock` while `keelwerk dev` runs, otherwise to an in-process runtime (connect without listen) as the operator |
| operator socket | `--socket <path>` or a profile whose URL is `unix://...` | operator, with logged tenant entry for tenant work |
| remote | a profile with an `https://` URL and a credential | whoever the credential resolves to |

The action part of the command tree is built from the API surface: from the local registry in
project mode, otherwise from `GET /_keelwerk/v1/surface`, cached by hash under
`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/keelwerk/surfaces/` and revalidated with `If-None-Match` on every run.

#### 16.9.2 The command tree

```
keelwerk
├── dev | build | start | generate | migrate | db | introspect | module | ...   framework commands (16.9.7)
├── call <module.entity.action>     call accounts.profile.deactivate prof_01j9... --reason "left the company"
├── call <module.action>            call accounts.register --display-name Jens --email jens@acme.example
├── call app.<action>               call app.health
├── call core.<entity>.<action>     call core.tenant.create ...   (backend, tenant and domain are framework aliases)
└── watch <subscription reference>  watch auth.sessionEvents      (call with --follow)
```

- Action commands sit under one verb, `call`, with the dotted action reference everyone already
  uses as its argument (decisions 16b and 81a, 2026-10-26):
  `keelwerk call deployments.deployment.run --project ...`. The reference is written as code
  writes it (`accounts.profile.changePassword`), and completion offers it segment by segment.
- The references under `call` are exactly the actions of the selected backend's app: a reference
  exists when the action exists, and a module that is not selected has none.
- Generated actions take their reference names, the set operations included:
  `call accounts.profile.get <id>...`, `.query`, `.changes`, `.queryChanges`, `.create`,
  `.update <id>`, `.archive <id>`, `.restore <id>`, `.set` (a batch read from JSON) and `.watch`.
- Instance commands take the id as the first positional argument; `cli.positional` names further
  positional inputs; `cli.aliases` adds shorter references under `call`.
- There are no hand-written project commands: composition of actions belongs in a script with the
  typed client (section 16.8.4), and behaviour belongs in actions.

#### 16.9.3 No reserved module ids

Action commands sit under `keelwerk call` (decisions 16b and 81a), so framework commands and
module ids never share a level, and no name is reserved because of the CLI, an integration, a
plugin or a module. The framework's commands (`backend`, `build`, `call`, `completion`,
`consumers`, `db`, `dev`, `doctor`, `domain`, `explain`, `fleet`, `flags`, `generate`, `help`,
`init`, `introspect`, `jobs`, `keys`, `login`, `logout`, `migrate`, `module`, `new`, `operator`,
`profile`, `rollout`, `start`, `surface`, `tenant`, `version`, `watch` and `x`) are free choices of
the CLI: a new framework command can arrive in a minor version, because it can never shadow an
action, and a module may be called `fleet`, `new` or `surface`. The only reserved module ids are
`core` and `app`, which action references themselves use (section 5.1).

#### 16.9.4 Flags from field nodes

Each input field becomes a flag with the parser of its kind (the CLI column of section 16.2.3): kebab
names (`--display-name`), `--no-` forms for booleans, enumerations with completion, TypeIDs checked
against their prefix, repeatable flags for lists and sets, dotted flags for nested shapes up to
depth 2 (`--address.city Gent`), `@file` for text, JSON and binary values, and secrets read from a
prompt without echo or from `--<name>-stdin`. `--input <json|@file|->` supplies the whole input
(or the parts that flags do not), and explicit flags win. The assembled input is validated by the
action's schema in the pipeline, like every other transport's input.

Common flags on every action command: `--profile`, `--backend`, `--tenant`, `--output` (`text`,
`table`, `json`, `yaml`, `ndjson`), `--fields`, `--async`, `--wait[=<seconds>]`,
`--wait-effects[=<seconds>]` (waits until the deferred effects the command requested settle, section
16.4.7), `--command-id`, `--if-version`, `--explain` (operator and development: prints the pipeline
stages, the plan and the matched rule ids) and `--trace` (prints the trace id).

#### 16.9.5 Output and exit codes

- On a terminal, rows print as key-value blocks, pages as tables (the id plus the fields that fit,
  or `--fields`), receipts as the command id and status. When standard output is not a terminal,
  the default is JSON. YAML output uses `yaml` 2.9.1.
- `watch` and every subscription print NDJSON (`{"state":"...","item":{...}}` per line) and resume
  automatically from the last token after a disconnect. A subscription command stops at the `head`
  frame unless `--follow` is given (`keelwerk call deployments.deployment.logs <id> --follow`, as
  section 17.3.6 expects); `watch` commands start at the present and always follow. Ctrl-C ends
  with exit code 130.
- Errors go to standard error as one line per problem (`error[accounts.email_taken]: This e-mail
  address is already in use.`), the issues with their paths, and the request id; with
  `--output json` standard error receives the `WireError`. Exit codes follow section 16.4.6.
- Commands generate a command id per invocation and reuse it for automatic retries of network
  failures, so retrying never applies a command twice.

#### 16.9.6 Profiles and credentials

```json
{
  "current": "lvj",
  "profiles": {
    "lvj": { "url": "https://lvj.example", "backend": "launchway", "tenant": "jens", "credential": "lvj" },
    "lvj-operator": { "url": "unix:///run/keelwerk/operator.sock" }
  }
}
```

- Profiles live in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/keelwerk/profiles.json` (default
  `~/.config/keelwerk/profiles.json`); credentials live apart in `credentials.json` in the same
  directory with mode 0600. `KEELWERK_PROFILE` and `KEELWERK_TOKEN` override both for CI.
- `keelwerk login` finds the actions that carry a `cli.login` hint in the surface (a password
  login, an API-key exchange, a later device-authorization flow), prompts for their inputs, invokes
  the chosen one and stores the value of its `tokenField` as the profile's credential;
  `--token` stores a pasted token instead. The CLI never knows which module authenticates.
- Every command accepts `--backend` and `--tenant` overrides (section 12).

#### 16.9.7 Framework commands

| Command | Connection | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `keelwerk init [dir]` | none | creates a project in the canonical layout of section 23.1: workspace, base TypeScript configuration, Biome preset, `knip.json`, the `.launchway/` directory (`deployment.ts`, `launchway.ts`, and until M4 `compose.yaml`; decision 90c), one app and one module |
| `keelwerk dev` | project | the watch loop of section 13.6 |
| `keelwerk build` | project | the checks of section 13.8, then emits JavaScript for production |
| `keelwerk start --role serve\|work\|all [--config <file>]` | project (built) | runs a process with the role of section 3.2, from the deployment file found as in section 16.9.1 |
| `keelwerk generate [--watch] [--check] [--only <producer>]` | project | writes or checks every artefact of section 13.7 |
| `keelwerk migrate` | project or operator socket | applies pending migration files (an alias of `db apply`) |
| `keelwerk db plan\|generate\|apply\|status\|check\|introspect\|retire\|rebuild\|verify\|restore\|reindex` | project or operator socket | the data layer's commands, with the semantics of sections 14.6.4, 15.2.4, 14.7.6, 14.7.9.7 and 14.8.4; `verify` also compares the chain heads with the anchors in the ledger sinks (section 15.1.8) |
| `keelwerk consumers list\|unpark`, `keelwerk jobs stats\|lanes\|list\|explain\|replay\|discard\|pause\|resume`, `keelwerk keys rotate [--index]`, `keelwerk tenant move` | operator socket | consumers and parked streams (section 15.2.3); statistics per queue and capability set, the busiest lanes, why a job waits, dead-letter jobs and pausing a queue (sections 9.5 and 21.9); key rotation, with `--index` a reindex (sections 14.7.4 and 14.7.9.7); tenant moves (section 14.4.5) |
| `keelwerk fleet [list\|show\|watch]`, `fleet cordon\|uncordon\|drain\|probe\|forget`, `fleet scale status\|explain\|history\|set\|pause\|resume` | operator socket or remote operator | nodes and processes with roles, capabilities, revision, state, slots and heartbeat; placement on nodes, drains with a deadline and probes; the scaler's plans, decisions and runtime limits within the deployment's (section 21.9) |
| `keelwerk operator token issue\|revoke\|list` | operator socket | short-lived operator tokens for remote operator profiles (section 3.5) |
| `keelwerk introspect [modules\|actions\|entity <ref>\|policies\|extensions\|diff]` | any | the surface and the composition report as a tree or JSON; `introspect diff` is an alias of `surface diff` |
| `keelwerk surface diff\|version new\|usage\|retire` | project; `usage` and `retire` on the operator socket | compatibility of every API version against a git base (section 18.6), a new API version in the ledger (section 18.2), usage per tenant and version, retirement once the sunset has passed (section 18.5) |
| `keelwerk rollout status\|finalize\|abort` | operator socket | processes, revisions and pending contract steps; finalization and abort of a rollout (section 19.4) |
| `keelwerk flags list\|get\|set\|history\|explain\|stale` | operator socket or remote operator | aliases of the `core.flag` operator actions (section 20.9) |
| `keelwerk new <kind> <reference>` | project | creates one part's file where its reference puts it; the generated manifest mounts it (sections 16.9.8 and 23.14) |
| `keelwerk module new\|rename\|retire` | project; rename and retire also on the operator socket | `module new` is an alias of `new module` (section 16.9.8); the operator actions of sections 5.1 and 6.6 |
| `keelwerk backend ...`, `tenant ...`, `domain ...` | operator socket or remote operator | aliases of `call core.backend...`, `core.tenant...` and `core.domain...` |
| `keelwerk call <ref> [--input ...]` | any | the action commands: invokes any action by its dotted reference, with flags from its input fields (sections 16.9.2 and 16.9.4) |
| `keelwerk watch <ref> [--input ...]` | any | `call <ref> --follow` for subscriptions |
| `keelwerk explain <ref> [--input ...] [--as <principal>] [--dry-run]`, `explain --trace <command, event or effect id>`, `explain --redecide <command id>` | operator socket, development | shows the authorization decision without executing (section 8.6); `--dry-run` runs admission, `prepare` and `decide` in a unit that rolls back and prints events, effects and the decision record; `--trace` prints a command's events, effects with outcomes and the continuations they caused; `--redecide` re-runs a recorded decision with the current build and compares (section 7.9.6); `--as` evaluates everywhere and executes only in development (decision 17a) |
| `keelwerk doctor` | any | the checks of section 13.12, then `app.health` and `app.ready` |
| `keelwerk login\|logout\|profile ...` | remote | profiles and credentials |
| `keelwerk completion bash\|zsh\|fish` | none | prints a completion script |

#### 16.9.8 Module scaffolding

`keelwerk new <kind> <reference>` scaffolds one part, located by its reference (section 23.14),
for the kinds `module`, `entity`, `action`, `flag`, `rule`, `reaction`, `service`, `error`,
`schedule`, `stream`, `topic`, `effect`, `executor`, `contribution`, `condition`, `version-change`,
`lib`, `shape`, `app` and `script`; `keelwerk module new` stays as an alias of
`keelwerk new module`.
`keelwerk new module <id> [--kind domain|transport|adapter] [--requires a,b] [--optional c]`
creates a package that already compiles, tests and type-tests:

```
packages/module-<id>/                     (modules/<id>/ in an application repository)
  package.json          name, "type": "module", exports "." to src/module.generated.ts with the source condition, publishConfig.exports without it (section 13.4)
  tsconfig.json         extends the base configuration; composite; rootDir src; references to the packages it requires
  tsconfig.test.json    includes src/**/*.test*.ts and test/
  src/base.ts           const <camelId>BaseDef = defineModuleBase({ id: '<id>', version: '0.1.0', requires: [...], optional: [...] })
                        export interface <PascalId>Base extends ModuleBaseType<typeof <camelId>BaseDef> {}
                        export const <camelId>Base: <PascalId>Base = <camelId>BaseDef
  src/module.generated.ts  written by the generator, the package entry: const <camelId>Def = defineModule(<camelId>Base, {})
                        export interface <PascalId> extends ModuleType<typeof <camelId>Def> {}
                        export const <camelId>: <PascalId> = <camelId>Def
  src/module.test-d.ts  type tests: composes alone, composes with each optional module, conditional parts appear only then
  test/alone.test.ts    a test through createLocalClient against an app made of this module alone
```

Scaffolds create files only and never edit a source (question 61, closed by decision 59b on
2026-10-28). `new module` runs the generator once, so the package compiles at once. A scaffold of
any other kind writes the part where its reference puts it (with a test beside actions, rules and
reactions), and the generator mounts it in `module.generated.ts` in the next `keelwerk generate`
or dev-server cycle; `--dry-run` lists the files. What only a hand-written file can hold, the
scaffold prints for the author to add: a declaration the base lists (an entity, stream, flag,
extension point, contribution or condition, in `base.ts`), an app-level part (in `app.ts`), the new
package's reference in the root `tsconfig.json` and, with `--app <id>`, the module's import and
tuple entry in that app's `modules.ts`. The layout pass reports any of them still missing (section
23.13).

#### 16.9.9 Completions and help

`keelwerk completion zsh` (or `bash`, `fish`) prints a script that calls back into the binary, and
Stricli's `proposeCompletions` answers from the route map, which comes from the cached surface:
framework commands, the action references after `call` (module, entity and action, segment by
segment), flag names and enumerations complete without a network call; TypeID values can
complete by calling the target entity's `query` within 500 milliseconds when a profile enables it.
Help text comes from action and field descriptions (`.describe()`), with examples derived from the
input shape. The CLI's artefact `generated/cli/<app>.json` (routes, flags, descriptions)
makes CLI changes visible in review and feeds packaging.

#### 16.9.10 Interfaces

```ts
import type { CommandContext, RouteMap, TypedFlagParameter } from '@stricli/core'

export interface CliContext extends CommandContext {
  readonly surface: ApiSurface
  readonly client: UntypedClient                         // AppClient keyed by runtime strings
  readonly output: OutputWriter                          // text, table, json, yaml, ndjson
  readonly profile: ResolvedProfile
  readonly signal: AbortSignal
}

/** The routes under `call`, one per action reference, from the surface; @keelwerk/cli adds the framework commands. */
export function buildActionRoutes(surface: ApiSurface, options?: { readonly listName?: string }): RouteMap<CliContext>

/** A field node as a Stricli flag: parser, brief, optionality, variadic and enumeration. */
export function flagFor(name: string, node: FieldNode): TypedFlagParameter<unknown, CliContext>

/** Exit code for an outcome; also Stricli's `determineExitCode`. */
export function exitCodeFor(error: WireError | 'usage' | 'interrupted'): number
```

### 16.10 User interfaces and other clients

The brief requires that a later user interface is fully pluggable while everything works as an API
first. A user interface is therefore a client like any other, and the framework never learns that
it exists:

- **Where it lives.** A user interface is a separate package or repository, built with whichever
  frontend framework is chosen later. It reaches a backend only through transports: REST (types
  from the committed OpenAPI document with `openapi-typescript` 7.13.0), GraphQL (the committed SDL
  with gql.tada 1.11.4), tRPC (the `TrpcRouter` type exported by the app package) or the typed
  client over the invocation protocol. Live updates come through the live carriers.
- **What the framework offers it, generically.**
  - Discovery: the API surface (`core.introspect`) describes entities, fields with kinds,
    enumerations and descriptions, relations, actions with their inputs, outputs and declared
    errors, and pagination. A generic administration screen can be rendered from it alone.
  - Abilities: `core.me` (section 8.7) returns the principal summary and the principal's effective
    rules in CASL's raw-rule shape, which ADR 0005 already provides for, so a client can hide or
    disable what the user cannot do with `@casl/ability` on its side. Rules with relation
    quantifiers arrive with their relations resolved to id sets, or marked `serverOnly` when the set
    is unbounded, because CASL can evaluate relations only against data embedded in the row.
    Enforcement stays on the server.
  - Browser sessions: the cookie hint, the CSRF check and per-tenant CORS of section 16.4.10.
- **User-interface metadata.** Labels per locale, widgets, list columns and form layouts are not
  part of the field model. A user interface that needs them is itself a module (or a set of
  modules) that lists the domain modules as `optional` and keeps its metadata in its own
  definitions and extension points; the domain modules never import it, following the rule of
  section 5.4. Metadata that is not specific to a user interface (descriptions,
  enumerations, formats, deprecations) stays in the field model, where every client benefits.
- **Serving it.** A later `@keelwerk/transport-static` module mounts a directory of built assets
  on the host for an app (default prefix `/`, with a fallback to `index.html` for client-side
  routing). It projects nothing from the surface; because mounts are per app and the host routes by
  tenant domain, the interface appears on every domain of every backend running that app.
- **Replacing it** touches no module and no transport.

### 16.11 Observability

The core opens one span per invocation and defines the metrics of section 11. The
interface layer adds:

#### 16.11.1 Traces

| Component | Span | Attributes beyond the core's |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP host | one server span per request, created by the host's middleware with OpenTelemetry's HTTP semantic conventions | `http.request.method`, `http.route` (the template, such as `/api/accounts/profiles/{id}`), `http.response.status_code`, `server.address`, `client.address`, `keelwerk.transport`, `keelwerk.backend`, `keelwerk.tenant` |
| GraphQL | one operation span (Envelop's OpenTelemetry plugin, `@envelop/opentelemetry` 9.2.2) | operation name and type; resolver spans off by default, since every data access is already an invocation span and a DataLoader batch is one invocation |
| tRPC | attributes on the HTTP span | `rpc.system: trpc`, `rpc.method: <path>` |
| invocation protocol | attributes on the HTTP span | `rpc.system: keelwerk`, `rpc.method: <action ref>` |
| live | a short span for the subscribe call; sampled `keelwerk.live.deliver` spans linked to the producing invocation through the trace context stored in the event envelope (section 11) | subscription id, carrier, items delivered |
| CLI | one client span per command, exported only when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set | `keelwerk.cli.route`; `traceparent` is propagated to the server and `--trace` prints the trace id |

A stream is not one long span: a span that lasts hours is useless in every trace viewer. Deliveries
link back to the command that caused them instead, so a trace reads "command, events, delivered to
N subscribers".

#### 16.11.2 Metrics

| Instrument | Kind | Attributes |
|---|---|---|
| `http.server.request.duration` | histogram, seconds | method, route, status, transport, backend |
| `http.server.active_requests` | up-down counter | transport |
| `keelwerk.transport.errors` | counter | transport, kind, code |
| `keelwerk.live.connections` | up-down counter | carrier, backend |
| `keelwerk.live.subscriptions` | up-down counter | action, backend |
| `keelwerk.live.items.delivered` | counter | action |
| `keelwerk.live.items.filtered` | counter | action, reason (plan or filter) |
| `keelwerk.live.delivery.lag` | histogram, seconds from commit to write | carrier |
| `keelwerk.live.resets` | counter | reason |
| `keelwerk.graphql.operation.cost` | histogram | operation type |

`backend` is always an attribute; `tenant` only when a backend opts in, because tenant counts are
unbounded and metric cardinality is not.

#### 16.11.3 Logs

One structured line per transport request at level `info`: request id, transport, route, status,
duration, backend, tenant, principal kind, a hash of the principal id, trace and span ids. Bodies
are never logged. Debug logs and explain output redact `.personal()`, `.secret()` and `.hidden()`
fields, using the field nodes. The default `Logger` implementation is pino 10.4.0 writing JSON
lines to standard output (section 11).

#### 16.11.4 Development and support

`KEELWERK_EXPLAIN=1` makes the invoker emit a per-invocation explanation (section 11);
`keelwerk dev` renders it, `--explain` requests it for one CLI call, and `keelwerk explain`
shows the authorization decision without executing. `/_keelwerk/health` and `/_keelwerk/ready`
serve orchestrators; `app.health` and `app.ready` serve per-backend checks through every transport;
`keelwerk doctor` runs all of them.

### 16.12 Multi-tenancy in the interface layer

The brief makes multi-tenancy a first-class requirement that every layer must state. For the
interface layer:

| Concern | How it is handled |
|---|---|
| Tenant resolution | only in the invoker (`open`), from the carrier the host or listener fills; no transport resolves a tenant |
| Routing | the host routes by the resolved app; mounts are per app; a tenant path prefix consumed by a resolver is stripped before routing |
| Documents | surface, OpenAPI and SDL are per app and served per backend with backend-specific server URLs; never per tenant |
| Domains, CORS, cookies | allowed origins are the tenant's domains plus configuration; session cookies carry the `__Host-` prefix (host-only, `Path=/`, no `Domain`), so one tenant's cookie never reaches another tenant's domain and sibling subdomains cannot shadow it; under path-based tenant resolution cookies are not used at all, only bearer tokens (section 16.4.10); WebSocket upgrades and cookie SSE requests are origin-checked |
| Configuration | transport configuration per backend with per-tenant overrides, read through the session's scope |
| Live | subscriptions bound to the session's scope; stream tokens bound to the principal and selector; the change feed filtered by scope in the data layer; admission limits per tenant |
| Operator work | deployment-scope actions only on the operator endpoint; tenant entry explicit and logged |
| CLI | profiles name a deployment, a backend and a tenant; `--backend` and `--tenant` override; operator profiles use the socket |
| Quotas | the `admit` stage's decisions surface as 429 with `Retry-After` in every transport and as exit code 8 in the CLI |
| Errors | an unknown host or tenant is `not_found` before any transport runs; a suspended backend is `unavailable` |
| Observability | `keelwerk.backend` and `keelwerk.tenant` on spans and logs; tenant as a metric attribute only by opt-in |

### 16.13 Later interfaces

- **JMAP** (mail platform): `transport-jmap` serves the session resource at `/.well-known/jmap` per
  tenant. `Foo/get`, `Foo/changes`, `Foo/set`, `Foo/query` and `Foo/queryChanges` map one to one to
  the generated entity actions (with a `jmap.method` hint where RFC 8621 fixes names such as
  `Email/get`); the method calls of one request run in order in one session, with result references
  resolved by the transport. Push uses the SSE carrier with JMAP `StateChange` frames built from
  pokes, and the WebSocket carrier with the RFC 8887 subprotocol. Errors follow RFC 8620, mapped
  from section 16.4.6. JMAP's `accountId` is the partition value of the partitioned mail entities
  (section 15.1.4), passed to the generated `changes` and `queryChanges`; JMAP `state` and `queryState`
  strings are the tokens of section 15.2.6 unchanged, and `cannotCalculateChanges` answers the
  `reset` cases there. `Email/query` pages by `position` and `anchor`, which the transport requests
  as positional paging (section 14.3.5); JMAP is therefore a projection with its own paging option,
  not a renaming of the generated actions. Section 17.4.8 decides which entities the mail app
  exposes.
- **Connect** (gRPC-compatible): needs stable field numbers (`.tag(n)`, allocated from day one,
  decision 18a). Descriptors would be built at runtime from field nodes with `@bufbuild/protobuf`
  2.16.0 (`createFileRegistry`) and the `.proto` file emitted as an artefact; a runtime-descriptor
  spike, scheduled with the Connect transport (decision 39a; roadmap, later milestones), decides
  whether `@connectrpc/connect` 2.2.0 accepts them.
- **oRPC** is no longer a later interface: it ships in the first release, section 16.7.7
  (decision 15b).
- **Outbound webhooks**: an `outbound-webhooks` module (distinct from the inbound `webhooks`
  transport of section 16.5.8), not a transport; it ships with Launchway's rebuild in M4 (decision
  49a). Endpoints are entities of the module;
  deliveries are async reactions (a keyed job per endpoint and event, section 7.7), authorized per
  event under the endpoint owner's principal exactly like live deliveries; payloads are signed
  according to the Standard Webhooks specification with `standardwebhooks` 1.1.1 (`webhook-id`,
  `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature`); the event type is `<module>.<entity>.<event>` with the
  generated names of section 15.1.5; requests go through the egress service (section 12.3); retries
  use the job queue with exponential backoff; secrets are per tenant (`field.secret()`).
- **Static sites** for user interfaces: `transport-static`, section 16.10.

## 17. Shared modules and platforms

This section specifies the shared accounts and authentication modules and maps the two proof
platforms of the brief onto keelwerk: the deployment platform (the existing Launchway product,
whose backend is re-architected on the framework) and a mail server for the domain
`jenspenneman.com`. It ends with the gaps the core must close before both platforms can be built
and where each one lands. Sources: Launchway's specification (release v0.3.0, 2026-10-07) and its
ADRs 0003, 0004, 0006, 0009 to 0012 and 0017 to 0019; the RFCs named in the text. Libraries were
checked with `npm view` and external components against their repositories on 2026-10-11
(Appendix A). Code uses the DSL of section 4; anything that depends on an open gap carries a
comment with its gap id (`// G3`); names of platform modules are proposals. Each platform lives in
its own repository and depends only on the published packages (decision 48c, 2026-10-27), so the
paths of its code are relative to that repository, in the layout of section 23.1. The mail
server's design stays as written while Jens has parked it (2026-10-26) until he has a stable,
permanent deployment option; its open questions wait with it (section 26.1).

### 17.1 Findings in brief

- Both platforms fit the composition model as specified. Every cross-module influence they need
  is a requirement, a contribution, a conditional part or an extension point: `github` contributes
  fields to `projects.project` and `deployments.deployment`, `previews` adapts itself when `github`
  is selected, `mail-store` adapts itself to `accounts`, `spam` contributes verdict fields to
  `mail-store.email`. No platform needs declaration merging, runtime module selection or an import
  cycle.
- The gaps were mostly in the runtime around the invoker: connection-oriented listeners and
  sessions, a scope directory for keys other than host names, jobs with timers and schedules,
  secrets with a key hierarchy, blob storage, streams for logs, commit-ordered change positions,
  HTTP ingress for webhooks and raw responses, process placement and tenant-editable
  configuration. Most are now specified in the core sections; G1, G2, G4 and G5, and the singleton
  leases of G9, remain proposals whose ADRs the roadmap schedules before the milestone that needs
  them (section 17.7).
  One composition rule needed a refinement and has it (G16, section 5.5): extension values and
  services that carry behaviour run with the context of the module that provides them.
- The mail server is built from framework modules for every protocol (SMTP for receiving and for
  submission, outbound delivery, IMAP, JMAP) over one store of entities and blobs. Spam scoring
  (rspamd), antivirus (ClamAV, optional), recursive DNS resolution (Unbound) and, from the home
  connection, an outbound relay are external components.
- The mail server does not need the raw SQL escape hatch: the data layer provides per-partition
  serials, full-text search (a keyed token index over personal text, section 14.7.9.9), positional
  paging for JMAP and partitioned change tokens (G7).
  Queue locking stays inside the job store.
- Launchway's limit of one API instance holding all agent connections (its ADR 0004) disappears:
  commands to a node become `agentCommand` effects that the agent performs (decision 80a), delivered
  through a subscription over its pending effects, so any process can hold the agent's connection.
- The residential connection constrains the mail server more than the framework does: outbound
  delivery needs a host with a static address and matching reverse DNS, and the MX host name must
  be an address record that follows the dynamic public address (question 21, parked with the mail
  server, section 26.1).

### 17.2 Accounts and authentication

The brief requires an authentication module in which users keep their login information and sign
in, and a separate accounts module that authentication influences and that influences
authentication. Both are shared modules (`@keelwerk/module-accounts`,
`@keelwerk/module-auth`) that both platforms select; section 5.4 shows how they influence each
other without an import cycle, and [api-sketch.ts](api-sketch.ts) shows them in code. ADR 0014
records the decisions of this section.

#### 17.2.1 Accounts

`accounts` is the lower module: a directory of people that needs no login.

| Part | Specification |
|---|---|
| `accounts.profile` | chain entity, `dataSubject: 'id'`: `displayName`, `email` (unique, personal), `locale`, `deactivatedAt`; domain event `deactivated` |
| `accounts.register` | creates a profile; public only when the backend's configuration `allowSelfRegistration` is on, otherwise operators and administrators |
| `accounts.profile.deactivate` | an entity command with a plain `decide`; deny rule `frozen` on the pre-image keeps deactivated profiles read-only |
| `accounts.profile.search` | an entity query whose `read` returns a query description over the caller's view (`ctx.target`) |
| `accounts.identities` | reads the `identityProviders` extension point, whose values are bound to their contributors (section 5.5) |
| subjects | with `accounts` selected, a user's auth subject is a profile id; principals carry `subjectRef: 'accounts.profile'`, so `ctx.principal.subjectAs('accounts.profile')` yields a branded profile id |

#### 17.2.2 Credentials, sessions and tokens

`auth` owns two entities and shares one token format with `api-keys` and `nodes`:

| Entity | History | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `auth.credential` | chain, `dataSubject: 'subject'`, generated set off | `subject`, `kind` (`password` or `passkey`), `identifier` (the normalised e-mail address of a password credential; unique among active password credentials), `verifier` (an Argon2id hash of the password; for passkeys the public key in a hidden field), passkey metadata (credential id, sign counter, transports), `label`, `lastUsedAt` (maskable), `revokedAt` |
| `auth.session` | state, `dataSubject: 'subject'` | `subject`, `credentialId`, `publicId` (unique), `tokenVerifier` (`field.verifier()`), `authenticatedAt` (the last full authentication), `lastSeenAt`, `idleExpiresAt`, `absoluteExpiresAt`, `revokedAt`, `rotatedFrom`, client metadata (user agent and address, personal) |

- **Tokens are not ids.** A session token is issued once by the key service, through the request
  `yield* ctx.secrets.issue({ prefix: 'pss' })`, which the decision record keeps without its
  plaintext (gap G4, section 7.9.3): `kws_<public id>_<secret>`, with a 128-bit public id and a
  256-bit secret. The row stores
  the public id and an HMAC-SHA-256 verifier of the secret under a key of the key service; the
  token itself is stored nowhere. Session ids appear in events, receipts, logs and
  `auth.sessionEvents`; they authenticate nothing. API keys, app passwords (`api-keys.key`) and node
  credentials use the same format with their own prefixes.
- **Passwords** are hashed with Argon2id, a computation of the core that module code requests
  (`yield* ctx.compute.argon2idHash(password, salt)` and `argon2idVerify(verifier, password)`, the
  salt a recorded random value): the core runs `node:crypto`'s `crypto.argon2` (which runs on Node
  24.21.0 without an experimental warning, checked on 2026-10-11) in a worker pool off the event
  loop, about 14 ms per hash, so `auth` imports no `node:*` module (section 7.9.3). The parameters
  are at least OWASP's current minimum (19 MiB of memory, two passes, one lane). The parameters are
  part of the stored hash, and a successful login rehashes with the current parameters. Verification
  of an unknown identifier runs against a dummy hash, so timing does not reveal which identifiers
  exist.
- **Passkeys** use `@simplewebauthn/server` (14.0.3) for registration and authentication ceremonies;
  the challenge lives in a short-lived row of the session or of the pending registration, never in
  process memory, so any process can finish a ceremony.
- **App passwords and API keys** are `api-keys.key` rows with scopes and allowed transports (rules
  over credential scopes, gap G13); they are not `auth` credentials, because they authenticate
  programs and protocol clients (IMAP, SMTP submission), not people at a login page.

#### 17.2.3 Expiry, rotation and revocation

- Sessions expire after an idle period (default 12 hours) and an absolute lifetime (default 30
  days), both configurable per backend and tenant. `lastSeenAt` and `idleExpiresAt` are extended at
  most every five minutes, so active sessions do not write on every request: when the resolver sees
  a session last extended more than five minutes ago, it returns, beside the principal, an `enqueue`
  effect of an `auth` command that writes the new times, keyed by session so that concurrent
  requests coalesce (section 7.9.5).
- Every login creates a new session; a session is never reused across logins. Changing the password
  revokes every other session of the subject and rotates the current one; a privilege elevation
  (a role or membership granted, observed at revalidation) rotates a cookie session on the next
  response.
- `auth.logout` revokes the caller's session (the session id is the principal's credential
  reference) and clears the cookie. `auth.session.revoke` revokes one of the caller's sessions;
  `auth.revokeSubject` revokes every credential and session of a subject and is invoked by auth's
  own reactions (a deactivated profile, an erased subject) under `auth.system`.
- Revocation reaches live connections through revalidation: the session resolver names the events
  it depends on (the session's own change records, its credential's `revoked`, the profile's
  `deactivated`, membership changes), and a connection whose session they touch is revalidated at
  once and closed when it fails (section 16.3.4).

#### 17.2.4 The resolver's read path

The session resolver is a principal resolver of `auth`, a pure generator bound to auth's context
(section 5.5) that yields loads and returns the principal. It runs in `resolvePrincipal`, after
`resolveScope` has fixed the tenant:

1. It reads the token from the `__Host-keelwerk_session` cookie or from `Authorization: Bearer`
   in the carrier it receives as a parameter.
2. It yields a load of the session by public id, which the kernel answers in a read-only unit of
   the resolved tenant with auth's module authority, and a verification request
   (`ctx.secrets.verify(token, session.tokenVerifier)`), which compares the HMAC of the secret with
   the stored verifier in constant time.
3. It checks revocation and both expiries against the invocation's time and returns a
   `UserPrincipal` whose `ref` names the resolver, the subject, the credential and the session
   (auth's `principalRef`, section 8.5), and whose
   `expiresAt` is the earlier expiry, together with the idle extension due, if any (section
   17.2.3).
4. The kernel caches validated sessions per process for at most 30 seconds, keyed by public id (the
   resolver itself keeps no state), and drops a cache entry when the change feed reports a change
   record for that session, so a revocation applies within the wake-up latency (and within a second
   if a wake-up is lost).

Session tokens are looked up in the tenant the carrier already names (host name, header or the CLI
profile's tenant). Long-lived credentials that must work without a tenant host (API keys, node
credentials) carry a public id that is also a scope key in the scope directory (gap G2).

An unknown, expired or revoked cookie session makes the request anonymous and clears the cookie;
an invalid bearer token fails with `unauthenticated` (section 16.3.4).

#### 17.2.5 Re-authentication and recovery

- Changing a credential (`accounts.profile.changePassword`, adding or removing a passkey, creating
  an app password, changing the login identifier) requires either the current password in the input
  or a session whose `authenticatedAt` is at most ten minutes old (configurable); otherwise it fails
  with `forbidden` and code `auth.reauthentication_required`. `auth.reauthenticate` (password or
  passkey assertion) refreshes `authenticatedAt`. A stolen session therefore cannot become a
  permanent takeover by setting a new password.
- Nobody sets another person's password. `auth.requestPasswordReset` (public, rate-limited, the
  same answer whether or not the identifier exists) issues a one-time reset token, valid for 30
  minutes and stored as a verifier, and hands it to the `auth.resetDelivery` extension point (the
  mail platform delivers it by mail; without a filler, an operator command shows a reset link).
  `auth.resetPassword` consumes the token, sets the new password and revokes every session of the
  subject.
- Operators help users through `core.tenant.enter` and these actions, never by reading verifiers.

#### 17.2.6 Rate limits and abuse

`auth` contributes to `invocationMiddleware` a pure admission rule that runs at `admit` and returns
the token buckets to consume, which the kernel takes: buckets per remote address (after
trusted-proxy rules) and per identifier for `auth.login`, the passkey ceremonies,
`auth.reauthenticate`, `auth.requestPasswordReset` and `auth.resetPassword` (defaults: 10 attempts
per minute per address, 5 failed attempts per 15 minutes per identifier, configurable). Buckets are
the shared buckets of the quota model (section 12.2), so the limits hold across processes. Failures
are counted in metrics and in the decision log.

#### 17.2.7 Login flows

- **Browser.** `auth.login` (password) or the passkey ceremony (`auth.passkey.options`, then
  `auth.passkey.verify`) returns the token; the `http.cookie` hint sets `__Host-keelwerk_session`
  and leaves the token out of the body (section 16.4.10); `auth.logout` clears it. Under path-based
  tenant resolution, a browser client keeps the token in memory and sends it as a bearer token.
- **CLI.** `keelwerk login` finds the actions with a `cli.login` hint in the surface: the password
  login prompts for the identifier and the password (without echo) and stores the token in the
  profile's credentials file (mode 0600). Passkey-only accounts use a device authorization flow
  (`auth.device.start`, approval in a browser session, `auth.device.poll`), delivered with
  Launchway's rebuild in M4; passkeys themselves come in M3, because Trail signs in with passkeys
  only.
- **Protocols.** IMAP and SMTP submission use app passwords over TLS (section 17.4.9); the agent
  uses its node credential (section 17.3.4).

#### 17.2.8 Rules

```ts
// modules/auth/src/policies/public-actions.ts: one rule over several module-level actions, the rule auth.public-actions
export const publicActions = defineRule(authBase, [login, requestPasswordReset, resetPassword], { effect: 'allow', public: true })
// modules/auth/src/policies/passkey/ceremony.ts: the passkey ceremony's actions
export const ceremony = defineRule(authBase, passkey, { effect: 'allow', actions: ['options', 'verify'], public: true })
// modules/auth/src/policies/signed-in.ts: auth.signed-in
export const signedIn = defineRule(authBase, [logout, reauthenticate], { effect: 'allow', principal: 'user' })
// modules/auth/src/policies/credential/self.ts, self-revoke.ts and already-revoked.ts
export const self = defineRule(authBase, credential, { effect: 'allow', actions: ['read'], principal: 'user', where: (ctx) => ({ subject: ctx.principal.subject }), fields: ['lastUsedAt'] })
export const selfRevoke = defineRule(authBase, credential, { effect: 'allow', actions: ['revoke'], principal: 'user', where: (ctx) => ({ subject: ctx.principal.subject }) })
export const alreadyRevoked = defineRule(authBase, credential, { effect: 'deny', actions: ['revoke'], where: () => ({ revokedAt: { isNull: false } }), reason: 'This credential is already revoked.' })
// modules/auth/src/policies/session/self-sessions.ts
export const selfSessions = defineRule(authBase, session, { effect: 'allow', actions: ['read', 'revoke'], principal: 'user', where: (ctx) => ({ subject: ctx.principal.subject }) })
```

Each tenant is its own authentication realm: credentials and sessions are tenant rows, the same
e-mail address in two tenants is two credentials, and a token of one tenant is never found in
another tenant's namespace. One login across tenants or backends would be federation through a
later OpenID Connect module.

### 17.3 The deployment platform

#### 17.3.1 What carries over and what changes

Launchway's product model stays as specified: GitHub repositories are the source, Compose is the
runtime contract, an agent per machine connects outbound over WebSocket and owns Docker there,
Caddy is the edge and is configured through its admin API (on keelwerk, the first provider of the
shared `edge` module, section 17.3.7), DNS providers are plugins, pull requests get previews. What
changes is the control plane: the hand-wired Hono and Drizzle API (`apps/api`) becomes a keelwerk
app in the Launchway repository (decision 48c). The agent, Docker, Caddy and the web UI stay outside
the framework; the agent and the UI become clients of the generated interfaces, rebuilt together and
shipped at one cutover: a clean break, with no compatibility layer for the old agent protocol or the
old API paths (decision 23c, 2026-10-26).

**The `.launchway/` directory** (decision 90c, 2026-10-28). Every app repository carries a
`.launchway/` directory, and the rebuilt Launchway deploys the app from it: its project model reads
the directory, which replaces the per-project `composeFiles` setting of today's Launchway.
`.launchway/deployment.ts` is the app's keelwerk deployment file (`defineDeployment`: the app, data
stores and placements, ports, providers, scaling limits; section 4.6), and `.launchway/launchway.ts`
holds what only the platform needs (domains and routes, previews, environment, node). The framework
stays neutral: `keelwerk start --config <file>` runs any deployment file, and the default lookup is
`keelwerk.config.ts`, then `.launchway/deployment.ts` (section 16.9.1). Before the rebuild, Trail
(M3) is deployed by the current Launchway from `.launchway/compose.yaml`, which runs `keelwerk start
--config .launchway/deployment.ts`.

| Launchway v0.3.0 | On keelwerk |
|---|---|
| User, Session, Passkey | `accounts.profile`, `auth.credential`, `auth.session` (shared modules) |
| ApiToken (`lwy_`, scopes `read`, `write`, `admin`) | `api-keys.key` (shared) with scopes |
| Invitation; roles `owner`, `admin`, `member`, `viewer` | `members.membership`, `members.invitation` (shared); roles reach the principal through an enricher |
| GitHubConnection | `github.connection` |
| App, EnvVar | `projects.project`, `projects.envVar` (the UI keeps the word "app"; section 17.6.5) |
| Deployment and its log lines | `deployments.deployment` (chain) and the stream `deployments.log` (G6) |
| Preview | `previews.preview` |
| Node, join token, node credential | `nodes.node`, `nodes.credential`, `nodes.presence`; messages to a node are `agentCommand` effects that its agent performs (section 17.3.4) |
| DnsProviderAccount, DnsZone | `dns.providerAccount`, `dns.zone`, `dns.record` (shared) |
| Domain, Route | `domains.domain`, `domains.route` |
| Setting (singleton row) | module configuration per tenant (section 17.3.12, G10) |
| AuditEvent | `audit.entry` (shared), projected from the chain, the receipts and the decision log |
| Webhook deliveries table (replay protection) | command receipts keyed by the delivery id (G8) |
| `startJob` loops (ADR 0012), the 15-second deployment worker | schedules, timers and event-driven dispatch (G3) |
| Composition root with a deferred deployment sink (ADR 0010) | lifecycle phases; the cycle disappears because the agent calls actions through the invoker as a typed client |
| SSE `GET /events` | subscriptions of the `live` module |
| REST `/api/v1`, OpenAPI from Zod routes, RFC 9457 problems | `transport-rest` projection and the error taxonomy mapping of section 16.4.6, under the projection's own paths: the UI is rebuilt against them, and no `/api/v1` path is kept (decision 23c) |
| TypeID prefixes (`dep_`, `node_`, ...) | the entity `prefix`; the same prefixes are kept |
| AES-256-GCM secrets, HKDF subkeys, AAD per record (ADR 0009) | the secrets key hierarchy (G4) |

#### 17.3.2 Module map

| Module | Package | Owns | Requires | Optional | Contributes to | Fills |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `accounts` | shared | `profile` | | | | |
| `auth` | shared | `credential` (password, passkey), `session` | | `accounts` | `accounts.profile` | `principalResolvers` |
| `api-keys` | shared | `key` (verifier hash, scopes, expiry, last use) | | `accounts` | | `principalResolvers` |
| `members` | shared, new | `membership` (subject, role), `invitation` | | `accounts`, `auth` | | `principalEnrichers` |
| `audit` | shared | `entry` | | observes every module (G12) | | none: an `observes: 'all'` reaction and the receipts' request metadata (G12) replace the earlier middleware |
| `dns` | shared, new | `providerAccount`, `zone`, `record`; the effect `applyRecord` with its executor | | | | declares `providers` (executor-side provider adapters) |
| `dns-cloudflare`, `dns-manual` | shared, new | | `dns` | | | `dns.providers` |
| `projects` | Launchway | `project`, `envVar` | | | | declares `gitProviders` |
| `nodes` | Launchway | `node`, `credential`, `presence`; the external effect `agentCommand` (performed by the agent) | `live` (contract) | | | `principalResolvers`; claims node-credential scope keys (G2); declares `heartbeatObservers` and `commandResolvers` |
| `deployments` | Launchway | `deployment`, stream `log` | `projects`, `nodes` | | | `nodes.heartbeatObservers` and `nodes.commandResolvers` (bound to deployments, G16) |
| `domains` | Launchway | `domain`, `route`; reactions that turn each route and the running deployment it points at into edge sites | `projects`, `deployments`, `nodes` | `dns`, `edge` | | |
| `edge` | shared, new (decision 82a) | `site` (the desired state, with owners), `render` (the last applied configuration, its hash and the status per site); the external effect `apply` (performed on the edge host) | | | | declares `providers` (single) |
| `edge-caddy` | shared, new | | `edge` | | | `edge.providers` (renders the Caddyfile) |
| `github` | Launchway | `connection`; effects with executors for GitHub's API (the status mirror, release reads, the manifest conversion) | `projects`, `deployments` | `webhooks` | `projects.project`, `deployments.deployment` | `projects.gitProviders` (bound to github, G16), `webhooks.receivers` |
| `previews` | Launchway | `preview` | `projects`, `deployments`, `domains` | `github` | `projects.project`, `deployments.deployment` | |

Infrastructure modules in the app: `live`, the transports `transport-rest`, `transport-graphql`,
`transport-trpc` and `transport-webhooks` (G8), and the shared `outbound-webhooks` module, which
ships with Launchway's rebuild (decision 49a, section 16.13). The PostgreSQL adapter, the
HTTP host (which also serves the invocation protocol for the CLI) and the job queue are
infrastructure of the deployment (section 17.5.1), not modules of the app.

What toggling does:

- Without `previews`: projects have no preview settings, deployments have no `previewId`, and no
  pull request reaction exists. Nothing else changes.
- Without `github`: no webhook receiver, no mirror, no automatic deployments; `previews` loses its
  pull request reactions (conditional part) and can only be opened by hand through another git
  provider. As of 2026-10-11 no other provider exists, so `projects.gitProviders` declares
  `min: 1` and an app without `github` fails at boot with `emptyExtensionPoints` (section 5.5).
- Without `domains` and `edge`: projects still deploy; services publish ports directly, which is
  how a service that needs raw TCP ports runs in Launchway v0.3.0.
- Without `dns`: domains are not bound to zones and users create records by hand, as with the
  `manual` provider of Launchway v0.3.0.
- Without `members`: only the operator and API keys act; no roles exist.

#### 17.3.3 Tenancy and scope

- The deployment has a backend `launchway` that runs the app `launchway`. A tenant is an
  organisation that deploys its own projects on its own machines. Jens's installation is one
  tenant whose core domain is `deploy.jenspenneman.com`.
- All Launchway entities are tenant data (`tenancy: 'tenant'`): nodes, projects, deployments,
  domains, DNS provider accounts, GitHub connections. Nodes and the edge belong to one tenant, so
  containers of two tenants never share a Docker host or the proxy network (decision 25a,
  2026-10-27).
- Scope resolution per carrier, all through the pipeline's `resolveScope`:
  - the UI and REST clients: the host name (`core.domain`);
  - API tokens and node credentials: the token carries a public id that is a scope key (G2);
  - the agent WebSocket: the join token or node credential, the same way;
  - GitHub webhooks: the receiver path `/hooks/github/<connection id>`, registered as a scope key
    when the connection is created and turned into `carrier.scopeKey` by the deployment's carrier
    enricher before scope resolution (G2, G8, section 16.5.8).
- The operator (Jens) creates the backend and tenants and issues the first owner invitation from
  the CLI. Launchway's public first-run endpoint (`POST /setup`) is not needed any more.

#### 17.3.4 Agents

The agent remains a separate program (Node, the Docker CLI with Compose, git) that keelwerk does
not contain. Decision 23c (2026-10-26) makes the move a clean break: the agent and the UI are
rebuilt against the generated interfaces and ship together at the cutover (roadmap M4); no
compatibility transport serves Launchway's agent protocol v1, and no legacy path stays. The agent
is a typed client (section 16.8.4) pinned to an API version and connected over the live module's
WebSocket carrier (`keelwerk.live.v1`, `subscribe` and `invoke` on one connection, section
15.4.7): it holds its command channels as subscriptions and calls actions for everything it
reports. What the agent did with the messages of Launchway's ADR 0004 and their additions in ADR
0009 maps onto actions as follows:

| The agent (the protocol v1 message it replaces) | Direction | On keelwerk |
|---|---|---|
| connects with `Authorization: Bearer <join token or node credential>` (the upgrade) | agent to server | `invoker.open` over the live carrier (section 16.3.4) with the token in the carrier; the `nodes` resolver yields a `service` principal (`via: 'nodes.credential'` or `'nodes.join'`) |
| joins or reconnects (`hello`, `hello.ok`) | agent to server; the result back | `nodes.join` (join token: returns the node credential once) or `nodes.node.connect` (agent version, API version, Docker facts); the action's result is the answer |
| sends a heartbeat every 15 s with its active deployment ids (`heartbeat`) | agent to server | `nodes.node.heartbeat`: a presence draft, a `setTimer` effect that resets the offline timer, and the decisions of the `heartbeatObservers` |
| reports a phase (`deployment.progress`) | agent to server | `deployments.deployment.reportPhase` |
| appends build output (`deployment.log`) | agent to server | `deployments.deployment.appendLog` (batched stream append, G6) |
| reports the result (`deployment.result`) | agent to server | `deployments.deployment.reportResult` |
| reports runtime state (`app.status`) | agent to server | `deployments.deployment.reportRuntime` |
| streams container logs on demand (`logs.chunk`, `logs.end`) | agent to server | `nodes.node.publishLogs`, whose decision publishes the lines to the topic `nodes.containerLogs` (G6) |
| performs commands (`deploy`, `stop`, `remove`, `status`, `logs.start`, `logs.stop`, `deployment.cancel`) | server to agent | `agentCommand` effects with the agent as their external performer (section 7.9.5), emitted by the subscription `nodes.channel` and settled with `nodes.ack` |
| applies the edge configuration (the edge node's agent only) | server to agent | the `edge.apply` effect, emitted by the subscription `edge.channel` and settled with `edge.ack` (section 17.3.7) |
| errors (`error`) | both | a `WireError` (`{ code, message, retryable }`) of the live carrier |

The command channel is the part that changes most:

- A module that must tell a node something returns, from its decision, what the pure service
  `ctx.services.nodes.send(nodeId, command, { continueWith, with, deadline })` builds: an `agentCommand`
  effect, which `nodes` declares with `performer: 'external'` (decision 80a). Its `requested`
  record commits in the caller's unit, so a state change and the message to the node commit
  together, and the effect record is the outbox.
- The agent holds one subscription, `nodes.channel`, whose source is
  `ctx.live.effects(agentCommand, { where: { nodeId } })`: the pending effects of its own node, in
  position order and resumable. Any process can hold the connection: the change feed wakes
  whichever process serves the subscription. Launchway's single-instance limitation goes away. The
  edge node's agent holds `edge.channel` beside it on the same connection.
- Delivery is at least once. Commands carry their effect id; the agent ignores ids it has already
  handled, and unsettled effects are emitted again after a reconnect. The agent settles each
  through `nodes.ack`, whose decision returns `settle(...)`; the requesting module's continuation
  receives the outcome, and an effect left unsettled past its `deadline` is settled as failed
  (`core.effect_deadline`), so every command to a node has one record with its outcome and its
  follow-up.
- Secrets never sit in an effect's input. The `deploy` command holds references (deployment,
  project, environment variable ids). At emit time, the generator item map of `nodes.channel`
  delegates to its `commandResolvers` extension point, which `deployments` fills with a generator
  bound to its own context (G16): it loads the deployment to check that it is assigned to the
  subscribing node and delegates to `ctx.services.projects.environmentFor`, a service of `projects`
  that reveals its own secret fields with reveal requests (logged with the deployment id as the
  reason and never recorded, G4).
- Presence: the session's open and close hooks call `nodes.node.connected` and
  `nodes.node.disconnected` (G1). Each heartbeat returns a `setTimer` effect that replaces the keyed
  durable timer `node-offline:<id>` set 45 seconds ahead; when it fires, `nodes.node.markOffline`
  runs under the service principal `nodes.system`, not under the node's credential (section 9.5).
  This also covers a crashed process, which never calls the close hook.
- Join tokens are single use, expire after 15 minutes and are stored as verifiers (section 17.2.2);
  the bundled local agent of the installer gets a bootstrap token issued by the operator.
- Versions: the agent has no protocol of its own any more. Its compatibility is the app's dated API
  version, which its typed client pins, and the live carrier's major (sections 18.7 and 19.7);
  `nodes.node.connect` records `agentVersion` and `apiVersion`, and an agent pinned below the floor
  gets `core.api_version_retired` (section 18.5).
- Cutover (decision 23c): the existing v1 agents are redeployed with the new agent, not kept, and
  the new UI ships with it; the old Launchway installation (v0.3.0) stays in place as the rollback
  until the new one is verified on the home server (roadmap M4).

#### 17.3.5 Deployments

- `deployments.deployment` is chain-backed. Its status follows Launchway's state machine with one
  added state, `dispatched` (sent to the node, not yet cloning), which makes the hand-over
  explicit: `queued`, `dispatched`, `cloning`, `building`, `starting`, `running`, then
  `superseded` or `stopped`; `failed` and `cancelled` from any state before `running`.
- One running deployment per project and environment is a partial unique index
  (`unique` on `projectId, environment` where `status = 'running'`, G7). A successful result marks
  the previous running deployment `superseded` and the new one `running` in one transaction, as
  Launchway's ADR 0009 point 14 requires.
- Dispatch is event-driven instead of a 15-second loop. An async reaction keyed by project
  (`ordering: 'fifo-per-key'`, section 7.7) runs when a deployment is created or finishes, when a
  node comes online and when a retry timer fires. It picks the oldest due deployment of the
  project whose node is online and invokes `deployments.deployment.run`, which returns the
  `dispatched` event and the `agentCommand` effect `deploy` with the continuation `dispatchSettled`
  and a 60-second deadline, in one unit (section 7.9.8): a refusal or silence requeues the
  deployment, up to three retries, and then fails it. One build per project at a time (Launchway's
  dispatch lane) is the key's FIFO order.
- Durable timers (G3) carry every waiting rule of Launchway:
  - a deployment for an offline node fails after 10 minutes (`deployment-node-offline:<id>`);
  - an automatic deployment whose image does not exist yet returns to `queued` and waits 1, 2, 4,
    8, 15, 15 and 15 minutes (Launchway ADR 0019; `deployment-retry:<id>`);
  - a deployment missing from two heartbeats is failed (result lost) or sent again (never
    started), decided by the `heartbeatObservers` filler that `deployments` contributes to
    `nodes`.
- Image retries are domain logic (state machine plus timers), not job retries. The job queue only
  retries infrastructure failures, driven by the error taxonomy's `retryable` flag.
- Events of `deployment` drive the edge (re-render), the GitHub mirror, preview status and audit.

#### 17.3.6 Logs

- Deployment logs are a stream `deployments.log` keyed by deployment (G6): the agent appends
  batches through `deployments.deployment.appendLog`, records are ordered per key and kept (decision
  47c, 2026-10-27: Jens wants to look back on deployments years later), and a log longer than 50,000
  lines moves its older lines into the blob store (`offload`, section 15.1.12) instead of being cut.
  `deployments.deployment.logs` is a subscription that tails from the start, offloaded lines
  included, and follows with a resume token. REST serves it as SSE, GraphQL as a subscription, the
  CLI as `--follow`.
- Runtime is reclaimed, data is kept (decision 47c). When a deployment is superseded or a preview
  closes, the agent's `remove` command reclaims its containers, images, volumes and build caches on
  the node; the deployment's or preview's row, its events and its log stay, and no Launchway module
  suggests a purge rule (section 14.7.1).
- Container logs on demand (`GET /apps/{id}/logs?follow=true` in Launchway v0.3.0) are an
  ephemeral topic `nodes.containerLogs` that is never stored. The first subscriber triggers
  `logs.start` to the node and the last one leaving triggers `logs.stop`: the topic's subscriber
  lifecycle hooks (G6) are pure and return `agentCommand` effects, which the kernel records and the
  agent performs. Slow subscribers lose lines with a gap marker rather than holding the agent back.

#### 17.3.7 Domains and the edge

- `domains.domain` keeps Launchway's statuses (`pending`, `verified`, `misconfigured`, `active`)
  and the `force` flag; `domains.route` keeps the kinds `app`, `external` and `redirect`, the
  options `protected`, `compress` and `hsts`, and the admin-only `extraDirectives`. The DNS
  preflight is an action (`domains.domain.verify`, execution `either`) and a schedule (G3).
  Managed domains ask `dns` for a `CNAME` to the anchor host name.
- Three different "domain" concepts exist in one deployment and must not be confused:
  `core.domain` maps a host name to a backend and tenant for keelwerk's own HTTP host;
  `domains.domain` is a host name a Launchway tenant's edge serves for its projects;
  `mail-domains.mailDomain` is an e-mail domain of a mail tenant (section 17.4.4).
- The edge is a shared module with providers (decision 82a, 2026-10-26), built like `dns` (section
  17.3.8): `edge` (`@keelwerk/module-edge`) owns a provider-neutral desired state and declares
  the `providers` extension point (`extensionPoint.single`), and `edge-caddy` (`@keelwerk/edge-caddy`)
  is the first provider. A custom `edge-native` listener module, Traefik or Envoy can follow as
  further providers without a change to `edge` or its callers. Both are keelwerk packages,
  because a provider package may depend only on published packages (decision 48c) and because any
  app on keelwerk may need an edge.
- Desired state in. `edge.site` rows hold a host name, its owner (`module`, `entity`, `id`), the
  upstreams or the redirect target, the TLS mode and the route options (`protected`, `compress`,
  `hsts` and the admin-only `extraDirectives`). Other modules call pure services instead of writing
  rows: `ctx.services.edge.ensure(owner, sites)` and `ctx.services.edge.release(owner)` return the
  site drafts for the caller's decision. In Launchway, `domains` is the caller: its reactions to
  route, domain, deployment and node changes turn each route and the running deployment it points
  at into sites, a pure function as the render was in Launchway v0.3.0.
- Apply and status out. `edge.render` (state) holds the last applied configuration, its hash and
  the status per site. The reconciler, a keyed and coalescing job per tenant triggered by site and
  configuration changes (G3, G10), plus a drift-repair schedule every 10 minutes and never twice at
  the same time for one tenant (G9), asks the provider to render the complete desired state (pure:
  for `edge-caddy` the complete Caddyfile, as Launchway v0.3.0 renders it) and, when the hash
  differs, returns the `edge.apply` effect with the rendered configuration. Its continuation records
  the outcome, and the provider maps it to a status per site; `domains`, reacting to those statuses
  in a conditional part on `edge`, marks the verified domains whose sites are applied `active`.

```ts
// @keelwerk/module-edge, src/extension-points/providers.ts
export interface EdgeProvider {
  readonly id: string                                                         // 'caddy'
  render(desired: EdgeDesiredState): EdgeConfiguration                        // pure: the provider's configuration and its hash
  status(outcome: EdgeApplyOutcome, desired: EdgeDesiredState): EdgeStatus    // pure: per site applied, pending or failed, with the reason
}
export const providers = extensionPoint.single<EdgeProvider>()
```

- `edge.apply` is an external effect (decision 24a: through the edge node's agent). The program on
  the edge host performs it: it holds the subscription `edge.channel` over the pending `apply`
  effects of its tenant, checks the configuration with the provider's own validation (Caddy's
  `/adapt`), loads it (`/load` on Caddy's admin socket, which only a process on that host can
  open) and settles the effect through `edge.ack`. In Launchway, the edge node's agent is that
  program, beside `nodes.channel` on the same connection (section 17.3.4); `edge.config.performer`
  names the node principal that may hold the channel. No keelwerk process has to run on the edge
  host, and any number of keelwerk processes can serve. An apply left unsettled past its 60-second
  deadline fails, and the next reconcile tries again.
- `edge.rendered` (query) returns the rendered configuration with the reason above each site,
  replacing `GET /edge/config`.
- The keelwerk deployment's own HTTP host sits behind this edge: `external` routes in the
  Launchway tenant point at the keelwerk container with the `Host` header preserved, for
  `deploy.jenspenneman.com` and for the mail tenant's HTTPS host names (section 17.5.3).

#### 17.3.8 DNS (shared with the mail server)

- `dns.providerAccount` holds the provider kind and its credentials as `field.secret()` values
  (G4); `dns.zone` is discovered from the account; `dns.record` holds the desired record, its
  owner (`module`, `entity`, `id`), the provider's external id and the applied status.
- Providers fill the extension point `dns.providers` with an executor-side provider adapter and a
  credentials `shape()`: the adapter is imperative, and only the `applyRecord` executor uses it
  (`ExecutorContext.extensions`, section 7.9.5); the walkable field model yields the JSON Schema the
  UI renders as a form, which Launchway does with Zod in v0.3.0. The provider contract grows from
  Launchway's `A`, `AAAA`, `CNAME` and `TXT` to `MX` and `SRV` for the mail server, with `CAA` and
  `TLSA` later.
- Other modules call pure services instead of writing records:
  `ctx.services.dns.ensure(owner, records)` and `ctx.services.dns.release(owner)` return the record
  drafts and one `applyRecord` effect per changed record, with the continuation
  `dns.record.applied`, for the caller's decision. The executor applies a change with mechanical
  retries (429 and 5xx: the upsert is idempotent) in a group per provider account that respects the
  provider's rate limits (G3), and `applied` marks the record applied or failed (section 7.9.8).
- The public-address schedule (every 5 minutes, two independent services must agree; the lookups
  are an effect whose continuation decides) updates the anchor `A` record and every record marked
  `followPublicAddress`. The mail server needs the
  latter: an MX target must be an address record, never an alias (RFC 2181 section 10.3), so
  `mail.jenspenneman.com` cannot be a `CNAME` to the anchor.
- The module only modifies records it created (stored external ids, plus a comment tag where the
  provider supports it). Two backends can therefore manage disjoint records in one zone, which is
  the case for `jenspenneman.com` (section 17.5.3).

#### 17.3.9 GitHub

- `github.connection` holds the kind (`app` or `token`), the GitHub App ids and installation id,
  and the private key, client secret, webhook secret or personal access token as secrets (G4).
- The manifest flow is two actions with redirect results (G8): `github.startManifest`
  answers with a redirect to GitHub carrying a `state`, and `github.completeManifest`
  receives the `code`, converts it through an inline effect in its `prepare` (GitHub returns the
  App's secrets once, inside the request; section 7.9.4) and seals the secrets in its decision. The
  installation callback works the same way.
- Webhooks arrive through a receiver of `transport-webhooks` at `/hooks/github/<connection id>`
  (G8). The deployment's carrier enricher turns the path into the scope key before scope
  resolution; the receiver's verification resolver, a pure generator bound to `github`, checks
  `X-Hub-Signature-256` with the connection's webhook secret (a reveal request) in constant time over
  the raw body (`hmacSha256` and `timingSafeEqual` of `@keelwerk/core/crypto`), and only then does
  the request act as `github.webhook` (section 16.5.8). `X-GitHub-Delivery` is
  the command id (receipts drop replays; the deliveries table goes away), and `github.ingest`
  parses the payload and appends domain events to the connection's chain: `releasePublished`,
  `pushed`, `pullRequestChanged`, `installationChanged`.
- Automatic deployments are async reactions to those events. They invoke
  `deployments.createAutomatic` with the command id `release:<tag>` or `push:<sha>`, whose
  idempotency window is 30 days (`idempotency: { window: 'P30D' }`); beyond it, a unique
  `(projectId, environment, triggerKey)` on automatic deployments is the deduplication of record, so
  a delivery GitHub repeats weeks later never deploys twice.
- The deployment mirror is an asynchronous reaction to `deployments.deployment` events, keyed by
  deployment and coalescing (G3), so steps of one deployment run one at a time and GitHub converges
  on the latest status. The reaction returns an effect whose executor calls GitHub's API;
  rate-limited answers are `rate_limited` errors with `retryAfter`, which the executor's mechanical
  retries honour. A refusal settles the effect as failed, and its continuation sets `refusedUntil`
  on the connection, pausing it for 5 minutes.
- Release polling for token connections is a schedule every 5 minutes per tenant (G3); each run
  requests a GitHub read as an effect whose continuation records the new releases.
- Contributions: `projects.project` gains `githubConnectionId`, `repository`,
  `autoDeployReleases`, `autoDeployPrereleases`, `autoDeployBranch` and `githubDeployments`;
  `deployments.deployment` gains `githubDeploymentId`; `projects.gitProviders` receives the
  GitHub implementation of `GitProvider` (`listRepos`, `listReleases`, `resolveRef`,
  `cloneCredentials`, `getPullRequest`), whose calls to GitHub are effects; how a user interface
  reads them (the repository picker) is an open question of section 26.3.
- Libraries: `@octokit/app` 16.1.4, `@octokit/rest` 22.0.1 and `@octokit/webhooks` 14.2.0 (all
  MIT).

#### 17.3.10 Previews

- `previews.preview` keeps Launchway's fields and statuses (`pending`, `deploying`, `running`,
  `failed`, `closing`, `closed`) and its limits (10 per project, 20 in total), checked
  synchronously in `previews.open` because they are cross-entity invariants. Expected versions
  cannot see a concurrently inserted preview, so `previews.open` locks the project row and the
  tenant's preview counter (a usage counter, section 12.2) for its unit before counting; two
  concurrent opens on one project queue instead of both counting nine (section 14.3.6).
- Contributions: the preview settings become fields of `projects.project` (`previewsEnabled`,
  `previewSkipBots`, `previewRequireLabel`, `previewHostTemplate`, `previewEnvOverrides`,
  `previewComposeFiles`) and `previewId` a field of `deployments.deployment`. Without the module,
  none of them exists in the types or the tables.
- A conditional part on `github` adds the reaction to `pullRequestChanged` (opened, reopened,
  synchronize, labeled, unlabeled, closed), keyed by repository and pull request number (G3).
  Without `github`, previews are opened by hand through `previews.open`, which reads the pull
  request through the project's git provider.
- Closing removes the route and domain through `domains` actions and sends `remove` to the node,
  which reclaims the preview's containers, images, volumes and build caches; a step that cannot
  finish leaves the preview `closing` and a timer retries it (G3). The closed preview's row, events
  and logs are kept: nothing purges them unless Jens adopts a rule (decision 47c, section 14.7.1).

#### 17.3.11 Accounts, authentication, tokens and roles

The shared modules are used unchanged; Launchway's rules live in Launchway's modules, reference
roles from the `members` enricher and combine them with conditions, which is the point of the
CASL-style engine over plain roles.

```ts
// modules/projects/src/policies/project/read.ts (Launchway repository): the rule projects.project.read
export const read = defineRule(projectsBase, project, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['read'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => hasRole(ctx, 'viewer', 'member', 'admin', 'owner'),
})

// modules/projects/src/policies/project/manage.ts
export const manage = defineRule(projectsBase, project, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['create', 'update'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => hasRole(ctx, 'member', 'admin', 'owner'),
  fields: ['name', 'slug', 'dockerfile', 'context', 'nodeId'],   // the fields members may change; the deployment comes from the repository's .launchway/ (section 17.3.1)
})

// modules/projects/src/policies/project/admin-fields.ts
export const adminFields = defineRule(projectsBase, project, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['create', 'update'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => hasRole(ctx, 'admin', 'owner'),
  fields: ['trustedMounts', 'proxyServices'],
  reason: 'Bind mounts and proxy attachments change what a node and the edge expose.',
})

// modules/projects/src/policies/project/archive.ts: members edit; only admins archive
export const archive = defineRule(projectsBase, project, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['archive', 'restore'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => hasRole(ctx, 'admin', 'owner'),
})

// modules/projects/src/policies/env-var/read-env.ts
export const readEnv = defineRule(projectsBase, envVar, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['read'],
  principal: 'user',
  where: (ctx) => hasRole(ctx, 'member', 'admin', 'owner'),          // viewers never see variables; `value` is a secret field (G4)
})

// modules/deployments/src/policies/deployment/assigned-node.ts: a node reports only on its own work.
export const assignedNode = defineRule(deploymentsBase, deployment, {
  effect: 'allow',
  actions: ['reportPhase', 'reportResult', 'reportRuntime', 'appendLog'],
  principal: 'service',
  where: (ctx) => (ctx.principal.via === 'nodes.credential' ? { nodeId: ctx.principal.idAs('nodes.node') } : false),
  reason: 'A node reports only on deployments assigned to it.',
})

// @keelwerk/module-api-keys, src/policies/read-only-key.ts: the rule api-keys.read-only-key;
// read-only keys cannot run commands in any module.
export const readOnlyKey = defineRule(apiKeysBase, { kinds: ['command'] }, {   // G13: a selector across modules
  effect: 'deny',
  when: (ctx) => ctx.principal.via === 'api-keys.key' && !hasScope(ctx, 'write'),
  reason: 'This API key has the read scope only.',
})
```

The gate authorizes `reportResult` for the node; inside the handler, `deployments` reads and
supersedes the previous running deployment with its own authority (section 8.4), so the node
principal needs no rule on other deployments.

- The owner cannot be removed: a deny rule on `members.membership` with
  `where: () => ({ role: 'owner' })` and a reason; ownership moves through a dedicated command.
- Session cookies, origin checks (`Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site`) and trusted proxies for the client
  address are concerns of the HTTP host (sections 16.3.3 and 16.4.10); rate limits on login,
  passkey and token actions are `auth`'s admission rule at `admit` (section 17.2.6).
- Passkeys stay on `@simplewebauthn/server` (14.0.3, MIT) inside `auth` (section 17.2.2).
- The home node that runs keelwerk and PostgreSQL is itself a Launchway node, and its agent
  controls Docker. A project with `trustedMounts` could mount keelwerk's volumes or the Docker
  socket, so on that node `allowedBindRoots` excludes keelwerk's volumes and the Docker socket by
  default, and the admin role of the tenant that owns the node is treated as operator-equivalent in
  the threat model (section 17.5.2).

#### 17.3.12 Settings as module configuration

Launchway's settings row becomes the configuration of the modules that use it. Owners and admins
edit it in the UI of v0.3.0, so configuration must be editable by tenant principals through actions,
under policies, with change events (G10).

| Launchway setting | Module configuration |
|---|---|
| `publicUrl` | the tenant's `core.domain`, plus `edge.config.platformHost` |
| `acmeEmail` | `edge.config.acmeEmail` |
| `anchorHostname`, dynamic DNS on or off | `dns.config.anchor`, `dns.config.detectPublicAddress` |
| `forwardAuthUrl`, `forwardAuthTarget` | `edge.config.gate` (a union of the two) |
| `edgeNodeId` | `edge.config.performer`: the edge node's principal (its `nodes.credential` subject), which may hold `edge.channel` |
| `previewBaseDomain`, `previewMaxPerApp`, `previewMaxTotal` | `previews.config.baseDomain`, `.maxPerProject`, `.maxTotal` |

#### 17.3.13 The app definition

The app is the package `@launchway/app-launchway` in the Launchway repository (`apps/launchway/`),
and each of its own modules is a package in `modules/<id>/` named `@launchway/module-<id>`, in the
layout of section 23 (section 23.10 shows the trees). The repository depends only on the published
`@keelwerk/*` packages, pinned to exact 0.x versions (decision 48c); paths in the code below are
relative to it, and each module's `src/module.generated.ts` is written by the generator (section
23.5).

```ts
// apps/launchway/src/modules.ts
import { accounts } from '@keelwerk/module-accounts'
import { auth } from '@keelwerk/module-auth'
import { apiKeys } from '@keelwerk/module-api-keys'
import { members } from '@keelwerk/module-members'
import { audit } from '@keelwerk/module-audit'
```
