| `dns`, `dns-cloudflare`, `dns-manual` | shared, new | yes | yes (`dns-manual` optional) |
| `certificates` | shared, new | no (the edge obtains certificates) | yes |
| `blobs`, `blobs-fs`, `blobs-s3` | shared, new (G5) | yes (long deployment logs, decision 47c) | yes |
| `transport-webhooks` | shared, new (G8) | yes | no |
| `transport-jmap` | shared, new | no | yes |
| `adapter-postgres`, `transport-http` (with the invocation protocol), `blobs-fs` | infrastructure of the deployment | yes | yes |
| `live`, `transport-rest` | shared modules | yes | yes |
| `transport-graphql`, `transport-trpc` | shared infrastructure | yes | optional |
| `transport-orpc` | shared infrastructure (decision 15b) | optional | optional |
| `edge`, `edge-caddy` | shared, new (decision 82a) | yes | no (its HTTPS host names go through Launchway's edge, section 17.5.3) |
| `outbound-webhooks` | shared, new (decision 49a) | yes | optional |
| `projects`, `nodes`, `deployments`, `domains`, `github`, `previews` | Launchway, in the Launchway repository | yes | no |
| `mail-domains`, `mail-store`, `sender-auth`, `spam`, `smtp-in`, `smtp-submission`, `mail-delivery`, `imap`, `mta-sts`, `autoconfig`; later `sieve`, `antivirus`, `dmarc-reports` | mail, in the mail server's repository (parked) | no | yes |

#### 17.6.2 Commands that must stay synchronous

Launchway:

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `projects.project.set` (create, slug change) | slug unique per tenant; Compose project names and proxy aliases derive from it |
| `projects.envVar.set` | key unique per project; keys starting with `LAUNCHWAY_` refused |
| `nodes.join`, `nodes.node.issueJoinToken`, `api-keys.create` | a secret is shown exactly once |
| `auth.login`, passkey ceremonies, `auth.logout` | token issuance and revocation |
| `members.invitation.accept` | single use |
| `domains.domain.set` (create) | host name unique per tenant |
| `domains.route.set` | one route per domain; proxy aliases unique across projects |
| `deployments.create` | resolves the ref to a commit and returns the id; deduplicates automatic triggers per tag or commit |
| `deployments.deployment.cancel`, `.stop` | the state change is visible at once; the node message follows as an `agentCommand` effect, whose record is the outbox |
| `deployments.deployment.report*`, `nodes.node.heartbeat` | node reports must be ordered with the state machine |
| `previews.open` | limits per project and in total (cross-entity invariant) |
| `github.completeManifest` | GitHub returns the App's secrets once, to the inline effect of its `prepare` |
| `github.ingest` | signature check and receipt before GitHub gets its answer |
| `<module>.config.set` (G10) | settings apply to the next request |

Asynchronous by design: edge reconciliation, DNS record application, the GitHub deployment
mirror, release polling, preview teardown steps, and automatic deployments created by reactions to
webhook events.

Mail:

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `mail-store.acceptInbound` | durable before the SMTP `250` |
| `mail-delivery.submit` | durable before the SMTP `250` or the JMAP response |
| `mail-domains.addDomain` | scope key unique across the deployment (G2) |
| `mail-store.address.set` | address unique per tenant, aliases included |
| `mail-store.mailbox.set` (create, rename) | name unique among siblings (IMAP, JMAP) |
| `mail-store.importEmail`, `mail-store.email.copyTo`, `.moveTo` | IMAP clients receive the new UIDs (UIDPLUS) |
| `mail-store.email.setKeywords` from IMAP `STORE` | IMAP clients receive the new MODSEQ (CONDSTORE) |
| `api-keys.create` (app passwords) | a secret is shown exactly once |
| `sender-auth.createKey` | the private key is generated and sealed; publication follows asynchronously |
| `mail-delivery.testRelay` | the operator waits for the relay's answer: an inline effect in `prepare` (section 17.4.7) |

Asynchronous by design: `mail-store.inbound.file`, the `smtpDeliver` effects with their
continuation `mail-delivery.submission.recordAttempt`, `.retryDomain` and `.bounce`, DNS
publication, spam learning, DKIM rotation steps and retention purges.

#### 17.6.3 Offline authorship and live updates

| Data | Live updates | Offline authorship |
|---|---|---|
| Every Launchway entity | yes (UI refresh, logs, deployment progress) | no: every command touches machines, DNS or GitHub, or checks a uniqueness or a quota; offline edits would be proposals that mostly fail |
| `mail-store.email.keywords` (`$seen`, `$flagged`, ...) | yes | yes, merge `set` |
| `mail-store.email.mailboxIds` (moving and labelling) | yes | yes, merge `set`; the rule "at least one mailbox" is checked at ingest |
| Drafts (new `email` rows in the Drafts mailbox) | yes | yes; the blob is uploaded on reconnect |
| `mail-store.mailbox.sortOrder`, `.subscribed`; `identity` fields; `vacationResponse` | yes | yes, merge `lww` |
| Mailbox names, addresses, domains, submissions, app passwords | yes | no: unique fields or external side effects |

JMAP clients already work offline in their own way (state strings and `ifInState`); the
keelwerk push protocol of section 15.3 applies to clients that use the framework's
own client.

#### 17.6.4 The SQL escape hatch

The mail server does not force it. Mailbox search uses the keyed token index over personal text
(section 14.7.9.9) combined with the authorization plan, UIDs use a per-partition serial, JMAP and
IMAP synchronisation use partitioned, commit-ordered change positions and positional paging for JMAP
(all G7), and queue locking lives inside the job store behind `JobQueue`. On an adapter that lacks
one of these capabilities, `mail-store` still runs: the kernel's paths of section 14.3.3 serve it at
the cost `keelwerk doctor` reports (brief addendum 5). The escape hatch remains useful for
operator reports and DMARC aggregate statistics, which are optional modules.

#### 17.6.5 Names that differ from the first draft

The first draft of this specification (2026-10-08) named the proof apps' modules provisionally.

| First draft | Now | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `teams` (Launchway) | `members` | Launchway's roles and invitations are tenant-wide memberships; `teams` stays free for groups inside a tenant |
| `projects` | `projects`, shown as "apps" in Launchway's UI | "app" is keelwerk's word for a composition and `app` is a reserved module id |
| `domains` (mail) | `mail-domains` | an e-mail domain differs from a Launchway domain and from `core.domain` |
| `mailboxes`, `messages` | `mail-store` | one cohesive store; the protocol modules around it are what can be switched off |
| `smtp` | `smtp-in`, `smtp-submission`, `mail-delivery` | receiving, submission and delivery are toggled independently |
| `queues` | the kernel job queue and `mail-delivery` | the queue is the kernel's `JobQueue` over the adapters' job store; delivery is a module |
| `dkim` | `sender-auth` | SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC belong together |

#### 17.6.6 Where platform modules live

Shared platform modules (`module-members`, `module-dns`, `dns-cloudflare`, `dns-manual`,
`module-edge`, `edge-caddy`, `module-outbound-webhooks`, `module-certificates`, `blobs-fs` and later
`blobs-s3`, `transport-webhooks`, `transport-jmap`) are packages of this repository (section 22).
Every app built on keelwerk lives in its own repository and depends only on the published
packages, never on this repository (decision 48c, 2026-10-27): Launchway's own modules are packages
in the Launchway repository, `modules/<id>/` (`@launchway/module-<id>`), with the app in
`apps/launchway/` (section 23.10); Trail's backend is rebuilt in the Trail repository first (roadmap
M3); the mail server's modules get a repository of their own when Jens unparks it (section 23.11).
This repository keeps `examples/portal` for its own CI. Moving a module between repositories changes
its package name and nothing inside it.

### 17.7 Gaps for the core and where they land

Mapping both platforms onto the core found sixteen gaps. The ids are stable references, because
other sections cite them; G16 was found last and therefore carries the highest id, although it
ranks third. Most gaps are now specified in the core sections; the rest are proposals whose ADRs
the roadmap schedules before the milestone that first needs them ([roadmap.md](roadmap.md)).

| Id | Gap | Needed by | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | Connection-oriented listeners and invoker sessions | Launchway agents; SMTP, IMAP, JMAP | sessions specified; listener contract proposed, ADR before the mail foundations (parked) | sections 9.2 and 16.3.4; proposal below |
| G2 | Scope directory for keys other than host names | tokens, node credentials, webhook paths, mail domains | proposed, ADR before M4 | proposal below |
| G16 | Extension values bound to their contributor's context | git providers, heartbeat observers, DKIM signers, inbound checks | specified (ADR 0003; pure values since ADR 0026) | sections 5.5 and 7.9.2 |
| G3 | Jobs, durable timers and schedules | both platforms throughout | specified (ADRs 0015 and 0025) | sections 7.7, 9.5, 14.3.9 and 21 |
| G4 | Secrets and a key hierarchy | Launchway environments and credentials; DKIM keys, relay password, certificates | key service and sealing specified; the `ctx.secrets` interface proposed, ADR before M3 | sections 6.6 and 14.7.4; proposal below |
| G5 | Blob storage | deployment logs past their offload threshold (decision 47c); messages, attachments, uploads | proposed, ADR before M4 | section 5.2 (the `blobs` contract); proposal below |
| G6 | Streams, topics and a live feed for state entities | deployment logs, container logs, the agent channel, delivery attempts | storage and live delivery specified; the DSL lands in M2 | sections 15.1.10, 15.1.12 and 15.4 |
| G7 | Change positions and data capabilities | IMAP and JMAP synchronisation, mail search, UIDs, Launchway's one-running-deployment rule | specified | sections 14.3.3, 14.3.5, 14.5.1, 14.7.9 and 15.1.4 |
| G8 | HTTP ingress beyond JSON actions | GitHub webhooks and manifest flow; MTA-STS, autoconfig, JMAP downloads | specified | section 16.5.8 |
| G9 | Process capabilities and singleton work | mail ports, the edge, reconcilers | named processes and capabilities specified (ADR 0025); singleton leases proposed, ADR 0018 before M4 | section 21; proposal below |
| G10 | Tenant-editable configuration with change events | Launchway settings, mail policies | specified | section 5.7 |
| G11 | Retention and purge | Trash and Junk, previews, logs, delivery queues, command rows | specified | section 14.7.1 |
| G12 | Cross-cutting observers and request metadata | audit, later outbound webhooks and search indexers | request metadata specified; `observes: 'all'` proposed | sections 11 and 15.1.7; proposal below |
| G13 | Rules over credential scopes | API key scopes, app passwords per listener | specified (ADR 0005) | section 8.1 |
| G14 | Extension-point cardinality and carrier coverage checks | git providers, SASL-capable resolvers | specified | sections 5.2 and 5.5 |
| G15 | Hyphenated module ids in the context types | every module with a hyphen in its id | specified | sections 3.4 and 5.1 |

#### G1. Connection-oriented listeners and invoker sessions

Status: sessions (`Invoker.open`, `InvocationSession`) are specified in sections 9.2 and 16.3.4; the
listener contract below is a proposal, and its ADR lands before the mail foundations milestone
(roadmap; parked with the mail server).

Problem. The pipeline resolves scope and principal per invocation from a carrier. SMTP, IMAP and
the agent WebSocket are long-lived connections: the scope is known only after `AUTHENTICATE` or
`LOGIN` (IMAP, submission), or once per recipient (an SMTP transaction can reach several tenants),
and a connection performs hundreds of invocations under the same principal. Section 16.3.4 has
`invoker.open(carrier)`, which returns an `InvocationSession` (scope, app, principal, `expiresAt`,
`revalidate()`) that invocations reuse, and section 16.3.7 sends non-HTTP listeners through the
same call. What the platforms still need from the core is the listener side:
ports are a deployment resource while listener modules belong to apps (one port 25 must serve every
backend that runs `smtp-in`), the `Listener` extension point of section 5.6 has no
contract, and `Carrier.connection` is unspecified.

Proposal:

```ts
interface Connection {
  readonly id: string
  readonly listener: string                                   // 'smtp-in.mx', 'imap.imaps', 'smtp-submission.submission'
  readonly remote: { address: string; port: number }          // after PROXY protocol or trusted-proxy rules
  readonly local: { address: string; port: number }
  readonly tls?: { serverName?: string; protocol: string; cipher: string }
}
interface Carrier {                                            // section 9.2, extended
  readonly transport: string
  readonly connection?: Connection
  readonly sasl?: { mechanism: 'PLAIN' | 'LOGIN' | 'OAUTHBEARER' | 'XOAUTH2'; authcid: string; authzid?: string; secret: string }
  readonly scopeKey?: { kind: string; value: string }         // G2
  // host, path, headers, token, local as before
}
interface ListenerSpec {
  readonly id: string
  readonly ports: Readonly<Record<string, { default: number; tls: 'none' | 'starttls' | 'implicit'; proxyProtocol?: 'off' | 'optional' | 'required'; enabled?: boolean }>>
  readonly capability?: string                                // G9
  start(kit: ListenerKit): Promise<{ accept(socket: Socket, port: string): void; updateCertificates(options: SecureContextOptions): void; drain(deadline: Temporal.Instant): Promise<void> }>
}
interface ListenerKit {
  readonly hostname: string
  readonly certificates: { sniCallback: SniCallback }        // filled by the certificates module
  readonly blobs: { stage(body: ReadableStream<Uint8Array>, options: { maxBytes: number }): Promise<StagedBlob> }   // G5
  readonly limits: Readonly<Record<string, number>>           // from the module's config; the largest value over backends
  /** invoker.open (section 16.3.4) plus invocations and subscriptions bound to the session. */
  readonly sessions: { open(carrier: Omit<Carrier, 'transport'>): Promise<Outcome<BoundSession>> }
  readonly telemetry: Telemetry
}
interface BoundSession {
  readonly scope: Scope
  readonly principal: Principal
  invoke(ref: string, input: unknown, options?: { commandId?: string; prefer?: 'sync' | 'async' }): Promise<Outcome<unknown>>
  subscribe(ref: string, input: unknown, resume?: { after: StateToken }): AsyncIterable<Emitted<unknown>>
}
```

- `defineDeployment({ ports })` binds sockets; one socket per listener port serves every backend
  running that module. Two different listener modules claiming one port number fail at boot.
- A connection may open several sessions (one per recipient tenant on an SMTP transaction) or open
  its session late (after `AUTHENTICATE`). `admit` runs at connection time (connections per remote
  address and per listener) as well as per invocation.
- A listener can present its own service principal for protocol steps without client
  authentication (the MX), so actions that only a listener may call are never public. The carrier
  is produced in-process, so this principal cannot be forged from the network.
- Revalidation (section 16.3.4: at `expiresAt` and at least every 60 seconds) also runs on
  revocation events of the session's credential, membership and tenant, so a revoked app password
  or node credential ends its IMAP or agent connection within seconds; the listener then closes
  with its protocol's goodbye (SMTP `421`, IMAP `BYE`, WebSocket close).
- Open and close hooks map to actions for presence (`nodes.node.connected`, `.disconnected`).
- A connection span is the parent of the invocation spans, so one IMAP session or SMTP transaction
  reads as one trace.
- TLS material comes from the deployment-level certificate directory of section 17.4.12 (SNI callback,
  reload without restart).

#### G2. Scope directory for keys other than host names

Status: proposal; its ADR lands before M4, the first milestone whose app resolves tenants from
tokens and webhook paths (Launchway's node credentials and GitHub's receiver paths; Trail, in M3, is
one tenant resolved by its host name) (roadmap).

Problem. `resolveScope` runs before any tenant data is reachable, and tenant data may live in
another database (placements). Resolvers by host name work because `core.domain` lives in the
control store. Launchway and mail need the same for other keys: an API token or node credential
(which tenant issued it), a webhook path (which tenant owns GitHub connection `gh_...`), a mail
domain (which tenant receives `jens@jenspenneman.com`). Some of these keys must also be unique
across the deployment: two tenants must never both claim one mail domain.

Proposal:

```ts
type ScopeKey = { kind: 'hostname' | 'mail-domain' | 'webhook-endpoint' | 'node-credential' | 'api-key' | (string & {}); value: string }
interface ScopeDirectory {                        // kernel-internal: module code returns the effects below
  /** Unique across the deployment; `conflict` when another scope holds the key. */
  claim(key: ScopeKey, owner: { module: string; entity: string; id: string }): Promise<void>
  release(key: ScopeKey, owner: { module: string; entity: string; id: string }): Promise<void>
  /** Cached per process and invalidated by the control store's change feed. */
  resolve(key: ScopeKey): Promise<{ backendId: string; tenantId: string } | undefined>
}
// module code:   claimScopeKey({ kind: 'mail-domain', value: 'jenspenneman.com' }, owner, { continueWith: claimed })   // a kernel effect after commit (section 7.9.5)
// resolver:      byScopeKey()  reads carrier.scopeKey, set by listeners, receivers and token parsers
```

- `core.domain` becomes the `hostname` kind of the same directory.
- Tokens carry a public id (`<prefix>_<public id>_<secret>`, section 17.2.2); the public id is the scope
  key, the secret is verified against the hash in the tenant's data.
- The claim lives in the control store and the owning row in the tenant's placement, so the two
  cannot share a transaction. Decision 50a settles the choice the ADR had to make (claim first with
  a compensating release on rollback, or an outbox with a reconciler) as the outbox:
  `claimScopeKey` and `releaseScopeKey` are kernel effects whose `requested` records commit with the
  owning row and which the kernel performs after commit in the control store. The continuation
  (`continueWith`) receives the outcome, so a `conflict` (another scope holds the key) becomes a decision of
  the owning module, such as marking the mail domain rejected; an effect left unsettled after a
  crash is performed again, and claims are idempotent per owner (section 7.9.5).
- Release and claim of security-sensitive kinds (mail domains, webhook endpoints) need care because
  the directory is cached per process and invalidated asynchronously: a released key stays
  quarantined for longer than the cache staleness before another scope may claim it, or the
  resolver checks those kinds synchronously against the control store. The SMTP listener does the
  latter (section 17.4.4).

#### G16. Extension values bound to their contributor's context

Problem. The declaring module reads an extension point's values through `ctx.extensions`; when a
value is a function, it used to run with the declaring module's context, so the password provider
of `auth` could not read `auth.credential`, GitHub's `GitProvider.cloneCredentials` could not reach
the connection's secret, the `heartbeatObservers` filler of `deployments` could not read
deployment rows, the DKIM signer of `sender-auth` could not reach its keys, and the inbound check of
`spam` could not read its own configuration. Services had the same defect: callers passed their own
context, so a provider ran with the caller's configuration and data view.

Status: specified in section 5.5 and ADR 0003. Behavioural fillers are factories
`(own) => value` that the kernel binds per invocation to the contributor's pure context (same
scope, principal and trace; the contributor's load authority, write boundary, services,
configuration and secret requests; no unit of its own); behavioural values return values or
generators, never promises (section 7.9.2). Services are bound to their provider the same way, and
call sites pass no context. The principal never widens.

#### G3. Jobs, durable timers and schedules

Problem. The platforms need per-project dispatch lanes (FIFO per key), per-destination
concurrency (mail), debounced reconcilers (edge, DNS, the GitHub mirror), durable timers keyed by
business ids (node offline after 45 seconds, deployment offline after 10 minutes, image retries,
preview teardown retries), schedules per tenant (public address every 5 minutes, release polling,
certificate renewal, DKIM rotation, retention), retry policies with explicit schedules (mail
delivery for up to 5 days), heartbeats for long jobs, cancellation by key and dead letters, on
every adapter the proof apps run on.

Status: specified in sections 7.7, 9.5, 14.3.9 and 21 and ADRs 0015 and 0025. The kernel job queue
runs over the data adapters' job store with keys (keep, replace, coalesce), fair lanes with caps
and weights per tenant and queue, a queued cap with backpressure, groups with concurrency and
rates, priority classes, FIFO per key, retry schedules driven by the error taxonomy, leases fenced
by (worker, attempt), expiry, dead letters and schedules (`backend` or `each-tenant`). Jobs store
a principal reference that is resolved again when they run; timers, schedules and reactions run
under the module's service principal. pg-boss 12.38.0 now has groups, FIFO per key, heartbeats,
Kysely enqueue and PGlite, but no MySQL, SQLite or in-memory store, no scope predicate and no fair
shares; the queue stays replaceable by an infrastructure entry (decision point 6 of section 26.1).

#### G4. Secrets and a key hierarchy

Problem. Both platforms need module code to read secrets on purpose: Launchway builds deploy
payloads with environment values and calls GitHub with the App's private key and DNS providers
with stored tokens; the mail server signs with DKIM private keys, authenticates to the relay and
serves certificates. The brief makes secrets per tenant, and erasure and purges need per-record
keys.

Status: the key service (master key, deployment, backend and tenant keys, subject and value keys),
sealing of credential material with per-value keys destroyed on overwrite, and the rule that only
the owning module reads its secrets are specified in sections 6.6 and 14.7.4. The `ctx.secrets`
interface below is a proposal; its ADR lands before M3 (roadmap).

```ts
interface SecretRequests {                         // ctx.secrets in handlers: requests the key service answers (section 7.9.3)
  /** The only read path for a `field.secret()` value: the owning module's handlers (and its bound services and extension values); logged with the reason, never recorded. */
  reveal(value: SecretRef, reason: string): Request<string>
  /** One-time secrets: the plain token goes to the caller once; the decision record keeps only the public id and the verifier. */
  issue(options: { prefix: string; bytes?: number }): Request<{ plain: string; publicId: string; verifier: string }>
  /** Constant-time comparison of a presented token with a stored verifier. */
  verify(presented: string, verifier: string): Request<boolean>
}
interface ExecutorSecrets {                        // ctx.secrets in effect executors only (section 7.9.5)
  reveal(value: SecretRef, reason: string): Promise<string>
}
// Sealing is no call: a draft that sets a `field.secret()` field carries the plain value, and the kernel seals it at append
// with a fresh value key bound to (entity, id, field), destroying the previous value's key.
```

- Verifier-only secrets (API keys, app passwords, join tokens, node credentials, session tokens)
  never use `reveal`; reversible secrets (provider credentials, DKIM and TLS private keys, the
  GitHub App key, environment values) do, always from the module that owns the field. Other modules
  reach them through that module's services, as `deployments` reaches environment values through
  `projects.environmentFor` (section 17.3.4).
- Secrets in module configuration (`relayPassword`, provider tokens) are sealed under the backend's
  key, or the tenant's for tenant overrides.

#### G5. Blob storage

Problem. `field.binary()` is a `Uint8Array`, fit for small payloads only. Mail needs streaming
writes with a size limit, hashing while streaming, range reads (IMAP partial fetches), a
deployment-level staging area for SMTP data that is adopted into several tenants, per-tenant
encryption, purge by key destruction, quotas, and uploads and downloads through JMAP, REST and the
CLI.

Status: the `blobs` contract (deployment level) and the `blobStores` deployment extension point
are specified in sections 5.2 and 5.6; the interfaces below are a proposal whose ADR lands before
M4, where Launchway's long deployment logs move into the blob store (decision 47c), and the mail
server then needs it for messages (roadmap).

```ts
// field kind; the value is a reference
raw: field.blob({ mediaType: 'message/rfc822', maxBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024 })      // BlobRef { id, size, sha256, mediaType }

interface Blobs {                                                                  // ExecutorContext.blobs and the listener kit, for modules that require contracts.blobs
  put(body: ReadableStream<Uint8Array>, options: { mediaType: string; maxBytes: number }): Promise<BlobRef>
  get(ref: BlobRef, options?: { range?: { start: number; end?: number } }): Promise<ReadableStream<Uint8Array>>
  adopt(staged: StagedBlobRef): Promise<BlobRef>                                   // from the deployment staging area
}
interface BlobStore {                                                              // deployment extension point `blobStores`
  readonly capabilities: { range: boolean; copy: boolean }
  write(namespace: string, key: string, body: ReadableStream<Uint8Array>): Promise<{ size: number }>
  read(namespace: string, key: string, range?: { start: number; end?: number }): Promise<ReadableStream<Uint8Array>>
  copy?(from: { namespace: string; key: string }, to: { namespace: string; key: string }): Promise<void>
  remove(namespace: string, key: string): Promise<void>
}
```

- Each blob is encrypted with its own data key wrapped by the tenant's key, or by the data subject's
  key for personal blobs (section 14.7.4). Purge and erasure destroy the key; the collector removes
  the bytes later, never before the deployment's backup retention has passed (section 14.7.6).
- A blob belongs to the rows that reference it; reading it is reading that field, so field masks
  and plans apply. Transports project blob inputs as uploads and blob outputs as downloads with
  range support. Blob bytes count towards the tenant's storage quota (section 12.2).
- Handlers hold `BlobRef` values and never read bytes: effect executors and listeners use `Blobs`
  (section 7.9.5), and adopting a staged blob is a kernel step before the unit of the command that
  references it, so no row references a missing blob (section 17.4.6; whether it should be a
  deferred kernel effect instead is an open question of section 26.3).
- Stores: a file system first (`blobs-fs`), an S3-compatible API second (`blobs-s3`).

#### G6. Streams, topics and a live feed for state entities

Problem. Deployment logs (thousands of lines per build), delivery attempts and SMTP transcripts are
append-only records that are not entities: a chain event per line would multiply storage, and
`history: 'state'` rows have no chain events, so the live feed of section 9.6 does
not cover them. Container logs requested on demand must never be stored at all. The agent channel
and node presence are `history: 'state'` entities that still need live updates.

Status: storage (section 15.1.12), transient change records for `state` entities (section
15.1.10) and live delivery of streams and topics (section 15.4) are specified; the DSL below lands
with the live module in M2 (roadmap).

```ts
const log = defineStream({
  key: field.ref.own('deployment'),                           // ordered per key
  record: shape({ at: field.instant(), source: field.enum(['stdout', 'stderr', 'system']), line: field.text() }),
  offload: { afterPerKey: 50_000 },                           // older lines move to the blob store; nothing is purged (decision 47c)
  readAs: 'deployment',                                       // may read the stream when it may `get` the keyed row
})
ctx.write.deployments.log.append(deploymentId, records)                         // a draft: a batch append in the decision's unit
ctx.live.stream('deployments', 'log', { key: deploymentId, from: 'start' })     // a source description: tail and follow, resumable

const containerLogs = defineTopic({                           // never stored
  key: shape({ projectId: field.string(), service: field.string() }),
  record: logLineShape,
  onFirstSubscriber: (key, ctx) => startContainerLogs(ctx, key),       // pure: returns the agentCommand effect logs.start (section 17.3.6)
  onLastSubscriberLeft: (key, ctx) => stopContainerLogs(ctx, key),     // and logs.stop
})
```

- The change feed also carries changes of `history: 'state'` entities, with positions, so
  subscriptions such as `nodes.channel` resume after a reconnect.
- Slow subscribers on topics lose records with a gap marker; streams resume from a token.

#### G7. Change positions and data capabilities

Requirements from the mail server first: commit-ordered positions (a reader must never see a
later position while an earlier one can still commit, or IMAP and JMAP clients miss changes for
good); change tokens partitioned by a field (`accountId`); per-partition serials for IMAP UIDs;
full-text search on declared indexes combined with the authorization plan; positional paging for
JMAP's `Email/query`; partial unique indexes (one running deployment per project and environment,
one active DKIM key per domain and algorithm); atomic increments with the resulting value for
quota counters.

Status: specified. Positions come from a counter per scope (section 15.1.4); `partition` on entities
and `field.serial` are in sections 15.1.4 and 14.5.1; the `search` and `positionPaging` capabilities
and partial unique indexes are in sections 14.3.3, 14.3.5 and 14.5.1, and search over personal text
through keyed token indexes in section 14.7.9.9; rows locked for writes make increments atomic and
`update` returns the resulting row (section 15.1.6). Search ships with the mail foundations
milestone, before the mail server needs it (roadmap; parked with the mail server).

#### G8. HTTP ingress beyond JSON actions

Problem. GitHub webhooks need the raw body for HMAC verification before parsing, a delivery id that
deduplicates, scope resolution from the path and a service principal. GitHub's manifest flow (and
later OpenID Connect) needs redirect responses. MTA-STS policy files are `text/plain`, autoconfig
documents are XML, JMAP downloads are byte streams with ranges.

Status: specified in section 16.5.8: receivers with deployment-level path enrichers, verification
by a principal resolver of the owning module before any principal is granted, delivery ids as
command ids, and the response kinds `raw`, `redirect`, `download` and `empty`.

#### G9. Process capabilities and singleton work

Problem. Process roles are `serve`, `work` or `all`. Some work can only run where a resource is:
the public mail ports on a host that sees real client addresses, outbound mail on a host with a
clean address. Reconcilers (edge, DNS) must run at most once per tenant at a time across
processes.

Status: named processes, capabilities, probes and placement are specified in section 21 (ADR 0025,
before the mail foundations for the mail listeners); the singleton lease remains a proposal, with
ADR 0018 before M4 (the edge and DNS reconcilers); roadmap.

Proposal for singleton work: a `singleton: true` option holds a lease with a fencing epoch per
(action, scope) in the control store, so two processes never run the same reconciler for one
tenant, and a draining process hands its leases over (section 21.2). The process registry of
section 19.1 (`core.process`) already records each process's name, roles, capabilities and the
singleton lease holders, so ADR 0018 builds on it. Named processes with a start flag, declared and
probed capabilities, and the capabilities a process advertises are section 21's. With the edge
configuration applied through the edge node's agent (decision 24a, section 17.3.7), no keelwerk
process needs the Caddy admin socket.

#### G10. Tenant-editable configuration with change events

Problem. Module configuration is stored per backend with per-tenant overrides, but nothing said who
may change it. Launchway's owners and admins edit settings in the UI, and a change must re-render
the edge or republish DNS records.

Status: specified in section 5.7: `configAccess: { level: 'tenant', edit: 'policy' }` generates
`<module>.config.get` and `<module>.config.set` under ordinary rules (secret fields sealed, section
6.6) and a typed `config.changed` event that reactions consume.

#### G11. Retention and purge

Problem. "Nothing deleted without a retention rule the operator chose" needs a mechanism. Mail
Trash and Junk, archived emails, closed previews (purged after seven days in Launchway v0.3.0),
deployment logs, delivery attempts and acknowledged node commands all need one.

Status: specified in section 14.7.1. Rules are adopted by the operator per backend with
per-tenant overrides. Launchway's modules suggest none and keep deployment records, logs, previews
and effect attempts (decision 47c, 2026-10-27); only runtime artefacts of closed previews and
superseded deployments are reclaimed (section 17.3.6). The mail modules' suggestions (30 days for
Trash, Junk and archived mail, 90 days for delivery attempts) wait with the mail server. Purges,
once a rule is adopted, remove payloads, destroy per-record and blob keys in the same unit and drop
projections such as search indexes, while the chain keeps tombstones; rules cover stream records
and blobs. Operator-adopted retention ships in M4 (roadmap).

#### G12. Cross-cutting observers and request metadata

Problem. A reaction to another module's events requires that module in `requires` or `optional`.
`audit` must see every event of every module, as Launchway v0.3.0 records every mutation, and it
needs the request's remote address and user agent.

Status: the request metadata on the receipt is specified (sections 11 and 15.1.7). Proposal for the
rest: a module declares `observes: 'all'` in its base, which allows `defineReaction(base, { on:
'all', timing: 'async', react })` (an async reaction to every event, dispatched like any other,
section 7.7) and is listed in the registry and by `keelwerk doctor`. It lands with `audit` in M2
and needs no ADR beyond ADR 0015. The experiments module (section 20.8) observes all events too,
which costs one job per event per tenant; the proposal must bound that cost, possibly with a
dispatch-time event-type filter held as data (section 26.3).

#### G13. Rules over credential scopes

Problem. A rule's subject was one module (and optionally an entity). API keys with the `read` scope
must be denied every command in every module, and app passwords must work only on the listeners
they were made for. Writing that rule in every module defeats composition.

Status: specified in section 8.1 and ADR 0005: rule subjects that match action kinds or transports
across modules, evaluated at the gate with the usual explanation.

```ts
// policies/read-only-key.ts and policies/app-password.ts of @keelwerk/module-api-keys: rules over selectors
export const readOnlyKey = defineRule(apiKeysBase, { kinds: ['command'] }, { effect: 'deny', when: (ctx) => isReadOnlyKey(ctx), reason: 'This API key has the read scope only.' })
export const appPassword = defineRule(apiKeysBase, { transports: ['imap', 'smtp-submission'] }, { effect: 'allow', when: (ctx) => keyAllowsTransport(ctx) })
```

#### G14. Extension-point cardinality and carrier coverage checks

Status: specified in sections 5.2 and 5.5. `extensionPoint.set<T>({ min: 1 })` turns an
empty slot into a named boot error (`emptyExtensionPoints: 'projects.gitProviders'`); a contract
provided by several modules is an error unless it is `set`-valued; and every carrier a listener
produces (SASL for IMAP and submission) must have at least one principal resolver that accepts it.

#### G15. Hyphenated module ids in the context types

Status: specified in sections 3.4 and 5.1. Module ids keep their hyphens in references
(`mail-store.email.get`) and appear in lower camel case in the context (`ctx.load.mailStore`,
`ctx.services.apiKeys`); ids that camel-case to the same name cannot be selected together.

## 18. Versioning and compatibility

Every contract carries an explicit version. Old API versions are served from one head
implementation by translation in the invoker, and CI refuses any change that breaks a supported
version. [ADR 0021](adr/0021-api-versioning-and-compatibility.md) records the decisions and
[research/versioning-rollouts-flags.md](research/versioning-rollouts-flags.md) the evidence.

### 18.1 What carries a version

Whatever crosses a process boundary or outlives its writer names the version it was written with.
A value without one is refused (`validation` on the wire, `internal` in storage), never guessed; a
request without a version header still resolves one, through pins that always exist.

| What | Version | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Packages and modules | semantic version (a module's `version` is its package's), bumped from surface and declaration diffs | `package.json`, changelog, build manifest, surface |
| App | dated API versions, a surface hash each | `defineApiVersions`, ledger, `Keelwerk-Version` |
| Deployment build | build id (manifest hash) and the revision assigned at start | build manifest, `core.process` |
| API surface | `format`; hash per API version | per-version artefacts, `ETag` of `/surface` |
| Action input and output | `since`, `changedIn`, schema hashes | surface |
| Entity schemas and events | track versions, shape ids | snapshots, `kw_shapes`, envelope `shape` |
| Protocols, stream tokens, cursors | integer major | path, subprotocol, `v1.` prefix, `hello.protocol` |
| Module configuration | configuration version | each stored value |
| Generated artefacts | producer version, format, API version, surface hash | file header |
| Clients and the CLI | semantic version, API version spoken | `Keelwerk-Client`, `Keelwerk-Version`, `sync.client` |
| Flags | definition: its module's version; targeting: `ruleVersion` | code, control store, the events' `flags` |
| Events, jobs, receipts | writer's build and revision; API version of input or output | `kw_events.meta`, job row, receipt |

### 18.2 Named API versions

- An app's public contract has dated API versions (`YYYY-MM-DD`, strictly increasing). Handlers
  implement only the head, the code as written; each version is served by translating requests
  forward and responses backward through the version changes it lacks, as Stripe's version change
  modules do (decision point 52 of section 26.1).
- Additive and neutral changes (section 13.8) reach every supported version; clients ignore output
  members they do not know.
- A breaking change to a module's surface is a version change beside what it changes, in a major
  of the module's package. Until an API version adopts it, it is translated for every version, so
  a module upgrade never alters a released version.
- Removed behaviour (an action, a module, a field no transform can produce) goes only when the app
  raises its floor, the app's major.

```ts
// modules/accounts/src/versions/display-name.ts: one version change per file
export const displayName = defineVersionChange({
  since: '2.0.0',                                        // the module version that made the change
  surface: [{ entity: profile, field: 'displayName', renamedFrom: 'name' }],   // also addedRequired, removed, action renames
  input: {}, output: {},                                 // custom transforms, typed by the shapes the change names
  errors: { 'accounts.display_name_invalid': 'accounts.name_invalid' },
  fixtures: [{ ref: 'accounts.profile.update', older: { id: 'prof_1', name: 'J' }, newer: { id: 'prof_1', displayName: 'J' } }],
})
// modules/accounts/src/module.generated.ts: the generated module literal lists its changes (src/versions/) beside the
// parts they refer to, which checks them; the keys, from the file names, are the change ids the ledger records and never
// change once released.
const accountsDef = defineModule(accountsBase, { entityActions: { profile: { update } }, changes: { displayName } })

// apps/portal/src/api-versions.ts
export const portalApi = defineApiVersions({
  '2026-10-23': { deprecated: { at: '2027-01-12', sunset: '2028-01-12' } },   // deprecated the day the newer version exists, retired 12 months later (decision 53)
  '2027-01-12': { changes: [healthDetails] },            // app-level changes; module changes come from the ledger
})
// apps/portal/src/app.ts
const portalDef = defineApp({ id: 'portal', modules, api: portalApi })   // modules: the tuple of src/modules.ts
```

`keelwerk surface version new <date>` appends to `generated/api-surface/<app>/ledger.json` the
module versions in force, the changes the version adopts and its surface hash, and prints the entry
for `defineApiVersions`; `generate --check` fails while the two disagree.

A request at version D runs with the changes D lacks: `locate` maps an older reference to the head
reference, `validate` checks the input against D's schema, and `translate` applies input transforms
oldest first, filters, sorts and selections included. Handlers, rules and masks see head shapes
only. After `shape`, `translate` applies output and error transforms newest first, per item for
subscriptions; stream tokens are unaffected. Tests check translated inputs against the head schema
(`internal`, `core.version_change_failed`) and run every module's fixtures.

Transports project the session's version, one projection per supported version per mount, built
at first use; surface, OpenAPI and SDL documents are committed per version
(`generated/<kind>/<app>/`). `AppClient<App>` and the tRPC router type describe the head they were
compiled with; the generated file exports it as `apiVersion`, which `createRemoteClient` and the
tRPC link helpers require and send.

### 18.3 Selecting a version

The session's version is the first of:

1. the request: header `Keelwerk-Version`, query parameter `keelwerk-version` on `GET`
   (`EventSource` sends no headers), `hello.apiVersion` on WebSocket, `--api-version` in the CLI;
2. the credential: an API key created with a version, so an integration does not move with its
   tenant;
3. the tenant's pin, set at creation to the backend's default;
4. the backend's default, set at creation to the app's head (at deployment level, the core's
   newest version).

`resolveVersion` runs in `Invoker.open` after `resolvePrincipal`; responses echo
`Keelwerk-Version`, and receipts and spans (`keelwerk.api_version`) record it. Pins are fields
of `core.backend` and `core.tenant`, changed as reversible events by `core.tenant.setApiVersion`
(tenant scope, governed by rules) and operator actions; no deploy changes a pin except the floor
rise. The typed client, the CLI and the Launchway agent also send
`Keelwerk-Client: <name>/<version>`.

### 18.4 Compatibility per transport

| Contract | Compatible | Breaking |
|---|---|---|
| Surface (every transport) | new actions, entities, optional inputs, output fields; dangerous: new output enum values, union members, declared errors | the breaking list of section 13.8 |
| REST | new paths, optional parameters, members, headers | a changed path, status or header meaning |
| CLI | new commands, optional flags | a renamed route or flag, a new required flag, another exit code |
| Protocols, module protocols included | optional members, new message types | anything else: a new major beside the old |
| Events | optional or defaulted fields, new event types | renames and type changes (upcasters, the N-1 rule); removals are contract steps |
| Module configuration | fields with defaults | removed, renamed or narrowed fields, through a configuration migration |

### 18.5 Deprecation, sunset and usage

- `deprecated: { at, sunset? }` marks a version entry (`sunset` is `at` plus 12 months unless it
  says otherwise, and never earlier), and the action option `deprecated` gains `at` and `sunset`.
  From `at`, responses carry `Deprecation: @<seconds>` (RFC 9745), `Sunset: <HTTP-date>` (RFC 8594,
  never before `at`) and a `Link` with `rel="deprecation"`; GraphQL adds
  `extensions.keelwerk.deprecations`, the CLI warns on standard error, live connections get a
  `notice` frame.
- Processes count requests per day, backend, tenant, version and transport (per action or field
  for deprecated items) into `core.apiUsage`, read by `keelwerk surface usage`.
- Support window (decision 53, 2026-10-28): a version is deprecated the day a newer one exists, its
  sunset is 12 months later, and after the sunset it is retired regardless of use; there is no
  zero-use gate and no `--force`. The floor rises when entries leave `defineApiVersions`, which CI
  accepts only after each removed version's sunset and with a major in the app's changelog (the CI
  check is unchanged). `keelwerk surface retire <version>` records the retirement and refuses only
  before the sunset. Usage counters stay as information: `keelwerk surface usage` shows who still
  calls a version, so that they can be told before the sunset. A retired version is then
  `not_found`, `core.api_version_retired` (REST 410); tenants and credentials pinned below the
  floor are re-pinned to it by an event.
- A module or core major never ends a pinned version: the app's next version adopts its changes,
  and new protocol majors run beside the old.

### 18.6 `keelwerk surface diff`

`keelwerk surface diff --base <git ref>` takes over step 9 of section 13.8 (`introspect diff`
becomes its alias). For every API version on both sides it derives the surface twice and fails on a
breaking difference; removed versions pass only under the floor rule; dangerous changes need a
changelog acknowledgement; ledger entries on the base must stay unchanged. Each changed module
package's own surface (the module composed alone) and declaration files must fit its version
bump: breaking needs a major with a version change per surface break, additive a minor, neutral a
patch, as section 5.1 requires.

### 18.7 Protocol versions and negotiation

Each protocol carries an integer major in its own place (path, subprotocol, prefix, `format`,
`hello.protocol`). Within a major only optional members and message types are added and readers
ignore what they do not know; a new major runs beside the old until counters show 30 days without
use. `core.capabilities` (public query, `GET /_keelwerk/v1/capabilities`) lists, like a JMAP
session object, the majors served and the API versions with status and dates; clients declare
what they use, as JMAP's `using` does, and the server picks the highest common major or answers
`not_found`, `core.protocol_retired`. The Launchway agent has no protocol of its own since decision
23c: it speaks the live carrier's protocol as a typed client pinned to an API version, so its majors
start at the new protocol, `keelwerk.live.v1`, and Launchway v0.3.0's agent protocol v1 is not
served at all (section 19.7).

### 18.8 Pipeline stages and errors

The pipeline of section 9.2 runs `resolveVersion` in `open` after `resolvePrincipal`, and
`translate` after `validate` and after `shape`; `admit` also checks kill switches and suspensions,
`authorize` flag gates, `execute` records writer and flags per event, and `complete` flushes
counters and exposures.
Every failure fits an existing kind of section 10:

| Code | Kind | REST | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core.api_version_invalid` | `validation` | 400 | not `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `core.api_version_unknown` | `validation` | 400 | not a version of the app |
| `core.api_version_retired` | `not_found` | 410 | below the floor |
| `core.protocol_retired` | `not_found` | 410; WebSocket 4404 | a major no longer served |
| `core.rollout_in_progress` | `unavailable` | 503, `Retry-After` | an older process meets a version, action or protocol it does not know while a target exists |
| `core.version_change_failed` | `internal` | 500 | a transform failed |
| `core.feature_disabled` | `forbidden` | 403 | a gate's flag is false for the caller |
| `core.feature_suspended` | `unavailable` | 503 | a kill switch is false or a suspension matches |
| `core.rollout_not_finalized` | `conflict` | 409 | the registry refuses a contract step or finalization |

### 18.9 Backends and tenants

A version's surface depends only on the app and the version; version changes are the same for every
backend and tenant. Pins are per backend, tenant and credential, so one build serves tenants on
different versions, and a tenant principal changes only its own tenant's pin.

## 19. Rollouts

A new build never interrupts running clients or processes: two builds of adjacent revisions run
side by side under an N-1 rule, and incompatible formats and destructive steps wait for a
finalization that the process registry gates, as CockroachDB's upgrades do
([ADR 0022](adr/0022-rolling-upgrades-expand-and-contract.md)).

### 19.1 Builds, revisions and the process registry

`keelwerk build` writes the build manifest: package versions and the compatibility content
(migration files per track, event shapes, configuration versions, job formats, protocol majors,
version change ids, and each app's API versions with their surfaces). `core.rollout` records the
finalized revision and its content. At `connect` a starting process compares: equal content joins
the finalized revision; content that only adds runs at the target revision (finalized plus one), as
the new target or one more process of it; content lacking anything the finalized build has, retired
versions and majors apart, refuses to start (`buildTooOld`), as does content that differs from a
current target's (`targetConflict`). One rollout runs at a time.

```ts
export interface ProcessRecord {                         // core.process, in the control store
  readonly id: string                                    // UUIDv7, new per start
  readonly name: string | null                           // the named process (section 21.1)
  readonly node: string
  readonly roles: readonly ('serve' | 'work')[]
  readonly capabilities: readonly string[]
  readonly build: { readonly id: string; readonly revision: number }
  readonly protocols: Readonly<Record<string, readonly number[]>>     // 'invocation', 'live', 'sync', module protocols
  readonly apiVersions: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>   // per app
  readonly state: 'starting' | 'ready' | 'draining' | 'stopped'
  readonly heartbeatAt: Temporal.Instant                             // every 10 s; presumed gone after 30 s of silence
  // section 21.1 adds provider, instance, slots per queue, reserved connections, drain and interruption
}
export interface RolloutState {                          // core.rollout, chain-backed: its events are the history
  readonly finalizedRevision: number
  readonly finalizedContent: string                      // hash of the finalized compatibility content
  readonly target: { readonly revision: number; readonly buildId: string; readonly startedAt: Temporal.Instant } | null
}
// defineDeployment({ rollout: { finalize: 'auto' | 'manual', graceSeconds: 600 } }); 'auto' is the default
```

A process registers at `connect`, is `ready` at `listen` and `draining` at `stop`; the registry has
a change feed like the scope directory (section 3.2) and records singleton lease holders (gap G9).
A process that finds itself below the finalized revision, after a partition for example, stops.

### 19.2 The N-1 rule

| Shared thing | Rule while the finalized build and a target run |
|---|---|
| Namespaces, the control store included | expand steps only, none adding a constraint the older build's writes violate (a new required column gets a database default until a contract step) |
| Events | the target writes the finalized track versions: new optional fields, renamed fields under the old name, type changes through a `downcast` beside the migration's `upcast`; older live sources skip unknown event types |
| Consumers | leases move to target processes, so reactions the target adds see every event; rebuilds wait for finalization |
| Jobs | a job records its enqueuer's build and revision and, from an external caller, the input as sent with its API version; workers take jobs at or below their revision, run external input through the pipeline at that version and translate internal input with the version changes the enqueuer's manifest lacks |
| Receipts | the outcome's API version is recorded and fingerprinted; a replay returns the stored outcome, re-reading entity outcomes at that version |
| Requests | an older process meeting a version, action or protocol it does not know answers `unavailable`, `core.rollout_in_progress`, `Retry-After: 2`; clients retry, commands under the same command id |
| Configuration | the target reads older stored values through their migration and writes the older version until finalization |

### 19.3 Migrations in two phases

`keelwerk db plan` shows per namespace and track the expand steps (`db apply`, before the target
takes traffic), the data steps (idempotent, batched backfills) and the contract steps
(`db apply --contract`), each with the revision that introduced it. `--contract` and rewrites of
stored configuration refuse with `conflict`, `core.rollout_not_finalized`, unless the finalized
revision covers them and no live process is below it. For one process or many:

- a field rename is a new column under the new derived name, which the target writes beside the
  old one (the migration file's `renames` entry) while reading the old one, a backfill
  (`copyColumn`) after finalization, reads moving to the new column per namespace once its backfill
  is recorded, and a contract step dropping the old column (decision 55b, 2026-10-28): physical
  names always equal the derived names, and the snapshot aliases no column;
- a type change or a split column is a new column that the target writes beside the old one
  (through `downcast`) while reading the old one, a backfill through `upcast` after finalization,
  reads moving to the new column per namespace once its backfill is recorded, and a contract step
  dropping the old column. Both replace the multi-process procedure that section 14.6.4 had
  scheduled for the data-breadth milestone.

### 19.4 Finalization and rollback

`keelwerk rollout status` lists processes, revisions and pending contract steps.
`keelwerk rollout finalize` raises the finalized revision when every live process runs at the
target revision, and with `finalize: 'auto'` a singleton finalizer does so once that has held for
the grace period (decision point 54 of section 26.1). Finalization switches writers to the new formats and starts backfills; contract
steps stay explicit because they destroy data. Before finalization, rollback is a redeploy of the
finalized build, which reads everything the target wrote, then `keelwerk rollout abort`: once
none of the target's processes is live, it clears the target, moves the target's jobs the
finalized build can run to its revision and parks the rest as dead letters. After finalization,
going back means a restore (section 14.7.6).

### 19.5 Clients during a rollout

Draining processes end streams with `going_away` (section 15.4.5); clients resume from their token
on any process at the same API version. The WebSocket `welcome` frame and a new SSE `welcome` event
carry `apiVersion`, `surfaceHash` and the protocol major, and a client whose cached hash differs
refetches its surface. When the floor passes a connection's version, the stream ends with reason
`version_retired` and a user interface reloads onto a supported build: the forced refresh.

### 19.6 Deployment strategies

Rolling replacement is the default; blue-green moves traffic at the edge in one step, switchable
back until finalization, and a canary build uses weighted edge routes. On the home server (section
17.5.2): start the new container, wait for `/_keelwerk/ready`, move the Caddy upstream, drain the
old one. Two containers cannot publish one host port, so the mail listeners (ports 25, 465, 587,
993) get their own container, a named process of gap G9, replaced by stop and start within seconds;
SMTP senders retry and IMAP clients reconnect (question 56, parked with the mail server).

Deploying and releasing are separate: new behaviour ships behind a tenant-level release flag, moves
from canary tenants to a percentage and to everyone
(`keelwerk flags set checkout.newFlow --backend launchway --tenants home --percent 10`), and
leaves the code when the stale report asks.

### 19.7 Sync and agent protocols

`sync.register` records the client's API version and sync major; push and pull run at the
session's version; a cursor of an older format gets `reset: 'shapes'`. The Launchway agent has no
protocol of its own (decision 23c, 2026-10-26): it is a typed client pinned to an API version over
the live carrier, so its compatibility is the app's dated API version and the carrier's major
(`keelwerk.live.v1`, section 18.7), and `nodes.node.connect` records its `agentVersion` and
`apiVersion`. Launchway v0.3.0's agent protocol v1 is not served: the cutover redeploys every agent
together with the new UI, and the old installation stays as the rollback until the new one is
verified (roadmap M4).

### 19.8 Backends and tenants

The registry, revisions and finalization are deployment-wide, because one build serves every
backend. Expand and contract run per namespace, so tenants with their own namespaces migrate one by
one (section 14.6.6).

## 20. Feature flags and experiments

### 20.1 Where they live

Flag definitions and evaluation are a small kernel concept in `@keelwerk/core`; experiments are
a module, `@keelwerk/module-experiments` (id `experiments`;
[ADR 0023](adr/0023-feature-flags-and-experiments.md)). Flags must be readable wherever behaviour
is decided (handlers, rules, `admit`, transports through the rules over transports of gap G13,
reactions, jobs, the kernel's own rollouts), and only the core is a dependency of all of them;
`ctx.flags` is typed from the module base like `ctx.config`. Experiments own data and actions, are
optional and observe events: by section 24, a module (decision point 51 of section 26.1).

### 20.2 Defining flags

```ts
// modules/checkout/src/flags/new-flow.ts, layout.ts and exports-enabled.ts: one flag per file
export const newFlow = defineFlag({          // listed by the base of its owning module
  kind: 'boolean',                           // 'boolean' | 'string' | 'number' | 'json' | 'variant'
  default: false,                            // keeps established behaviour; served when nothing else decides
  level: 'tenant',                           // whose key splits: 'deployment' | 'backend' | 'tenant' | 'principal'
  purpose: 'release',                        // 'release' | 'experiment' | 'operational' | 'kill-switch' | 'permission'
  expires: '2027-01-31',                     // required for release and experiment flags
  client: true,                              // readable by clients through core.flag.evaluate
})
export const layout = defineFlag({ kind: 'variant', variants: ['control', 'compact'], default: 'control', level: 'principal', purpose: 'experiment', expires: '2027-03-01' })
export const exportsEnabled = defineFlag({ kind: 'boolean', default: true, level: 'tenant', purpose: 'kill-switch' })

// modules/checkout/src/base.ts
const checkoutBaseDef = defineModuleBase({ id: 'checkout', version: '1.3.0', requires: [orders], flags: { newFlow, layout, exportsEnabled } })   // keys 'checkout.newFlow', ...
// modules/checkout/src/actions/place-order.ts and export-all.ts
export const placeOrder = defineCommand(checkoutBase, { gate: 'newFlow' /* ... */ })         // false: forbidden, core.feature_disabled
export const exportAll = defineCommand(checkoutBase, { gate: 'exportsEnabled' /* ... */ })   // false: unavailable, core.feature_suspended
```

`json` flags take a `schema` (a `shape`) and `number` flags optional bounds; `tenantEditable: true`
lets tenants override a flag that drives no experiment, through generated actions as for
configuration (section 5.7); `defineApp({ flags })` declares app-level flags. Flags belong to the
base, so every part is typed against them.

### 20.3 Evaluation

```ts
// DecideContext<M, W> (sections 7.6 and 7.9.7) has `flags: FlagRequestsOf<M, W>`: yield* ctx.flags.checkout.newFlow
// answers a boolean, yield* ctx.flags.checkout.layout 'control' | 'compact', yield* ctx.flagDetails(key) a FlagResolution.
export interface FlagContext {
  readonly scope: Scope
  readonly principal: { readonly kind: PrincipalKind; readonly id: string | null; readonly roles: readonly string[] }
  readonly attributes: Readonly<Record<string, string | number | boolean>>   // from flagContextEnrichers
  readonly targetingKey: string | null                                      // by level: backend, tenant or principal id
}
export interface FlagResolution<T> {
  readonly value: T
  readonly variant: string
  readonly reason: 'STATIC' | 'DEFAULT' | 'TARGETING_MATCH' | 'SPLIT' | 'DISABLED' | 'CACHED' | 'STALE' | 'ERROR'
  readonly errorCode?: 'FLAG_NOT_FOUND' | 'TYPE_MISMATCH' | 'TARGETING_KEY_MISSING' | 'PARSE_ERROR' | 'GENERAL'
  readonly ruleId?: string
  readonly ruleVersion?: number
  readonly provider: string
}
export interface FlagProvider {             // deployment-level ordered extension point `flagProviders`
  readonly id: string
  readonly sync: boolean                    // true: resolve never returns a promise
  start(signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void>
  /** undefined passes the decision to the next provider. */
  resolve<T>(flag: FlagSpec<T>, context: FlagContext): FlagResolution<T> | undefined | Promise<FlagResolution<T> | undefined>
  readonly changes?: AsyncIterable<{ readonly keys: readonly string[] }>
}
```

- Providers in order: `core.targeting` (the control store's targeting, always present);
  optionally `openFeatureFlags(provider)`, an infrastructure entry adapting an OpenFeature server
  provider (`@openfeature/server-sdk` 1.23.0, checked 2026-10-24); `env`
  (`KEELWERK_FLAG_CHECKOUT_NEW_FLOW=true`, development and tests only). The first resolution
  wins, else the default with `DEFAULT`.
- Handlers read flags as requests, answered from the invocation's snapshot and recorded in the
  envelope's `flags` (section 7.9.3); rules read the same snapshot as values (section 20.6).
  Building the snapshot is a kernel concern before `authorize`: synchronous providers resolve a flag
  on first use, and with an asynchronous one the kernel resolves every flag the invoked module can
  read before `authorize`. One invocation sees one snapshot; `core.targeting` keeps all targeting in
  memory, refreshed from the control store's change feed within about a second.
- An error never fails an invocation: the default is served with `ERROR` and counted, so the
  default must keep established behaviour.
- An anonymous principal has a targeting key only when the client sends `Keelwerk-Client-Id`;
  otherwise principal-level flags give the default with `TARGETING_KEY_MISSING`.
- `flagContextEnrichers` (app level, mode `set`) add attributes once per session. Clients read
  `client: true` flags with `core.flag.evaluate` (query, tenant scope).

### 20.4 Targeting, assignment and history

- A flag's targeting (`core.flag`, chain-backed, in the control store) exists per backend, plus an
  optional deployment-wide one for backends without their own: `enabled` (off serves the default
  with `DISABLED`), ordered rules that match listed tenants or principals and a condition over
  attributes (the condition AST of section 8.3, interpreted in memory) and serve a variant or a
  split, and a fallthrough; values are validated on write.
- Splits hash `SHA-256(salt ‖ ':' ‖ targetingKey)`; the first four bytes over 2^32 give a number
  in [0, 1), and variants own cumulative ranges in declared order, so raising a rollout's
  percentage never removes a key. The salt is the flag key, or `exp:<id>:<phase>` for an
  experiment, whose weights are frozen while it runs.
- Every change is an event with an actor and a required reason; the stream version is the
  `ruleVersion`, and `core.flag.restoreRules` goes back.

### 20.5 Exposure and provenance

Every event a command appends records, in the `meta` column of `kw_events` (section 15.1.2), its
writer's build and revision and the key, variant, reason and rule version of each flag the
invocation read; the envelope exposes them as `writer` and `flags`. Spans carry `keelwerk.flags`;
`keelwerk.flags.evaluations` counts by flag, variant and reason. The experiments module fills the
app-level extension point `flagObservers` (mode `set`, bound to its contributor, gap G16) with a
pure observer that returns the drafts of each targeting key's first exposure per phase of a running
experiment; the kernel writes them in the command's unit for commands, otherwise through a
per-process buffer flushed every second, so a crash loses at most a second of exposures, alike for
every variant.

### 20.6 What flags may gate

- Actions: `gate` names a boolean flag of the module, and the action runs only while it is true.
  It compiles to a deny rule `<action ref>.gate` at `authorize` (`forbidden`,
  `core.feature_disabled`), explained by `keelwerk explain` and visible through `core.me`; on a
  `kill-switch` flag it runs at `admit` instead (`unavailable`, `core.feature_suspended`). Gated
  actions stay in the surface.
- Policies: `where`, `check` and `when` read `ctx.flags`; the plan records the flags its rules
  read, and the token check of section 15.2.6 includes their values, so a flip that changes
  visibility resets tokens.
- Modules: a base with `flags: { enabled }` and `gate: 'enabled'` gates every action the module
  mounts, contributed ones included; reactions and schedules keep running. Configuration keeps
  durable settings (decision point 1, decided 2026-10-25: the compiled catalogue, section 26), flags
  temporary or targeted variation with an owner and an expiry; runtime module selection stays
  rejected.
- Transports: a rule over a transport subject (gap G13) whose `when` reads a flag.

### 20.7 Kill switches and stale flags

The operator suspends any action with a `core.suspension` row (action reference; deployment,
backend or tenant; reason), checked at `admit` beside quotas. `keelwerk flags stale` and
`keelwerk doctor` report flags past their expiry, serving one value to everyone for 14 days,
unevaluated for 30 days or with targeting no build defines. `doctor` warns when a release or
experiment flag's `expires` lies more than 40 days after its first build (Unleash's default
lifetime); an operational flag without `expires` is stale 7 days after its first build; kill
switches and permission flags never go stale by age.

### 20.8 The experiments module

- `experiment` (backend tenancy, chain-backed): key, driven flag, hypothesis, level (tenant or
  principal), variants and weights, allocation, status, phase, primary and guardrail metrics,
  planned sample size per variant. `metric` (backend tenancy): an event selector
  (`{ event: 'checkout.order.placed', value?: 'total' }`), kind `binomial` or `mean`, a window
  after first exposure (default 7 days). `exposure` (tenant tenancy, `history: 'state'`, unique per
  experiment, phase and targeting key, which is `.personal()`); `tally` (tenant tenancy:
  participants, conversions, sum and sum of squares per experiment, phase, variant and metric);
  `result` (backend tenancy: tallies summed over tenants).
- Starting writes the split into the flag's targeting; new weights need a new phase and salt. An
  asynchronous reaction over the selected events (`observes: 'all'`, gap G12) updates a tally when
  the event's actor (principal level) or tenant (tenant level) was exposed within the window; an
  hourly `each-tenant` schedule sends each tenant's counts to backend scope.
- `experiments.experiment.results` reports per variant and metric the participants, the rate or
  mean and, against control, the difference with a 95 % interval and a two-sided p-value: a
  two-proportion z-test for binomial metrics, Welch's t-test with a normal approximation for means.
  Before the planned sample size the result reads "inconclusive: planned size not reached",
  because repeated looks inflate false positives; a sample ratio mismatch (chi-squared against the
  weights, p < 0.001) marks it invalid; variants under 100 participants are marked too small; the
  primary metric decides, and guardrails get no multiple-comparison correction. Bayesian analysis,
  CUPED and sequential tests come later (decision point 57 of section 26.1).

### 20.9 Commands

New framework commands: `keelwerk surface diff|version new|usage|retire` (project; `usage` and
`retire` on the operator socket), `keelwerk rollout status|finalize|abort` (operator socket) and
`keelwerk flags list|get|set|history|explain|stale` (aliases of `core.flag` actions for
operators). `surface`, `rollout` and `flags` are framework commands that reserve no module id
(section 16.9.3); the module's actions run as `keelwerk call experiments...`.

### 20.10 Backends and tenants

Targeting addresses the tenants and principals of one backend and is written only by operator and
core-generated actions; a tenant principal changes only its own tenant's overrides. Evaluation runs
inside the session's scope, so no rule serves one tenant's value to another; exposures and tallies
stay in the tenant's namespace, and only counts reach backend scope.

## 21. Nodes, capacity and autoscaling

Jens's requirement of 2026-10-23: "This job queue should be thought out REALLY WELL: I plan to work
with an arbitrary number of nodes in the future, and they should all scale automatically, with
limits." [ADR 0025](adr/0025-nodes-capacity-and-autoscaling.md) records the decisions, ADR 0018 the
singleton leases (gap G9).

### 21.1 Nodes, processes and named processes

- A **node** is a host that runs keelwerk processes (a machine, a virtual machine, a Docker
  engine); a **process** is one `keelwerk start`; a **named process** is an entry of
  `defineDeployment({ processes })` with roles, declared capabilities, slots per queue, placements,
  a provider and scaling limits, whose replicas the scaler counts. Without `--process` a process
  belongs to the built-in, static `default`.
- `core.process` (section 19.1) gains the fields below and `core.node` is new; lifecycle changes
  write change records (`keelwerk fleet watch`), heartbeats and slot counts go to lease rows.

```ts
// keelwerk.config.ts: workers started on demand, a relay host with a clean address
processes: {
  home: { roles: ['serve', 'work'], slots: { '*': 4 } },
  mail: { roles: ['serve'], capabilities: ['smtp-public'] },
  worker: { roles: ['work'], slots: { reactions: 8, '*': 2 }, provider: 'docker', scale: { min: 0, max: 4 } },
  relay: { roles: ['work'], capabilities: ['smtp-out'], slots: { 'mail-delivery': 8 } },   // static, run by the operator
},
scaling: { maxProcesses: 8 },

export interface ProcessRecord {                      // core.process: the fields of section 19.1, and
  readonly provider: string                           // 'static', 'docker', ...
  readonly instance: string | null                    // the provider's handle
  readonly slots: Readonly<Record<string, { readonly total: number; readonly busy: number }>>   // per queue
  readonly connections: Readonly<Record<string, number>>                                       // pool reserved per placement
  readonly drain: { readonly deadline: Temporal.Instant; readonly reason: string } | null
  readonly interruption: Temporal.Instant | null                  // a provider's termination notice
}
export interface NodeRecord {                         // core.node, deployment scope
  readonly id: string                                 // --node, KEELWERK_NODE, the provider's, else the machine id
  readonly provider: string
  readonly labels: Readonly<Record<string, string>>   // region, zone, arch
  readonly capabilities: readonly string[]            // probed on the host
  readonly maxProcesses: number
  readonly state: 'active' | 'cordoned' | 'draining' | 'gone'   // gone: no heartbeat for 5 minutes
  readonly seenAt: Temporal.Instant
}
```

### 21.2 Capabilities and placement

- A process advertises a capability its named process declares (or `--capability` names) once its
  probe, if any, passes. Probes fill the deployment-level `capabilityProbes` extension point; the
  core ships `docker`, `smtp-out` (port 25 of an operator-chosen host is reachable), `gpu`, `arch`
  and `region`. They run at `connect`, every five minutes and on `keelwerk fleet probe`; a failing
  probe withdraws the capability, and running jobs finish.
- Only listeners and effect executors require capabilities (`smtp-public` for the port 25 listener,
  `smtp-out` for direct delivery). Every other job runs a pure handler (decision 50a) on any work
  process slotting its queue. A synchronous caller never waits for an effect job: the invoker never
  forwards a request. The only outside calls inside a request are the inline effects of `prepare`,
  whose executors need no capability and run in the invoking process (section 7.9.4).
- Unplaceable work fails closed: a static capability that no named process declares is refused at
  boot (`unplaceableCapability`), a computed one at enqueue (`unsupported`,
  `core.capability_unplaceable`). Declared but not live: jobs wait in their lane while the scaler
  starts a process that declares it, if a provider can; otherwise `keelwerk doctor` names it and
  `giveUpAfter` applies.
- Singleton work (reconcilers, the finalizer of section 19.4, the scaler) holds leases with a
  fencing epoch in the control store (ADR 0018); a draining process hands them over.

### 21.3 Capacity and the connection budget

- Each placement has a connection budget, `placements.<name>.maxConnections` (default 80 percent of
  the server's `max_connections`); a starting process reserves its pool per placement when it
  registers, and over budget the start is refused (`connectionBudget`). The default pool is the
  action queues' slots, plus three (notifier, listener, effect completions), plus the serve role's
  pool: under decision 50a no job holds a connection while it waits on the network. A named process
  connects only to the placements it lists (default all).
- Workers added to a saturated database slow the queue, so the scaler adds none while a placement's
  take latency (p95) exceeds 250 milliseconds or its budget is spent.

### 21.4 The scaler

The scaler runs under a singleton lease every 15 seconds, in a work process of a named process whose
`min` is at least 1. Its plan is a pure function of its inputs (decision 50a); the kernel gathers
the inputs and executes the plan's provider calls as recorded effects; tests drive it with the fake
provider and clock of `@keelwerk/testing`.

```ts
export interface WorkClassStats {                     // JobQueue.stats per queue and capability set, over every namespace
  readonly queue: string
  readonly capabilities: readonly string[]
  readonly due: number                                // available and due now
  readonly oldestDueSeconds: number
  readonly arrivalsPerSecond: number                  // smoothed over a minute
  readonly meanRunSeconds: number
  readonly running: number
  readonly nextDueAt: Temporal.Instant | null
  readonly sloSeconds: number                         // queues.<q>.slo (an ISO 8601 duration, default 'PT30S') in seconds: target wait from due to start
}
export interface ScaleLimits {                        // processes.<name>.scale
  readonly min: number                                // 0 allows scale-to-zero, except for the scaler's own process
  readonly max: number
  readonly maxPerNode?: number
  readonly up?: { readonly percent: number; readonly processes: number }   // per evaluation; default 100 percent or 4
  readonly down?: { readonly processes: number; readonly window: string }  // default 1, after a '5m' window
  readonly tolerance?: number                         // default 0.1
  readonly activationLead?: string                    // default '60s'
}
export declare function plan(inputs: ScalerInputs, scaling: DeploymentScaling, at: Temporal.Instant): ScalePlan   // scaling: maxProcesses, maxCostPerHour, per provider
// ScalerInputs: class stats, named processes, provider offers, placements, recent decisions
```

1. Slots needed per work class: `ceil(meanRunSeconds × (arrivalsPerSecond + due / sloSeconds))`
   (Little's law plus the backlog drained within one target wait), times the oldest age over the
   target, at most 2, while the target is missed; never fewer than the class's running jobs, because
   a plan from backlog alone scales in on top of busy workers (KEDA issues 7368 and 8249); at least
   one when work is due within `activationLead`.
2. Static processes' slots are subtracted; the rest goes to the named processes that advertise the
   class's capabilities and slot its queue, cheapest provider first, then in declaration order.
3. Limits clamp the result, the binding one recorded as `limitedBy`: `min`, `max`, `maxPerNode`
   times the provider's nodes, provider maximums, `maxProcesses`, `maxCostPerHour`, each placement's
   connection budget, the database guard.
4. Stabilisation, after Kubernetes' defaults (checked on 2026-10-25): up at once by at most 100
   percent or 4 processes, whichever is more; changes within 10 percent ignored; down to the highest
   value wanted in the last 5 minutes, but one process per evaluation (Kubernetes allows 100
   percent), because every stop is a drain. Starting processes count as present and idle, so a
   backlog is answered once.
5. Starts are spread (0 to 2 seconds of random delay); stops are drains. Each acting evaluation
   writes a `core.scaleDecision` row (inputs, plan, bound, actions, outcomes), kept for 30 days.

With `min: 0` a named process reaches zero after a down window without work and starts again for
work due within the activation lead. With the static provider the plan is a recommendation in
`keelwerk fleet scale status`; the scaler with the static provider ships with Launchway's rebuild
in M4 and the opt-in docker provider one milestone later, in M5 (decision 63a), while a Kubernetes
provider stays a named later milestone of the roadmap.

### 21.5 Node providers

`nodeProviders` is a deployment-level extension point (set), filled by infrastructure entries that
are imperative like adapters and called only by the kernel.

```ts
export interface NodeProvider {
  readonly id: string                                 // 'static', 'docker'
  offer(): Promise<ProviderOffer>                     // what it can start, its maximums, cost per process hour, startup time
```
